221:
“They abide constantly in their own respective views” means: There are some ascetics and brahmins who hold views. Among the sixty-two types of views, they accept one or another view, particularly grasping it, firmly holding it, touching it, and adhering to it; they live, dwell together, reside, and abide solely within their own views. Just as householders live in houses, or as those with offenses live in their offenses, or as those with defilements live in their defilements, even so, some ascetics and brahmins who hold views accept one or another of the sixty-two views, particularly grasping it, firmly holding it, touching it, and adhering to it; they live, dwell together, reside, and abide solely within their own views. This is the meaning of “They abide constantly in their own respective views.”

“Disputing, they each say they are experts” means: Having accepted, particularly grasped, firmly held, touched, and adhered to (their own views), they speak differently, speak in various ways, speak against one another, and speak much. They do not speak of a single view, but they speak, recite, show, and express (diverse views). “Experts” means: those who, based on their own doctrine, call themselves experts, call themselves wise ones, call themselves firm ones, call themselves logical ones, call themselves reasoners, call themselves those who possess the characteristics, call themselves those who have the grounds, and call themselves those who have the opportunity. This is the meaning of “Disputing, they each say they are experts.”

“He who knows thus, he knows the Dhamma” means: Whoever knows this Dhamma, this view, this practice, this path. That person has known, has understood, has seen, and has penetrated the Dhamma. This is the meaning of “He who knows thus, he knows the Dhamma.”

“He who rejects this is incomplete” means: Whoever rejects this Dhamma, this view, this practice, this path. That person is incomplete, unfinished, unfulfilled, inferior, very inferior, low, base, insignificant, and meager. This is the meaning of “He who rejects this is incomplete.”

Therefore, the created one said:
“Abiding constantly in their own respective views, disputing, they each say they are experts. ‘He who knows thus, he knows the Dhamma; he who rejects this is incomplete,’ they say.”

In this way, they dispute and argue, and they also say, “The other is a fool and unskilled.” Which of their doctrines is true? For all of them say they are experts.
222:
“In this way, they dispute and argue” means: Having thus accepted, learned, grasped, touched, and adhered (to their views), they argue, create quarrels, create strife, create disputes, and create contention—saying, “You do not understand this Dhamma and Vinaya... [etc.]... explain it if you can.” In this way, they dispute and argue.

“They also say, ‘The other is a fool and unskilled’” means: They say the other is a fool, inferior, very inferior, lacking in effort, lacking in reason, lacking in refuge, lacking in power, unskilled, ignorant, fallen into ignorance, unknowing, unable to distinguish, and of little wisdom. Thus they say, thus they speak, thus they recite, thus they show, and thus they express: “The other is a fool and unskilled.”

“Which of their doctrines is true?” means: Among the doctrines of these ascetics and brahmins, which doctrine is true, real, actual, factual, authentic, and unerring? This is the meaning of “Which of their doctrines is true?”

“For all of them say they are experts” means: All these ascetics and brahmins hold the view that they are skilled in their own doctrine, that they are wise, that they are firm, that they are proper, that they have reasons, that they have signs, that they have causes, and that they have a basis. This is the meaning of “For all of them say they are experts.”

Therefore, that created Buddha said:
“In this way, they dispute and argue, and they also say, ‘The other is a fool and unskilled.’ Which of their doctrines is true? For all of them say they are experts.”

If one who does not approve of another’s practice is a great fool and of very inferior wisdom, then all of them are fools and of very inferior wisdom, for all of them abide particularly in their own views.

“One who does not approve of another’s practice” means: One who does not know, does not see, does not attend to, does not reflect upon, and does not rejoice in another’s Dhamma, view, practice, or conduct. This is the meaning of “One who does not approve of another’s practice.”
223:
"Bālomako hoti nihīnapañño" means: Another is a fool, low, very low, inferior, insignificant, wretched, or of little account. One is of low wisdom, very low wisdom, inferior wisdom, insignificant wisdom, wretched wisdom, or of little wisdom. Therefore, it is said, "Bālomako hoti nihīnapañño."

"Sabbeva bālā sunihīnapaññā" means: All these ascetics and brahmins are fools, low, very low, inferior, insignificant, wretched, or of little account. All of them are of low wisdom, very low wisdom, inferior wisdom, insignificant wisdom, wretched wisdom, or of little wisdom. Therefore, it is said, "Sabbeva bālā sunihīnapaññā."

"Sabbevime diṭṭhiparibbasānā" means: All these ascetics and brahmins are those who dwell in views. Among the sixty-two views, they take up, grasp firmly, seize, misapprehend, and adhere to one or another view, and they live, cohabit, reside, and dwell within their own respective views. Just as householders live in houses, or as those with offenses live in offenses, or as those with defilements live in defilements; in the same way, all these ascetics and brahmins are those who dwell in views... and dwell within them. Therefore, it is said, "Sabbevime diṭṭhiparibbasānā."

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
"If one does not acknowledge another's Dhamma (view), one is a fool and of inferior wisdom.
All these are fools of very inferior wisdom, all these are established in their views."

"If they are not purified by their own view, (yet they claim to be) those of pure wisdom, skillful and sagacious.
None among them is of deficient wisdom, for their views are likewise perfected (in their own eyes)."

"Sandiṭṭhiyā ceva navīvadātā" means: They are not purified, not cleansed, not fully whitened by their own view, their own preference, their own liking, or their own doctrine; they are defiled and possess defiling qualities. Therefore, it is said, "Sandiṭṭhiyā ceva navīvadātā."

"Saṃsuddhapaññā kusalā mutīmā" means: One with pure wisdom, very pure wisdom, extremely pure wisdom, bright wisdom, or fully cleansed wisdom. Alternatively, one with pure vision, very pure vision...
224:
...extremely pure vision, bright vision, or fully cleansed vision—this is "pure wisdom." "Kusalā" means those who are skillful, wise, endowed with wisdom, powerful, knowledgeable, discerning, and sagacious. Thus, one with pure wisdom is "skillful." "Mutīmā" means those who are sagacious, wise, endowed with wisdom, powerful, knowledgeable, discerning, and sagacious. Thus, one with pure wisdom is "skillful and sagacious."

"None among them is of deficient wisdom" means: Among those ascetics and brahmins, there is no one who is of low wisdom, very low wisdom, inferior wisdom, insignificant wisdom, wretched wisdom, or of little wisdom. All of them possess only excellent wisdom, distinguished wisdom, foremost wisdom, supreme wisdom, or pre-eminent wisdom. Therefore, it is said, "None among them is of deficient wisdom."

"For their views are likewise perfected" means: The views of those ascetics and brahmins are perfected just like those of the wise; they are well-undertaken, grasped, misapprehended, attended to, firmly adhered to, and resolved upon. Therefore, it is said, "For their views are likewise perfected."

For that reason, the Blessed One said:
"Not being purified by their own view, they (claim to be) those of pure wisdom, skillful and sagacious.
None among them is of deficient wisdom, for their views are likewise perfected (so they say)."

"I do not say this is true, which fools say to one another; they have made their own views the truth, therefore they regard others as fools."

In the phrase "I do not say this is true," "Na" is a negation. "Etam" refers to the sixty-two views. I do not say, declare, teach, describe, establish, reveal, analyze, clarify, or manifest that this view is true, not vain, evident, factual, or unerring. Therefore, it is said, "I do not say this is true."

In the phrase "which fools say to one another," "Mithu" refers to two people who engage in disputes, quarrels, strife, many words, various arguments, legal questions, retorts, and talk. They say to one another, speak, utter, show, and call each other a fool, a low person, one of inferior application, one of inferior energy, one of inferior cause, one of inferior disposition, or one of inferior mindfulness.
225:
Fools say this to one another; they speak thus, they declare thus, they recite thus, they manifest thus, they designate thus. They establish their own respective views as the truth.

"The world is eternal; only this is the truth, anything else is futile"—thus they establish their own view as the truth. "The world is not eternal; only this is the truth, anything else is futile" ... "A Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death; only this is the truth, anything else is futile"—thus they establish their own view as the truth.

Therefore, for that reason, because of that cause, on account of that condition, on that basis, they regard others as "fools, low, inferior, insignificant, wretched, of little worth, and trifling." They see, behold, look at, contemplate, and examine them as such.

Therefore, the Blessed One said this:
"I do not say that what the fools say to one another is true. They establish their own respective views as the truth; therefore, they regard others as fools."

Some say that what they hold is the truth, the reality; others say that very same thing is empty and false. Thus, taking different views, they argue. Why do ascetics not speak one [and the same] thing?

Some ascetics and brahmins say of a certain teaching, view, practice, or path: "This is the truth, real, factual, actual, authentic, and unerring." Thus they say, speak, recite, manifest, and designate.

Other ascetics and brahmins say of that very same teaching, view, practice, or path: "This teaching is empty, this teaching is false, this teaching is unreal, this teaching is a lie, this teaching is not authentic." Thus they say, speak, recite, manifest, and designate.
226:
“Thus disputing and speaking differently” means: having taken up, grasped, seized, misapprehended, and adhered [to a view], they speak differently. They engage in quarrels, they engage in strife, they engage in disputes, they speak differently, they engage in verbal contention. “You do not understand this Dhamma-Vinaya... if you are able, resolve the original [point].” Thus disputing, they speak differently.

In the phrase “Why do ascetics not speak one word?”: “Why” (kasmā) means for what reason, because of what cause, on account of what condition, by what indication, from what origin, of what nature, from what source do they not speak one [thing] but speak variously, speak differently, speak diversely, speak against one another, speak many [things], preach, recite, manifest, and designate? Therefore, that created Buddha (Nimmitabuddha) said this:

“Some say that what they hold is the truth, the reality; others say that very same truth is empty and false.
Thus disputing, they speak differently. Why do ascetics not speak one [and the same] thing?”

“Truth is indeed one, there is no second, knowing which a person would not dispute.
They themselves praise various truths; therefore, ascetics do not speak one [and the same] thing.”

“Truth is indeed one, there is no second” means: Nibbāna, which is the cessation of suffering, is called the one truth. That which is the stilling of all formations (saṅkhāra), the relinquishing of all acquisitions (upadhi), the destruction of craving (taṇhā), dispassion (virāga), cessation (nirodha), Nibbāna. Alternatively, the Truth of the Path (maggasacca), the truth of leading out, the practice leading to the cessation of suffering, the Noble Eightfold Path, is called the one truth. Namely: Right View, Right Intention, Right Speech, Right Action, Right Livelihood, Right Effort, Right Mindfulness, Right Concentration. Thus, truth is indeed one, there is no second.

In the phrase “Knowing which beings would not dispute”: “In which” (yasmiṃ) means in which truth. “Beings” (pajā) is a designation for living beings. Those who know, understand, comprehend, fully realize, and penetrate that truth would not engage in quarrels, would not engage in strife, would not engage in disputes, would not speak differently, would not engage in verbal contention. They would abandon, dispel, destroy, and bring to non-existence quarrels, strife, disputes, different speaking, and verbal contention. Thus, it means “Knowing which beings would not dispute.”
227:
'nānā te saccāni sayaṃ thunantīti' means they themselves proclaim, teach, recite, demonstrate, and express various truths. They themselves proclaim, teach, recite, demonstrate, and express: 'The world is eternal; this alone is true, any other is false.' They themselves proclaim, teach, recite, demonstrate, and express: 'The world is not eternal... the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death; this alone is true, any other is false.' Thus, it is said: 'They themselves proclaim various truths.'

'tasmā na ekaṃ samaṇā vadantīti': In this passage, 'tasmā' means for that reason, because of that cause, depending on that condition, originating from that cause, [recluses] do not speak of one view; they speak of various [views], they speak of diverse [views], they speak differently from one another, they speak of many, they teach, recite, demonstrate, and express. Thus, it is said: 'Therefore, recluses do not speak of one [truth].'

Therefore, the Blessed One said:

'Truth is indeed one, there is no second,
Knowing which, the people do not dispute.
They themselves proclaim various truths,
Therefore, recluses do not speak of one [truth].'

'Why then do they speak of various truths, those who proclaim themselves as skilled? Have many various truths been heard, or do they follow their own reasoning?'

'kasmā nu saccāni vadanti nānāti': In this passage, 'kasmā' means for what reason, because of what cause, depending on what condition, originating from what cause do they speak of various truths, do they speak of diverse ones, do they speak of individual ones, do they speak of many, teach, recite, demonstrate, and express? Thus, it is said: 'Why then do they speak of various truths?'

'pavādiyāse kusalāvadānāti': In this passage, 'pavādiyāse' means they are called 'proclaimers' because they speak specifically. Alternatively, they speak, teach, recite, demonstrate, and express their own respective views. They speak, teach, recite, demonstrate, and express: 'The world is eternal; this alone is true, any other is false.' They speak, teach, recite, demonstrate, and express: 'The world is not eternal... the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death; this alone is true, any other is false.'
228:
'kusalāvadānā' refers to those who hold views, claiming to be skilled by their own view, wise, firm, reasonable, causal, having signs, having immediate causes, and having a basis.

'saccāni sutāni bahūni nānā' means it is said that many, various, diverse, and individual truths have been heard.

'udāhu te takkamanussarantī' means: Or do they arrive by thought, by right thought? Are they led, carried away, or well-conveyed? Thus, do they follow after reasoning? Alternatively, it means they speak, teach, recite, demonstrate, and express their own intuition, which is driven by reasoning, followed by investigation, and appears to themselves. Thus also, do they follow after reasoning?

Therefore, that created Buddha (Nimmitabuddha) asked:
'Why then do they speak of various truths,
Those who proclaim themselves as skilled?
Have many various truths been heard,
Or do they follow their own reasoning?'

'Apart from the views held as permanent in the world,
There are not indeed many various truths;
Having speculated on reasoning regarding views,
They speak of the dual dharma: "True" and "False".'

'na heva saccāni bahūni nānā' means there are not indeed many, various, diverse, and individual truths.

'aññatra saññāya niccāni loke' means that apart from the firm grasping of permanence through one's own perception, only one truth is spoken of, recited, demonstrated, and expressed in the world: Nibbāna, the cessation of suffering. That Nibbāna is the calming of all conditioned things, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, and the escape from craving. Alternatively, the Truth of the Path (Magga-sacca), which leads to the escape from suffering, is called the one truth. The practice leading to Nibbāna is the Noble Eightfold Path, namely: Right View... up to Right Concentration.

'takkañca diṭṭhīsu pakappayitvā, saccaṃ musāti dvayadhammamāhū' means having reasoned, speculated, and thought, they generate views, cause them to increase, make them manifest, and make them very manifest. Having generated views, they speak, teach, recite, demonstrate, and express: 'My view is true, your view is false.'

Therefore, the Blessed One said: 'There are not indeed many various truths... they speak of the dual dharma.' One who is well-dependent on these views in what is seen, heard, practiced as virtue, or sensed, and who does not see clearly, remains in the determined view and is like the many...
229:
They produce, they bring into existence, they bring forth fully. Having produced, brought into existence, and brought forth fully the views, they say: "My truth is real, yours is false." Thus they speak, thus they preach, thus they recite, thus they explain, thus they express. Having speculated on thoughts and views, they speak of the dual phenomena of "truth and falsehood."

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
"Indeed, there are not many and various truths, eternal in the world, apart from perception. Having speculated on thoughts and views, they speak of the dual phenomena of 'truth and falsehood'."

One who does not see clearly, relying on these things—on what is seen, heard, virtue and vows, or what is sensed—stands on their decision and, laughing, says: "The other is a fool, unskilled."

Regarding the phrase "One who does not see clearly, relying on these things—on what is seen, heard, virtue and vows, or what is sensed": this means living by relying on, depending on, grasping, misapprehending, and being obsessed with a view or the purity of a view, what is heard or the purity of what is heard, a habit or the purity of a habit, a practice or the purity of a practice, or what is sensed or the purity of what is sensed. "Vimānadassī" (one who does not see clearly/disparages) means not showing respect. Alternatively, causing displeasure is also called "vimānadassī."

Regarding the phrase "stands on their decision and, laughing": the sixty-two types of views are called "decisions" (vinicchaya). Standing, being firmly established, grasping, misapprehending, and being obsessed with that decision of views is called "standing on decision" (vinicchaye ṭhatvā). "Pahassamāno" (laughing) means being pleased, joyful, very joyful, delighted, and having fulfilled intentions. Alternatively, laughing while showing one's teeth is also called "pahassamāno."

Regarding the phrase "says the other is a fool, unskilled": this means they speak, preach, recite, explain, and express thus: "The other is a fool, low, very low, inferior, base, of poor disposition, insignificant, unskilled, ignorant, fallen into ignorance, unknowing, unable to distinguish, of little wisdom, or witless."

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
230:
“Whether in what is seen, heard, virtue, or what is sensed (muta), one who, relying on these, looks down upon others, and standing by their own judgment, laughs and says, 'The other is a fool, an unskilled person.' By whatever reason one regards another as a fool, by that same reason one calls oneself skilled. Being one who considers oneself skilled, he looks down on others and says that very thing,” (so said the Blessed One).

“By whatever reason one regards another as a fool” means: by whatever cause, by whatever condition, by whatever reason, by whatever origin one regards, sees, views, looks at, gazes at, or examines another as a fool, as inferior, as low, as base, as wretched, as one of low disposition, or as one of little power. This is the meaning of the phrase “By whatever reason one regards another as a fool.”

“By that same reason one calls oneself skilled” means: the self is called “ātumāna.” That person, by that same cause, by that same condition, by that same reason, by that same origin, says of himself, “I am skilled, I am wise, I am a person of wisdom, I am intelligent, I am possessed of knowledge, I am discerning, I am a sage who knows correctly.” This is the meaning of the phrase “By that same reason one calls oneself skilled.”

“Being one who considers oneself skilled” means: one who, by his own view, considers only himself as skilled, as wise, as firm, as proper, as logical, as consistent with characteristics, as having a reason, or as having a foundation. This is the meaning of the phrase “Being one who considers oneself skilled.”

“He looks down on others and says that very thing” means: “looking down on others” refers to not showing respect to others or causing them displeasure. “Says that very thing” means saying of that very view, “This person is one of wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi), one of perverted vision.” This is the meaning of the phrase “He looks down on others and says that very thing.”

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
“By whatever reason one regards another as a fool, by that same reason one calls oneself skilled; being one who considers oneself skilled, he looks down on others and says that very thing.”
231:
That person is complete with an overreaching view; intoxicated with pride, he considers himself perfect. He has anointed himself (as wise) with his own mind; for that view of his is thus fully grasped.

"Atisāradiṭṭhiyā so samatto" means: Overreaching views refer to the sixty-two views. Why are the sixty-two views called overreaching views? Because all those views transcend reason, transcend characteristics, and transcend proper grounds; for that reason, the sixty-two views are called overreaching views. All views are also overreaching views. Why are all views called overreaching views? Because those [holders of views] surpass, exceed, and go beyond one another to generate, produce, bring into being, and specifically manifest views; for that reason, all views are called overreaching views. "Atisāradiṭṭhiyā so samatto" means he is complete with that overreaching view, fully possessed of it, and not deficient in it.

"Mānena matto paripuṇṇamānī" means: He is intoxicated by his own view and by the pride associated with that view; he is heedless, crazed, and excessively intoxicated; thus, "intoxicated with pride." "Paripuṇṇamānī" means one who considers himself perfect, one who considers himself fully complete, one who considers himself not deficient; thus, "intoxicated with pride, imagining himself perfect."

"Sayameva sāmaṃ manasābhisitto" means: He anoints himself with his own mind, thinking, "I am skilled, a pundit, wise, intelligent, knowledgeable, discerning, and sagacious"; thus, "he has anointed himself with his own mind."

"Diṭṭhī hi sā tassa tathā samattā" means: That view of his is thus fully accepted, taken up, grasped, adhered to, entered into, and resolved upon; thus, "for that view of his is thus completed."

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
"That person is complete with an overreaching view; intoxicated with pride, he considers himself perfect. He has anointed himself with his own mind; for that view of his is thus fully grasped."

If one were inferior because of another's word, then he would be a person of inferior wisdom along with [the other]. If one were himself a wise man who has reached the end of knowledge, then there would be no fool among the recluses.

"Parassa ce hi vacasā nihīno" means: By another's word, by speech, because of blame, because of contempt, or because of accusation, another is a fool, inferior, very inferior, low, base, of mean disposition, or of mean courage.

"Tumo sahā hoti nihīnapañño" means: He too, along with that speech, is one of inferior wisdom, one of inferior wisdom, one of deficient effort in wisdom, one of low wisdom, one of base wisdom, one of mean doubt in wisdom, or one of mean courage in wisdom. If he himself...
232:
Therefore, the Blessed One said: 'That person is complete with an overreaching view; intoxicated with pride, he considers himself perfect. He has anointed himself (as wise) with his own mind; for that view of his is thus fully grasped. If one were inferior because of another's word, then he would be a person of inferior wisdom along with [the other]. If one were himself a wise man who has reached the end of knowledge, then there would be no fool among the recluses.'

'Parassa ce hi vacasā nihīno' means: By another's word, by speech, because of blame, because of contempt, or because of accusation, another is a fool, inferior, very inferior, of inferior effort, of inferior cause, of mean disposition, or of mean courage; thus, 'if one were inferior because of another's word.'

'Tumo sahā hoti nihīnapañño' means: He too, along with that speech, is one of inferior wisdom, one of deficient effort in wisdom, one of inferior effort in wisdom, one of inferior cause in wisdom, one of mean doubt in wisdom, or one of mean courage in wisdom; thus, 'he would be a person of inferior wisdom along with [the other].'

'Atha ce sayaṃ vedagū hoti dhီro' means: Furthermore, if he himself is one who has reached the end of knowledge, a wise man, a pundit, one who knows distinctly, one of great wisdom, one who possesses knowledge, one who can analyze, or one whose wisdom is like a true scale; thus, 'if one were himself a wise man who has reached the end of knowledge.'

'Na koci bālo samaṇesu atthi' means: Among recluses, there is no fool, no inferior person, no person of deficient effort, no person of inferior effort, no person of inferior cause, no person of mean disposition, or no person of mean courage. All of them possess praised wisdom, specially praised wisdom, chief wisdom, distinguished wisdom, supreme wisdom, or excellent wisdom; thus, 'there would be no fool among the recluses.'

Therefore, the Blessed One said: 'If one were inferior because of another's word, then he would be a person of inferior wisdom along with [the other]. If one were himself a wise man who has reached the end of knowledge, then there would be no fool among the recluses.'

Those who proclaim a doctrine other than this Right View have fallen away from purity and are incomplete. Thus do the many sectarians speak, for they are enamored with their own views.

'Aññaṃ ito yābhivadanti dhammaṃ, aparaddhā suddhimakevalီ te' means: Those who proclaim a doctrine, view, practice, or cause other than this Right View have fallen away from the stainless path, the faultless path, the well-purified path, the bright path, or the completely bright path. They have missed it, erred, declined, fallen from the cause, or failed through ignorance...
233:
They have failed [in purity], they are not complete, not perfect, they are low, base, inferior, mean, of poor intent, and of poor capability. Those who speak of a doctrine (view, practice, cause) other than this Sammādiṭṭhi have failed and fallen away from the pure path and the white path; they are not complete.

"Thus sectarians speak of many views" means: A view is called a "tittha." Those who hold views are called "titthiyas." Many sectarians speak, teach, recite, show, and express many views.

"They are deeply attached to their own views through the passion for views" means: They are attached and deeply devoted to their own views through the passion for views.

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
"Those who speak of a doctrine other than this [Sammādiṭṭhi] have failed in purity and are not complete. Thus sectarians speak of many views; they are deeply attached to their own views through the passion for views."

"They say purity is only in this [view], they do not say there is purity in other doctrines. Thus many sectarians are established, each speaking firmly of their own path."

"They say purity is only in this [view]" means: They speak, teach, recite, show, and express that in their own view alone there is purity, supreme purity, absolute purity, liberation, supreme liberation, and absolute liberation. "The world is eternal; this alone is the truth, any other is false"—thus they speak, teach, recite, show, and express that in this view alone there is purity, supreme purity, absolute purity, liberation, supreme liberation, and absolute liberation. "The world is not eternal... the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death; this alone is the truth, any other is false"—thus they speak, teach, recite, show, and express that in this view alone there is purity (suddhi), visuddhi, parisuddhi, mutti, vimutti, and parimutti.

"They do not say there is purity in other doctrines" means: Setting aside their own teacher, teaching, group, view, practice, and path, they cast away, reject, and discard all other doctrines. They say, "That teacher is not all-knowing, the doctrine is not well-expounded, the group is not well-practiced, the view is not good, the practice is not well-prescribed, the path does not lead out [of suffering]. There is no purity, supreme purity, absolute purity, liberation, supreme liberation, or absolute liberation here. In this [other] view, they are not purified, not supremely purified, not absolutely purified, not liberated, not supremely liberated, or absolutely liberated." Thus they speak, teach, recite, show, and express.
234:
"They are low, poor in effort, poor in intent, poor in cause, poor in disposition, and poor in capability"—thus they say, teach, recite, show, and express. Setting aside their own teacher, teaching, group, view, practice, and cause, they reject all other doctrines and say there is no purity in other doctrines. "That teacher is not all-knowing, the doctrine is not well-expounded, the group is not well-practiced, the view is not good, the practice is not well-prescribed, the path does not lead out [of suffering]. There is no purity, supreme purity, absolute purity, liberation, supreme liberation, or absolute liberation here. In this [other] view, they are not purified, not supremely purified, not absolutely purified, not liberated, not supremely liberated, or absolutely liberated."

"Thus many sectarians are established, each in their own way" means: A view is called a "tittha." Those who hold views are called "titthiyas." Many sectarians are well-established, fixed, attached, resorted to, deeply involved in, and convinced of many views.

"They speak firmly of their own views" means: The doctrine, the view, the practice, and the path are called one's own path (sakāyana). In their own path, they are firm-speakers, steady-speakers, strong-speakers, and established-speakers.

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
"They say purity is only in this Dispensation; they say there is no purity in other doctrines. Thus many sectarians are established, each speaking firmly of their own view."

One who speaks firmly of his own path, saying "Only this view is correct," whom among others would he regard as a "fool" based on that? He himself would bring about quarrels, calling another a fool and one of impure doctrine.

"One who speaks firmly of his own path" means: The doctrine, view, practice, and path are called one's own path. One who speaks firmly in his own path, saying "Only this view is correct," is one who has a determined view, a strong view, and is an established-speaker.

"Whom among others would he regard as a fool?" means: In one's own view, one's own preference, one's own liking, and one's own doctrine, whom would he regard as a fool, as low, as base, as inferior, as mean, as of poor cause, as of poor intent, or as of poor capability? Whom would he see, whom would he look upon, whom would he observe, whom would he contemplate, or whom would he investigate [as such]?
235:
He who says that another is a fool and of impure nature brings about disputes by himself. One who says that another is a fool, low, very low, extremely low, of low cause, of low disposition, of low power, of impure nature, of especially impure nature, of completely impure nature, or not of pure nature—such a person, speaking thus, talking thus, reciting thus, showing thus, and calling thus, brings about, well-brings about, carries, well-carries, pulls, well-pulls, takes up, grasps, and adheres to quarrels, strife, contention, disputes, and verbal conflicts by himself. Therefore, it is said: 'He who says that another is a fool and of impure nature brings about disputes by himself.'

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
'One who speaks while standing firmly in one's own view, whom could he regard as a fool in this matter?
He who says that another is a fool and of impure nature brings about disputes by himself.'

Standing in judgment (views) and measuring by oneself, one enters into great disputes in the world.
Having abandoned all judgments (views), a being does not engage in verbal conflict in the world.

'Vinicchaye ṭhatvā sayaṃ pamāya' means: 'Judgments' refers to the sixty-two types of wrong views. Standing, being established, grasping, adhering to, and being obsessed with those judgments (views) is called 'standing in judgment'. 'Measuring by oneself' means comparing and measuring by oneself. Thinking, 'This teacher is the Omniscient Buddha,' 'This Dhamma is well-expounded,' 'This Saṅgha is well-practiced,' 'This view is good,' 'This practice is well-prescribed,' 'This path leads out of suffering'—measuring and comparing in this way is called 'standing in judgment and measuring by oneself'.

'Uddhaṃsa lokasmiṃ vivādameti' means: 'Uddhaṃsa' refers to the future. Placing one's own view above, one enters, approaches, arrives at, grasps, adheres to, and becomes obsessed with quarrels, strife, contention, disputes, and verbal conflicts by oneself. Thus it is said, 'one enters into disputes in the world regarding the future.' Alternatively, one engages in quarrels, strife, contention, disputes, and verbal conflicts with another superior view, saying, 'You do not understand this Dhamma-Vinaya... and so on... explain it if you can.' This also is 'entering into disputes in the world regarding the future'.
236:
'Having abandoned all judgments (views)' means: The sixty-two types of views are called judgments (vinicchaya). Giving up, abandoning, relinquishing, discarding, rejecting, dispelling, making an end of, and causing the non-existence of all those judgments of views is 'having abandoned all judgments'.

'A being does not engage in verbal conflict in the world' means: He does not engage in quarrels, strife, contention, disputes, or verbal conflicts. For this was said by the Blessed One: 'Aggivessana, a monk whose mind is thus liberated does not argue with anyone, does not dispute with anyone; he uses the common language of the world without adhering to it.' 'Jantu' means a being, a man, a male, a person, a life, a creature. 'In the world' means in the world starting from the world of misery (apāya-loka) up to the world of the sense bases (āyatana-loka). Thus, 'a being does not engage in verbal conflict in the world'.

The Blessed One therefore said:
'Standing in judgment and measuring by oneself, thinking "This path leads out of suffering," one enters into disputes in the world, whether regarding the future or by placing one's view above, or together with another superior view.
Having abandoned all judgments, a being does not engage in verbal conflict in the world.'

## The Exposition of Cūḷaviyūha Sutta, the Twelfth, is finished.

## 13. Exposition of Mahāviyūha Sutta

Next, I shall speak the exposition of Mahāviyūha Sutta:
Those few recluses and brahmins who dwell immersed in views, and who say, "Only this is true," all of them bring about blame, and yet they also receive praise therein.

In the phrase 'Those few recluses and brahmins who dwell immersed in views': 'Those few' is a term that includes everyone without exception. 'Dwell immersed in views' means: There are some recluses and brahmins who hold views. They take up, grasp, hold onto, adhere to, and become obsessed with one or another of the sixty-two types of views, and they dwell, live together, dwell especially, and dwell all around with their own views.

Just as householders dwell in houses, or as monks with offenses dwell in those offenses, or as those with defilements dwell in those defilements, in the same way, there are some recluses and brahmins who hold views. They take up, grasp, hold onto, adhere to, and become obsessed with one or another of the sixty-two types of views, and they dwell, live together, dwell especially, and dwell all around with their own views. This is the meaning of 'Those few recluses and brahmins who dwell immersed in views'.

'And also "Only this is true"' means: (Saying) 'The world is eternal; only this view of mine is true'.
237:
Having grasped and adhered to them, they dwell, live together, reside, and inhabit their respective views. Just as householders dwell in houses, or as monks with offenses dwell in offenses, or as those with defilements dwell in defilements; in this very same way, some ascetics and brahmins dwell [in their views]. "Those who dwell attached to views" refers to all those who live clinging to such views.

They say, "Only this is true." They say, speak, utter, explain, and declare: "The world is eternal; only this is true, everything else is futile." They say, speak, utter, explain, and declare: "The world is not eternal... the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death; only this is true, everything else is futile." This is the meaning of the phrase "And they claim, 'Only this is true.'"

All of them incur blame. All those ascetics and brahmins follow only blame, follow only reproach, and follow only ill-repute. All of them are indeed blamed, reproached, and held in ill-repute. This is the meaning of the phrase "All of them incur blame."

Moreover, they also receive praise there. In that view of theirs, in their own preference, in their own liking, and in their own doctrine, they receive, obtain, arrive at, and experience praise, commendation, fame, and renown. This is the meaning of the phrase "Moreover, they also receive praise there."

Therefore, the Created Buddha (Nimmitabuddha) said:
"Those who dwell attached to views, and claim 'Only this is true,'
All of them incur blame, and moreover, they also receive praise there.
For this [praise] is small and not sufficient for calming; I say there are two fruits of contention.
Seeing this state also, one should not engage in contention, beholding the ground of non-contention as security."

"For this is small and not sufficient for calming": "For this is small" means this is insignificant, inferior, slight, low, trivial, and minor. "Not sufficient for calming" means it is not sufficient for the calming of greed, not sufficient for the calming of hatred, not sufficient for the calming of delusion.
238:
...not sufficient for the calming of anger (kodha), for the calming of malice (upanāha), for the calming of hypocrisy (makkha), for the calming of rivalry (palāsa), for the calming of envy (issā), for the calming of avarice (macchariya), for the calming of deceit (māyā), for the calming of treachery (sāṭheyya), for the calming of stubbornness (thambha), for the calming of impetuosity (sārambha), for the calming of conceit (māna), for the calming of arrogance (atimāna), for the calming of intoxication (mada), for the calming of negligence (pamāda). It is not sufficient for the calming of all defilements, all misconduct, all distress, all fever, all anguish, and all unwholesome volitional formations; it is not sufficient for their settling, their stilling, for Nibbāna, for relinquishment, or for tranquility. This praise is small and not sufficient for calming.

"I say there are two fruits of contention": There are two fruits of quarrels over views, disputes over views, conflicts over views, contentions over views, and strife over views. [These are:] victory and defeat, gain and loss, fame and disrepute, blame and praise, happiness and suffering, joy and grief, the liked and the disliked, attraction and repulsion, exaltation and depression, compliance and resistance. Alternatively, I say, declare, teach, describe, establish, reveal, analyze, clarify, and proclaim that such actions lead to hell, lead to the animal realm, or lead to the realm of hungry ghosts (petas). Thus, "I say there are two fruits of contention."

"Seeing this state also, one should not engage in contention": "Seeing this state also" means seeing, beholding, weighing, investigating, discerning, and making clear this danger in quarrels over views, disputes over views, conflicts over views, contentions over views, and strife over views. "One should not engage in contention" means one should not quarrel, should not dispute, should not conflict, should not contend, and should not engage in strife. One should abandon, dispel, destroy, and bring to non-existence quarrels, disputes, conflicts, contentions, and strife. One should be far from, abstain from, refrain from, emerge from, be released from, be detached from, and be disconnected from quarrels, disputes, conflicts, contentions, and strife, and should dwell with a mind that has made no boundaries. Thus, "Seeing this state also, one should not engage in contention."

"Beholding the ground of non-contention as security": The ground of non-contention (avivādabhūmi) refers to the Deathless, Nibbāna. That which is the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna. One should dwell seeing, beholding, looking at, contemplating, and investigating that ground of non-contention as security, as protection, as a shelter, as a refuge, as fearlessness, as the unshakable, as the Deathless, as Nibbāna. Thus, "Beholding the ground of non-contention as security."

For that reason, the Blessed One said:
239:
This dispute is indeed not sufficient for peace; I speak of the two fruits of dispute. Seeing this disadvantage, one should not dispute; one who sees safety should look to the ground of non-dispute.

Whatever conventions (sammuti) there are that have been produced by worldlings, the wise person does not adhere to those views. That person, unattached by defilements, not taking delight in what is seen or heard, to what attached state would he adhere?

In the phrase 'Yā kācimā sammutiyo puthujjā', 'yā kāci' is a term that includes everything, in every way, without exception, and without remainder. 'Sammutiyo' refers to the sixty-two types of views (diṭṭhi) and conventions. 'Puthujjā' is so called because they are conventions produced by worldlings (puthujjana), or because they are conventions produced by various individual people.

In the phrase 'Sabbāva etā na upeti vidvā', 'vidvā' refers to one who has attained knowledge (vijjā), who is wise, enlightened, sagacious, and intelligent. That wise person does not reach, does not approach, does not grasp, does not misapprehend, and does not adhere to all those conventions of views.

In the phrase 'Anūpayo so upayaṃ kimeyya', 'upaya' (attachment/clinging) is of two kinds: attachment through craving (taṇhūpaya) and attachment through views (diṭṭhūpaya). ...pe... This is called clinging through craving. ...pe... This is called clinging through views. For that person, attachment through craving has been abandoned, and attachment through views has been relinquished. Because craving has been abandoned and views have been relinquished, to what form would that person, who is unattached by defilements, approach, grasp, misapprehend, or adhere as 'this is my self'? To what feeling, what perception, what mental formations, what consciousness, what destination, what rebirth, what conception, what existence, what saṃsāra, or what round of rebirths would he approach, grasp, misapprehend, or adhere?

In the phrase 'Diṭṭhe sute khantimakubbamāno', it means living without producing delight, without producing desire, without producing affection, without producing lust (rāga), without cultivating, without fully cultivating, without manifesting, and without making fully manifest in what is seen, or in the purity of the seen, or in what is heard, or in the purity of the heard, or in what is sensed, or in the purity of the sensed.

For that reason, the Blessed One said—
240:
“Whatever conventions (views) of worldlings there are, the wise person does not approach any of them. That wise person, unattached (by craving and views), not forming (delight, desire, affection, or lust) in the seen or the heard, how could he approach (craving and views)?”

Those who hold the view that virtue is supreme say that purity comes through mere restraint; having undertaken and remained fixed in vows (such as the elephant-vow, horse-vow, etc.). Those who are led to existence, holding the view that (their own view) is good, think: “Let us train only in this (our own view/desire), then there will be purity.”

There are some recluses and brahmins who hold the view that virtue is supreme (sīluttamavāda). Those recluses and brahmins speak of, teach, recite, show, and designate purity, supreme purity, complete purity, liberation, supreme liberation, and complete liberation through mere virtue, mere restraint, mere control, and mere non-transgression.

The son of Samaṇamuṇḍikā said thus: “Householder, I designate a person endowed with four qualities as one who has accomplished wholesome deeds, who has the highest wholesome deeds, who has reached the supreme attainment, an invincible recluse. What are the four? Here, householder, he does not perform evil deeds with the body, he does not speak evil words, he does not think evil thoughts, and he does not lead an evil livelihood. Householder, I designate a person endowed with these four qualities as one who has accomplished wholesome deeds, who has the highest wholesome deeds, who has reached the supreme attainment, an invincible recluse whose defilements are stilled.” Just so, there are some recluses and brahmins who hold the view that virtue is supreme. They speak of, teach, recite, show, and designate purity, supreme purity, complete purity, liberation, supreme liberation, and complete liberation through mere virtue, mere restraint, mere control, and mere non-transgression.

‘Vows’ (vata) means taking up, fully taking up, undertaking, fully undertaking, grasping, and misapprehending (and remaining fixed in) the elephant-vow, the horse-vow, the cow-vow, the dog-vow, the crow-vow, the Vāsudeva-vow, the Baladeva-vow, the Puṇṇabhadda-vow, the Maṇibhadda-vow, the fire-vow, the nāga-vow, the supanna-vow, the yakkha-vow, the asura-vow, the gandhabba-vow, the Mahārāja-vow, the moon-vow, the sun-vow, the Indra-vow, the Brahma-vow, the deva-vow, or the vow of worshipping the directions.
241:
“Having undertaken vows, they remain attached and established” means—having well-undertaken the vows such as the practice of an elephant, the practice of a horse, the practice of a cow, the practice of a dog, the practice of a crow, the practice of Vāsudeva, the practice of Baladeva, the practice of Puṇṇabhadda, the practice of Maṇibhadda, the practice of fire, the practice of a Nāga, the practice of a Garuḍa, the practice of a Yakkha, the practice of an Asura, the practice of a Gandhabba, the practice of the Great Kings (Mahārāja), the practice of the Moon-god, the practice of the Sun-god, the practice of Sakka, the practice of Brahma, the practice of the Devas, or the practice of worshipping the directions; they remain attached, clinging, and considering them, being deeply immersed and inclined towards them.

“Let us train only in this, our own view; through such training, there will be purity” means—‘in this’ refers only to one’s own view, one’s own preference, one’s own desire, and one’s own doctrine. ‘Let us train’ means let us train in that doctrine, let us practice it well, let us undertake and follow it. ‘His purity’ through such training means his purity, special purity, complete purity, liberation, special liberation, and complete liberation.

“Led to existence, they speak of themselves as those with good views” means—‘those led to existence’ are those who have gone to existence, reached existence, are attached to existence, and are deeply inclined towards existence. ‘Those who speak of themselves as having good views’ are those who, according to their own doctrine, speak of themselves as having good views, wise views, firm views, appropriate views, logical views, characteristic views, causal views, and well-founded views.

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
“Some, regarding virtue as supreme, say that purity comes through restraint; having undertaken a vow, they remain attached to it.
Saying, ‘Let us train only in this, our own view; through such training, there will be purity,’ they are led to existence and speak of themselves as those with good views.”

“If one falls away from virtue and vows, one trembles, having failed in action;
One yearns and longs for purity, like a traveler who has lost his companions after leaving home.”

“If one falls away from virtue and vows” means—one falls away from virtue and vows due to two reasons: either due to the criticism and prohibition of others, or due to one’s own inability to accomplish it. How does one fall away due to the prohibition of others? Others criticize and prohibit, saying: “That teacher is not omniscient, the Dhamma is not well-proclaimed, the group (Gaṇa) is not well-practiced, the view is not good, the practice is not well-prescribed, the path does not lead out of suffering; in this view, there is no purity, no special purity, no complete purity, no liberation, no special liberation, no complete liberation; in this view, they are not purified, not liberated; they are inferior, very inferior, low, contemptible, insignificant, and trivial.” When others thus prohibit, one falls away from the teacher, from the teaching of the Dhamma, from the group, from the view, from the practice, and from the path. Thus...
242:
...one falls away due to the prohibition of others. How does one fall away due to inability? Being unable to fulfill virtue, one falls away from virtue; being unable to fulfill a vow, one falls away from the vow; being unable to fulfill virtue and vows, one falls away from virtue and vows. Thus, falling away due to inability is what is meant by “If one falls away from virtue and vows.”

“One trembles, having failed in action” means—having failed in virtue, or in a vow, or in virtue and vows, one thinks, “I have failed in the cause, I have erred, I have stumbled, I have slipped, I have erred through ignorance,” and thus one shakes, trembles, and is greatly agitated. “Having failed in action” means having failed in meritorious formations (puññābhisaṅkhāra), or non-meritorious formations (apuññābhisaṅkhāra), or imperturbable formations (āneñjābhisaṅkhāra), one thinks, “I have failed in the cause, I have erred, I have stumbled, I have slipped, I have erred through ignorance,” and thus one shakes, trembles, and is greatly agitated. Therefore, it is said, “One trembles, having failed in action.”

“One yearns and longs for purity” means—one yearns for virtue, or for a vow, or for virtue and vows; one yearns in various ways, one yearns excessively. “Longs for purity” means one longs for the purity of virtue, or for the purity of a vow, or for the purity of virtue and vows; one desires it and yearns for it excessively. Therefore, it is said, “One yearns and longs for purity.”

“Like a traveler who has lost his companions after leaving home” means—just as a man who has left his home and is traveling with a caravan, if he is left behind and separated from that caravan, he either follows that caravan or returns to his own home; in the same way, that person possessed of views (diṭṭhigatika) takes up that teacher or another teacher, that teaching of Dhamma or another teaching of Dhamma, that group or another group, that view or another view, that practice or another practice, that path or another path; he grasps it and becomes attached to it. Therefore, it is said, “Like a traveler who has lost his companions after leaving home.”

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
“If one falls away from virtue and vows, one trembles, having failed in action.
One yearns and longs for purity, like a traveler who has lost his companions after leaving home.”
243:
Having abandoned all virtue and vows, and this action both blameworthy and blameless, not longing for purity or impurity, one should wander detached, not grasping at [the peace of] views.

'Having abandoned all virtue and vows' means having abandoned, given up, dispelled, destroyed, and brought to non-existence all purities of virtue, all purities of vows, and all purities of virtue and vows.

'And this action both blameworthy and blameless' means: Blameworthy action (sāvajjakaṃma) is said to be dark action with dark results. Blameless action (anavajjakaṃma) is said to be bright action with bright results. It means having abandoned, given up, dispelled, destroyed, and brought to non-existence both blameworthy and blameless actions.

'Not longing for purity or impurity' means: They long for impurity (asuddhi), they long for unwholesome states (akusala dhamma). They long for purity (suddhi), they long for the five cords of sensual pleasure (pañca kāmaguṇa). They long for impurity, they long for unwholesome states, they long for the five cords of sensual pleasure. They long for purity, they long for the sixty-two views (dvāsaṭṭhi diṭṭhigata). They long for impurity, they long for unwholesome states, they long for the five cords of sensual pleasure, they long for the sixty-two views. They long for purity, they long for wholesome states belonging to the three realms (tedhātuka kusala dhamma). They long for impurity, they long for unwholesome states, they long for the five cords of sensual pleasure, they long for the sixty-two views, they long for wholesome states belonging to the three realms. They long for purity; noble worldlings (kalyāṇa puthujjana) long for the entry into the path of certainty (niyāmāvakkanti). Trainees (sekha) long for the highest state, Arahantship (arahatta-phala). When Arahantship is reached, the Arahant no longer longs for unwholesome states, nor for the five cords of sensual pleasure, nor for the sixty-two views, nor for wholesome states of the three realms, nor for the entry into the path, nor for the highest state of Arahantship. The Arahant, who has completely transcended longing, has transcended both growth and decline. He has lived the life, fulfilled the practice... there is no more saṃsāra consisting of birth, aging, and death; for that Arahant, there is no further rebirth. This is the meaning of 'not longing for purity or impurity'.
244:
The Arahant does not long for wholesome states, nor for the entry into the path, nor for the highest state of Arahantship. The Arahant has completely transcended longing. He has transcended both growth and decline. That Arahant has done what was to be done, has fulfilled the practice... the saṃsāra called birth, aging, and death does not exist for that Arahant; there is no further rebirth. This is the meaning of the phrase 'not longing for purity or impurity'.

'Wander detached, not grasping at peace' means: 'Detached' (virato) refers to one who abstains from purity and impurity, who especially abstains, who repeatedly abstains, who has gone out, who is released, who is especially liberated, who is disjoined, and who dwells with a mind that has made no boundaries. 'Should wander' (care) means one should practice, wander, dwell, maintain postures, carry on, protect, sustain, and keep oneself going. Thus it is said, 'wander detached'. 'Not grasping at peace' (santimanuggahāya) means the sixty-two views are called 'peace' (santi); dwelling without taking, without clinging, and without adhering to those 'peaces' of views is called 'wandering detached, not grasping at peace'.

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
'Having abandoned all virtue and vows, and this action both blameworthy and blameless, not longing for purity or impurity, one should wander detached, not grasping at peace.'

'Depending on that which is loathsome, or else on what is seen, heard, or sensed, they cry out for purity, those who are above, not having overcome craving for various states of existence.'

'Depending on that which is loathsome' (tamūpanissāya jigucchitaṃ vā) means some ascetics and brahmins have practices and views that are loathsome, such as self-mortification; they take such practice as the essence, they depend on it, especially depend on it, cling to it, approach it, enter into it, and are inclined towards it. Thus it is said, 'depending on that which is loathsome'.

'Or else on what is seen, heard, or sensed' (atha vāpi diṭṭhaṃ va sutaṃ mutaṃ vā) means dwelling by depending on, relying on, grasping, clinging to, and adhering to sight or purity through sight, hearing or purity through hearing, and sensing or purity through sensing.

'They cry out for purity, those who are above' (uddhaṃsarā suddhimanutthunanti) means some ascetics and brahmins hold the 'Uddhaṃsara' doctrine, which speaks of purity through saṃsāra. Who are those ascetics and brahmins of the Uddhaṃsara doctrine? Those ascetics and brahmins who desire extreme purity, purity through saṃsāra, who hold the view of non-action (akiriyadiṭṭhi), or the eternalist view (sassatavāda)—these are called those of the Uddhaṃsara doctrine. They speak of, preach, tell, recite, show, and designate purity, special purity, complete purity, liberation, special liberation, and complete liberation within saṃsāra. Thus it is said, 'they cry out for purity, those who are above'.

'Not having overcome craving for various states of existence' (avītatanhāse bhavābhave su) means: Craving (taṇhā) refers to craving for forms, craving for sounds, craving for smells, craving for tastes, craving for touches, and craving for mental objects. 'In various states of existence' (bhavābhave su) means in large and small existences, in the realm of action (kamma-bhava), in the realm of rebirth (upapatti-bhava), in the kamma-bhava of the sensual realm, in the upapatti-bhava of the sensual realm...
245:
In the fine-material existence, in the kamma-process of fine-material existence, in the rebirth-process of fine-material existence, in the immaterial existence, in the kamma-process of immaterial existence, in the rebirth-process of immaterial existence, in repeated existence, in repeated destinations, in repeated rebirth-process, in repeated conception, and in the repeated arising of individual existence—those with craving that is not gone, not departed, not abandoned, not vomited out, not released, not relinquished, and not forsaken, possess unextinguished craving in various existences.

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
“Depending on that (view), they repeatedly speak of purity regarding what is loathsome, or else regarding what is seen, heard, or sensed; those with unextinguished craving in various existences (bhava-abhava).”

For one who longs, there are mutterings through craving;
Trembling also occurs in things constructed by craving and views;
In this Dispensation, for that Arahant who has no passing away and rebirth,
By what lust would he tremble? Where would he perform mutterings through craving?

"Patthayamānassa hi jappitāni" means: Longing is called craving (taṇhā). That lust, infatuation ... (pe) ... covetousness, greed, the unwholesome root (is called craving). "Patthayamānassa" means for one who longs, for one who desires, for one who enjoys, for one who yearns, for one who mutters intensely. "Jappitāni" means mutterings are called craving. That lust, infatuation ... (pe) ... covetousness, greed, the unwholesome root (is called craving). Thus is the meaning of "Patthayamānassa hi jappitāni."

"Pavedhitaṃ vāpi pakappitesu" means: As for constructions (pakappanā), there are two kinds: construction through craving and construction through views. ... (pe) ... This is called construction through craving. ... (pe) ... This is called construction through views. "Pavedhitaṃ vāpi pakappitesu" means they tremble with the doubt that the constructed object will be snatched away; they tremble when it is being snatched away; they tremble when it has been snatched away. They tremble with the doubt that the constructed object will change; they tremble when it is changing; they tremble when it has changed; they tremble in various ways; they tremble intensely. Thus is the meaning of "Pavedhitaṃ vāpi pakappitesu."

"Cutūpapāto idha yassa natthi" means: "Yassa" refers to the Arahant, the one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava), who is unworthy of doing evil in secret. For that Arahant, there is no going, no coming, no going and coming, no death, no destination (gati), no various existences, no passing away (cuti), no rebirth (paṭisandhi), no manifestation, no breaking up of the aggregates, no birth, and no aging and death; they do not exist, they are not found, they are not obtained; they have been abandoned, completely cut off, calmed, stilled, made incapable of arising, and burnt by the fire of knowledge. Thus is the meaning of "Cutūpapāto idha yassa natthi."
246:
By what would that Arahant tremble? Where would he long? By what lust would he tremble? By what hatred would he tremble? By what delusion would he tremble? By what conceit would he tremble? By what view would he tremble? By what restlessness (uddhacca) would he tremble? By what doubt (vicikicchā) would he tremble? By what underlying tendencies (anusaya) would he tremble—as one who is lustful, or hateful, or deluded, or fettered, or misapprehending, or distracted, or undecided, or stubborn? Since those volitional formations (abhisaṅkhāra) have been abandoned, and because they are abandoned, by what destination (gati) would he tremble—as a hell-being, or as one in the animal realm, or as one in the peta realm, or as a human, or as a deva, or as one with form, or as one without form, or as one with perception, or as one without perception, or as one with neither-perception-nor-non-perception? The cause for which he would tremble, tremble in various ways, or tremble intensely does not exist; the condition does not exist; the reason does not exist—by what would he tremble? "Where would he long?" means where would he long, for what would he long, in what place would he long, long in various ways, or long excessively?—By what would that Arahant tremble? Where would he long?

Therefore, the Blessed One said:

'For one who longs, there are mutterings; trembling also exists in constructed views.
In this Dispensation, for the one who has no passing away and rebirth, by what would he tremble? Where would he long?'

Some say that a certain Dhamma is supreme, while others say that very same Dhamma is low.
Which of their claims is true? All of them are in the habit of saying, 'Only we are experts.'

'Some say that a certain Dhamma is supreme' means some recluses and brahmins say of a certain Dhamma, view, practice, or path: 'This is supreme, foremost, best, distinguished, chief, highest, and most excellent.' Thus they say, thus they speak, thus they recite, thus they show, thus they designate—'Some say that a certain Dhamma is supreme.'

'While others say that very same Dhamma is low' means some recluses and brahmins say of that very same Dhamma, view, practice, or path: 'This is low, very low, inferior, base, wretched, and insignificant.' Thus they say, thus they speak, thus they recite, thus they show, thus they designate—'While others say that very same Dhamma is low.'
247:
What is the doctrine of these ascetics and brahmins? Among the doctrines of these ascetics and brahmins, which one is true, unerring, real, factual, and non-perverted? — What is the doctrine of these ascetics and brahmins?

All these claim to be experts: All these ascetics and brahmins claim that they alone are experts in their own doctrine, wise, firm, logical, speaking with reason, speaking with signs, speaking with causes, and speaking with grounds in their own views.

Therefore, the Created Buddha (Nimmitabuddha) said:
“What some call the supreme Dhamma, others call inferior.
What is the doctrine of these? Which one is true? For all these claim to be experts.”

They say their own Dhamma is perfect, but they say the Dhamma of others is inferior.
Thus, they cling to their views and dispute, saying their own convention is the truth.

“They say their own Dhamma is perfect” means: Some ascetics and brahmins say, speak, recite, show, and declare regarding their own doctrine, practice, and path: “This is complete, perfect, and supreme.” — They say their own Dhamma is perfect.

“But they say the Dhamma of others is inferior” means: Some ascetics and brahmins say, speak, recite, show, and declare regarding the doctrine, practice, and path of others: “This is inferior, low, base, vile, contemptible, and insignificant.” — But they say the Dhamma of others is inferior.

“Thus, they cling to their views and dispute” means: Having thus taken up, grasped, seized, touched, and adhered to their views, they dispute, quarrel, fight, contend, argue, and engage in strife, saying: “You do not understand this Dhamma and Vinaya... if you are able, explain yourself to be free from fault.” — Thus, they cling to their views and dispute.

“They say their own convention is the truth” means: They say their own convention is the truth, saying: “The world is eternal; this alone is the truth, everything else is futile.” — They say their own convention is the truth. “The world is not eternal...”
248:
“The world is eternal (and so on) ... after death, the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist; this alone is the truth, everything else is futile.” Thus, they say their own view is the truth.

Therefore, the Blessed One said:

“They say their own Dhamma is perfect, but they say the Dhamma of others is inferior. Thus, they also cling and dispute, saying their own convention in their view is the truth.

If one were to become inferior by the disparagement of another, then no one would be distinguished in the teachings. For many speak of another's Dhamma as inferior, while speaking firmly of their own view.”

“If one were to become inferior by the disparagement of another” means: If, by reason of another's disparagement, blame, reproach, or criticism, another person becomes a fool, inferior, low, base, vile, contemptible, or insignificant. — This is the meaning of “If one were to become inferior by the disparagement of another.”

“No one would be distinguished in the teachings” means: Among the teachings, no one would be the foremost, the best, the distinguished, the leader, the supreme, or the most excellent. — This is the meaning of “No one would be distinguished in the teachings.”

“For many speak of another's Dhamma as inferior” means: Many people speak of, criticize, blame, and reproach the Dhamma of many others as inferior, low, base, vile, contemptible, or insignificant. Many people also speak of, criticize, blame, and reproach the Dhamma of one person as inferior, low, base, vile, contemptible, or insignificant. One person also speaks of, criticizes, blames, and reproaches the Dhamma of many others as inferior, low, base, vile, contemptible, or insignificant. One person also speaks of, criticizes, blames, and reproaches the Dhamma of one other person as inferior, low, base, vile, contemptible, or insignificant. — This is the meaning of “For many speak of another's Dhamma as inferior.”

“While speaking firmly of their own” means: They speak firmly and steadfastly regarding the Dhamma that is their own ground, the view that is their own ground, the practice that is their own ground, and the path that is their own ground...
249:
‘Balikavādā aṭṭhitavādā’ means firmly asserting one's own view in a very inferior manner.

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
“If one were to become inferior by the disparagement of others, then no one would be distinguished in the Dhamma. For many speak of another’s Dhamma as inferior while firmly asserting their own views.”

Just as they praise their own foundations (views), honoring one's own Dhamma is likewise considered true. All doctrines would be true, for their purity is individual to themselves.

‘Honoring one's own Dhamma is likewise considered true’—what is this honoring of one's own Dhamma? It is the respecting, honoring, venerating, and worshipping of one's own teacher, thinking, “This teacher is omniscient”—this is called ‘Saddhammapūjā’ (honoring the Dhamma). It is the respecting, honoring, venerating, and worshipping of one's own taught Dhamma, one's own group, one's own view, one's own practice, and one's own path, thinking, “This path leads to deliverance”—this is called ‘Saddhammapūjā’. ‘Honoring one's own Dhamma is likewise considered true’ means that honoring the Dhamma is thus true, real, factual, and non-erroneous.

‘Just as they praise their own foundations’—the Dhamma, view, practice, and path are called one's own foundations (sakāyana). Because they praise, laud, extol, and speak of the virtues of these foundations of theirs, it is said, “Just as they praise their own foundations.”

‘All doctrines would be true’ means that all doctrines would be unfailing, true, real, factual, and non-erroneous.

‘For their purity is individual to themselves’ means that the purity, supreme purity, absolute purity, liberation, supreme liberation, and absolute liberation of those recluses and brahmins are individual to themselves.

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
“Just as they praise their own foundations, honoring one's own Dhamma is likewise considered true. All doctrines would be true, for their purity is individual to themselves.”
250:
For the Brahmin (Arahant) who has put away evil, there is nothing to be led by others; among doctrines, there is no grasping after making a decision. Therefore, he has transcended disputes, for he does not see any other Dhamma as superior other than the foundations of mindfulness and so forth.

‘Na brāhmaṇassa paraneyyamatthi’—‘Na’ is a particle of negation. ‘Brāhmaṇa’ is so-called because he has put away seven things (evil)... [pe]... That Arahant who is independent of craving and views is called a Brahmin. ‘Na brāhmaṇassa paraneyyamatthi’ means that for the Brahmin, there is no state of being led by others; the Brahmin is not one to be led by others, not dependent on others, not convinced by others, and not bound to others. Being undeluded, possessed of wisdom and mindfulness, he knows and sees. Regarding the fact that “All formations are impermanent,” there is no state of being led by others for the Brahmin... he knows and sees. Regarding “All formations are suffering”... [pe]... Regarding “Whatever is of the nature to arise, all that is of the nature to cease,” there is no state of being led by others for the Brahmin; the Brahmin is not one to be led by others, not dependent on others, not convinced by others, and not bound to others. Being undeluded, possessed of wisdom and mindfulness, he knows and sees. Thus, it is said, ‘Na brāhmaṇassa paraneyyamatthi’.

‘Dhammesu niccheyya samuggahītaṃ’—‘Dhammesu’ refers to the sixty-two types of views. ‘Niccheyya’ means having decided, having specifically decided, having searched, having specifically searched, having weighed, having investigated, having made clear, and having manifested. Grasping by way of reference, grasping in groups, grasping as superior, grasping by parts, grasping specifically, or grasping by accumulation, such as “This alone is true, real, unfailing, and non-erroneous”—such grasping, handling, mental preoccupation, entering into, and immersion do not exist, are not present, are not found, and are not obtainable. They have been abandoned, cut off, stilled, calmed, and burnt by the fire of knowledge so that they cannot arise again. Thus, it is said, ‘Dhammesu niccheyya samuggahītaṃ’.

‘Tasmā vivādāni upātivatto’—‘Tasmā’ means for that reason, due to that cause, due to that condition, due to that origin, he has transcended, gone beyond, fully transcended, and specifically gone beyond disputes, quarrels, contentions, arguments, and verbal strife regarding views. Thus, it is said, ‘Tasmā vivādāni upātivatto’.

‘Na hi seṭṭhato passati dhammamaññaṃ’—This means he does not see any other teacher, teaching, group, view, practice, or superior Dhamma as a cause, other than the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) and the right efforts (sammappadhāna).
251:
Apart from the bases of power (iddhipāda), apart from the faculties (indriya), apart from the powers (bala), apart from the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga), and apart from the Noble Eightfold Path (ariya aṭṭhaṅgika magga), one does not see, look at, observe, contemplate, or examine the Dhamma that is supreme, praised, distinguished, chief, most excellent, and noble. Therefore, it means "one does not see any other Dhamma as supreme."

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
"For the Brahmin (Arahant), there is no being led by others;
Among the teachings, there is no fixed view that has been grasped.
Therefore, he has transcended disputes;
Indeed, he does not see any other Dhamma as supreme."

"I know, I see, this is just so,"
Some believe they reach purification through their own views.
Even if he saw something, what benefit would there be for him by that seeing?
Bypassing (the foundations of mindfulness, etc.), they speak of purification by other means.

In the phrase "Jānāmi passāmi tatheva etaṃ": "Jānāmi" (I know) means knowing by the knowledge of others' minds or by the knowledge of recollecting past lives. "Passāmi" (I see) means seeing with the physical eye or with the divine eye. "Tatheva etaṃ" means this is true, real, factual, as it is, and not otherwise. Thus, it means "I know, I see, this is just so."

In the phrase "Diṭṭhiyā eke paccenti suddhiṃ": Some recluses and brahmins believe they reach purity, supreme purity, absolute purity, liberation, supreme liberation, and absolute liberation through their views. Some recluses and brahmins believe, "The world is eternal; this alone is the truth, everything else is false," and thus believe they reach purity, supreme purity, absolute purity, liberation, supreme liberation, and absolute liberation through their views. Some recluses and brahmins believe, "The world is not eternal... (etc.) ... A Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death; this alone is the truth, everything else is false," and thus believe they reach purity, supreme purity, absolute purity, liberation, supreme liberation, and absolute liberation through their views. Thus, it means "Some believe they reach purification through their own views."

In the phrase "Adakkhi ce kiñhi tumassa tena": "Adakkhi" means he saw by the knowledge of others' minds, or by the knowledge of recollecting past lives, or with the physical eye, or with the divine eye. "Kiñhi tumassa tena" means what benefit is accomplished for him by that seeing? There is no full understanding of the truth of suffering, no abandoning of the truth of the origin, no development of the truth of the path, no realization of the fruit, no absolute eradication of lust, no absolute eradication of hatred, no absolute eradication of delusion...
252:
...no absolute eradication of all defilements, and no absolute cutting off of the round of rebirth. Thus, "Even if he saw something, what benefit would there be for him by that seeing?"

Those sectarians (titthiyas), having bypassed, completely bypassed, and transcended the path of purity, the path of supreme purity, the path of absolute purity, the path of clarity, and the path of absolute clarity—excluding the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna), excluding the right efforts (sammappadhāna), excluding the bases of power (iddhipāda), excluding the faculties (indriya), excluding the powers (bala), excluding the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga), and excluding the Noble Eightfold Path—speak of, teach, declare, show, and designate purity, supreme purity, absolute purity, liberation, supreme liberation, and absolute liberation. In this way, too, they speak of purification by other means, bypassing [the path].

Alternatively, the Buddhas, the disciples of the Buddhas, and the Paccekabuddhas, having bypassed, completely bypassed, and transcended the impure path, the non-supreme path of purity, the non-absolute path of purity, the non-clear path, and the non-absolute clear path of those sectarians, speak of, teach, declare, show, and designate purity, supreme purity, absolute purity, liberation, supreme liberation, and absolute liberation through the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the Noble Eightfold Path. In this way, too, they speak of purification by other means, bypassing [the sectarian paths].

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
"'I know, I see, this is just so,' some believe they reach purification through their own views. Even if he saw something, what benefit would there be for him by that seeing? Bypassing (the path of purification), they speak of purification by other means.
When a man looks (at name-and-form), he sees only name-and-form; having seen it, he knows only that name-and-form (as permanent, etc.). Let him look at much or little name-and-form as he wishes; the wise do not say that purification is obtained by such looking."

"When a man looks, he sees name-and-form" means that when a man looks with the knowledge of others' minds, or with the knowledge of recollecting past lives, or with the physical eye, or with the divine eye, he sees only name-and-form as permanent, as pleasant, and as self. He does not see the arising, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, or the escape from those phenomena. Thus, "When a man looks, he sees name-and-form."
253:
"Having seen, he knows only those" (disvāna vā ñāyati tānimeva) means that whether seeing through the knowledge of others' minds (paracittañāṇa), the knowledge of recollecting past lives (pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇa), the physical eye (maṃsacakkhu), or the divine eye (dibbacakkhu), one knows only mind-and-matter (nāmarūpa) as permanent, pleasant, and self. It means one does not know the origin (samudaya), the cessation (atthaṅgama), the gratification (assāda), the danger (ādīnava), and the escape (nissaraṇa) of those phenomena.

"Let him see much or little" (kāmaṃ bahuṃ passatu appakaṃ vā) means seeing much or little mind-and-matter as permanent, pleasant, and self.
