"The skilled do not say purity is by that" (na hi tena suddhiṃ kusalā vadanti) means those wise ones who are skilled in the aggregates (khandha), elements (dhātu), sense bases (āyatana), dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda), foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna), right efforts (sammappadhāna), bases of power (iddhipāda), faculties (indriya), powers (bala), factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga), the path (magga), the fruit (phala), and Nibbāna, do not say, preach, recite, show, or designate that purity (suddhi, visuddhi, parisuddhi) or liberation (mutti, vimutti, parimutti) comes merely from seeing mind-and-matter through the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of recollecting past lives, the physical eye, or the divine eye.

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
"A person looking sees mind-and-matter; having seen, he knows only those.
Let him see much or little mind-and-matter; the skilled do not say purity is by that."

One who speaks from a fixed view is not easy to lead; he is one who puts his preconceived view in the forefront.
In whatever he relies on, he says it is good; speaking of purity, he sees it as truth there.

"One who speaks from a fixed view is not easy to lead" (nivissavādī na hi subbināyo) means one who speaks from a fixed view (nivissavādī), saying, "The world is eternal; only this is the truth, everything else is futile," or "The world is not eternal... the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death... only this is the truth, everything else is futile." Such a dogmatist (nivissavādī) is difficult to lead, difficult to convince, and difficult to inspire.
254:
"One who speaks from a fixed view is not easy to lead, difficult to make see, difficult to inspire" means: one who always speaks with a fixed view such as 'The world is eternal, only this view of mine is true, other views are futile' is not easy to lead. Such a person who always speaks with a fixed view is difficult to lead, difficult to make understand, difficult to make see repeatedly, and difficult to inspire. Therefore, it is said, "One who speaks from a fixed view is not easy to lead."

"Preconceived, putting view in the forefront" (pakappitā diṭṭhipurekkharāno) means: having conceived, fashioned, and firmly established a view, one wanders about putting that view in the forefront. Because he is one who has a view as his banner, a view as his flag, who is dominated by a view, and who wanders about surrounded by a view, it is said, "Preconceived, putting view in the forefront."

"In what he relies on, he says it is good" (yaṃ nissito tattha subhaṃ vadāno) means: whatever teacher, doctrine, group, view, practice, or path one relies on, resorts to, enters into, or is intent upon, one says it is 'good' within one's own vision, desire, preference, and doctrine. Because he says it is beautiful, wise, firm, logical, characterized, grounded, and well-founded within his own doctrine, it is said, "In what he relies on, he says it is good."

"Speaking of purity, he sees it as truth there" (suddhiṃ vado tattha tathaddasā so) means: one who speaks of purity, great purity, complete purity, brightness, or great brightness (or one who sees in such a way) sees, observes, and penetrates it as true, real, factual, authentic, and unerring within his own vision, desire, preference, and doctrine. Therefore, it is said, "Speaking of purity, he sees it as truth there."

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
"One who speaks from a fixed view is not easy to lead, preconceived, putting view in the forefront. In what he relies on, he says it is good; speaking of purity, he sees it as truth there."

A Brahmin (Arahant) does not arrive at a concept through knowledge; he is not a follower of views, nor is he a kinsman of (mundane) knowledge. Having known the various conventions (sammuti) of worldlings, he remains equanimous, thinking, 'Others grasp (through craving and views).'

"A Brahmin does not arrive at a concept through knowledge" (na brāhmaṇo kappamupeti saṅkhā): 'Na' is a particle of negation. 'Brahmin' is so called because he has barred the seven evil qualities. Such a person of such nature, who does not resort to craving and views, is called a Brahma. 'Kappa' (conceptualization) is of two kinds: conceptualization through craving (taṇhākappa) and conceptualization through views (diṭṭhikappa). 'Saṅkhā' refers to knowledge. It is the wisdom, the act of knowing, non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, and right view. "A Brahmin does not arrive at a concept through knowledge" means the Brahmin (Arahant), having known through knowledge, having weighed, having investigated, and having made it clear...
255:
Non-delusion, the wisdom that investigates the Dhamma, and right view are called saṅkhā (wisdom). "The Arahant, knowing through wisdom, does not arrive at speculation" means: The Arahant, knowing through wisdom, weighing, investigating, making clear, and having made clear—knowing through wisdom, weighing, investigating, making clear, and having made clear that "All conditioned things are impermanent... all conditioned things are suffering... whatever is of the nature to arise, all that is of the nature to cease"—does not reach, approach, grasp, touch, or misinterpret the speculation of craving or the speculation of views. Thus, it is said: "The Arahant, knowing through wisdom, does not arrive at speculation."

"He is not one who relies on views, nor is he one who has knowledge as a relative" means: For that Arahant, the sixty-two types of views have been abandoned, cut off, calmed, stilled, made incapable of arising again, and completely consumed by the fire of knowledge. He does not follow the will of views; he is not led, carried away, or brought near by views. He does not believe in those views as having essence, nor does he return to them. Thus, it is said: "He is not one who relies on views." "Nor is he one who has knowledge as a relative" means: He does not make craving or views his relative, nor does he produce, generate, or bring them into existence through the knowledge of the eight attainments or the knowledge of the five supernormal powers. Thus, it is said: "He is not one who relies on views, nor is he one who has knowledge as a relative."

"And having known the conventions produced by worldlings" means: "Having known" means knowing, weighing, investigating, making clear, and having made clear—knowing, weighing, investigating, making clear, and having made clear that "All conditioned things are impermanent," "All conditioned things are suffering," ... "Whatever is of the nature to arise, all that is of the nature to cease." Thus, it is said: "And he, having known." Conventions (sammuti) refer to the sixty-two types of views, which are called the conventions of views. Worldlings (puthujjana) means those conventions are produced by worldlings, or they are conventions produced by many various people. Thus, it is said: "And having known the conventions produced by worldlings."

"He is indifferent to what is considered grasping" means: Others grasp, touch, and misinterpret through the power of craving and the power of views. The Arahant, however, is indifferent; he does not grasp, touch, or misinterpret. Thus, it is said: "He is indifferent to what is considered grasping."

## Therefore, the Blessed One said:
"The Arahant, knowing through wisdom, does not arrive at speculation; he is not one who relies on views, nor is he one who has knowledge as a relative.
Having known the conventions produced by worldlings, he is indifferent; (he is indifferent) to what is considered grasping (by others)."
256:
In this world, the muni, having abandoned the bonds, is not a partisan when disputes arise. Calm among the unpeaceful, that muni is indifferent and free from grasping; I consider that others alone grasp.

"In this world, the muni abandons the bonds" means: There are four bonds (gantha)—the bond of covetousness (abhijjhā-kāyagantha), the bond of ill-will (byāpāda-kāyagantha), the bond of adherence to rules and observances (sīlabbataparāmāsa-kāyagantha), and the bond of dogmatic attachment to 'this is the truth' (idaṃsaccābhinivesa-kāyagantha). Attachment to one's own view is the bond of covetousness. Malice and displeasure toward the doctrines of others is the bond of ill-will. Clinging to one's own virtue, practice, or virtue and practice is the bond of adherence to rules and observances. Dogmatic attachment to one's own view is the bond of dogmatic attachment to 'this is the truth'. 'Vissajja' means letting go of the bonds, especially relinquishing them. Alternatively, it means destroying and abandoning the knots, bonds, attachments, and hindering fetters. For example, just as one might destroy a carriage, chariot, cart, or palanquin so that it can no longer be used, in the same way, abandoning the bonds such as covetousness and not taking them up again is called 'vissajja'. Alternatively, it means destroying and abandoning the knots, bonds, attachments, and hindering fetters. 'Muni' refers to wisdom. One who has transcended the net (of craving and views) is called a muni. 'In this' (idha) means in this view... in this world of humans. This is the meaning of the phrase 'vissajja ganthāni munīdha loke'.

"He is not a partisan when disputes arise" means: When disputes have clearly arisen and others are following the path of favoritism, hatred, fear, or delusion, the muni does not follow the path of favoritism, hatred, fear, or delusion. He does not go by the power of lust, hatred, delusion, pride, views, restlessness, doubt, or underlying tendencies. He is not led, carried away, or brought near by partisan qualities. This is called 'vivādajātesu na vaggasārī'.

"Calm among the unpeaceful, he is indifferent" means: 'Santo' (calm) means one who is calm because of the stilling of lust, hatred, and delusion. (etc.) Because of the stilling, calming, especially calming, extinguishing, and quenching of all unwholesome formations (akusala-abhisaṅkhāra), he is one who is calm, thoroughly calm, especially calm, peaceful, and stilled. This is the meaning of the word 'santo'. 'Asantesu' (among the unpeaceful) means among those who are not thoroughly stilled, not especially calm, not peaceful, and not stilled. This is the meaning of the word 'asantesu'. 'Upekkako' (indifferent) means I, who am endowed with the six-factored equanimity...
257: One who is peaceful, calmed, especially tranquil, quenched, and again tranquil due to the cooling, disappearance, and subsiding of the heat of defilements is called 'Santo' (the peaceful one). Being peaceful among those who are not peaceful, not calmed, not especially tranquil, not quenched, and not again tranquil is called 'Santo asantesu' (peaceful among the unpeaceful). That Arahant, being endowed with six-factored equanimity (chaḷaṅgupekkhā), upon seeing a form with the eye, is neither glad nor sad, but dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending. Upon hearing a sound with the ear... (etc.). Having a developed and peaceful mind, he awaits the time. This is the meaning of the phrase 'Santo asantesu upekkhako so' (He is peaceful and equanimous among the unpeaceful). Others, through the power of craving (taṇhā) and through the power of views (diṭṭhi), grasp, misapprehend, and attend [to things]. The Arahant is equanimous; he does not grasp, does not misapprehend, and does not attend [to them in that way]. This is the meaning of the phrase 'Anuggaho ugghahaṇanti manye' (Not grasping, considering grasping as grasping). Therefore, the Blessed One said: 'In this world, the sage abandons bonds and does not follow factions where disputes arise. He is peaceful and equanimous among the unpeaceful, not grasping, considering grasping as grasping.' Abandoning past taints and not creating new ones, he does not follow the path of desire and the like, nor is he one who holds dogmatic views. That wise one is well-released from speculative views; not blaming himself, he is not stained by craving and views in the world. 'Pubbāsave hitvā nave akubbaṃ' means: Past rūpa, vedanā, saññā, saṅkhāra, and viññāṇa are called 'pubbāsava' (past taints). Abandoning, discarding, completely relinquishing, removing, dispelling, destroying, and bringing to non-existence those defilements that could arise based on past formations is called 'pubbāsave hitvā' (abandoning past taints). 'Nave akubbaṃ' means: Present rūpa, vedanā, saññā, saṅkhāra, and viññāṇa are called 'nava' (new). Dwelling without producing desire, without producing affection, without producing lust, without generating, without manifesting, and without bringing into being [defilements] based on present formations is called 'pubbāsave hitvā nave akubbaṃ'. 'Na chandagū nopi nivissavādī' means: He does not go by the way of desire (chandāgati), he does not go by the way of hatred (dosāgati), he does not go by the way of delusion (mohāgati), he does not go by the way of fear (bhayāgati), he does not go by the power of lust...
258: (He) goes, but he does not go by the power of hatred, he does not go by the power of delusion, he does not go by the power of conceit, he does not go by the power of views, he does not go by the power of restlessness, he does not go by the power of doubt, he does not go by the power of latent tendencies. Since he is not led, not taken, not carried away, and not gathered by dhammas that form factions, he is called 'one who does not follow the path of desire' (na chandagū). 'Nor a dogmatic speaker' (nopi nivissavādī) means he does not speak dogmatically, saying, 'The world is eternal; this alone is the truth, all else is false.' ... (etc.) ... Because he does not speak dogmatically, saying, 'The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death; this alone is the truth, all else is false,' he is called 'one who does not follow the path of desire, nor is he a dogmatic speaker.' 'That wise one is fully released from views' (sa vippamutto diṭṭhigatehi dhīro) means that for him, the sixty-two speculative views have been abandoned, cut off, calmed, tranquilized, rendered incapable of arising, and burnt by the fire of knowledge. He is fully released and disconnected from speculative views, dwelling with a mind that has no boundaries. 'Wise one' (dhīro) refers to one who is wise, a pundit, possessed of wisdom, intelligent, knowledgeable, discerning, and sagacious. Therefore, it is said, 'That wise one is fully released from views.' 'He is not stained in the world, not blaming himself' (na limpati loke anattagarahī) means there are two kinds of stains (lepa): the stain of craving and the stain of views. ... (etc.) ... This is the stain of craving. ... (etc.) ... This is the stain of views. For him, the stain of craving has been abandoned, and the stain of views has been relinquished. Because the stain of craving is abandoned and the stain of views is relinquished, he is not stained in the world of woe, he is not stained in the human world, he is not stained in the celestial world, he is not stained in the world of aggregates, he is not stained in the world of elements, he is not stained in the world of sense-bases; he is not especially stained, not closely stained. Being unstained, especially unstained, and not closely stained, he is one who has emerged, is relinquished, fully released, disconnected, and dwells with a mind that has no boundaries. Therefore, it is said, 'He is not stained in the world.' 'Not blaming himself' (anattagarahī) means he reproaches himself for two reasons: because of what was done and because of what was not done. How does he reproach himself because of what was done and what was not done? He reproaches himself, saying, 'I have committed bodily misconduct; I have not practiced bodily good conduct.' 'I have committed verbal misconduct... (etc.) ... I have committed mental misconduct; I have committed the taking of life... (etc.) ... I have committed wrong view; I have not practiced right view.' Thus, he reproaches himself because of what was done and what was not done. Alternatively, he reproaches himself, saying, 'I am not one who fulfills the virtues,' 'I am one whose sense-doors are unguarded,' 'I am one who knows no moderation in eating,' 'I am one who is not devoted to wakefulness,' 'I am not endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension,' 'I have not yet developed (the foundations of mindfulness).'
259:
I have not developed the four foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna); I have not developed the four right efforts (sammappadhāna); I have not developed the four bases of power (iddhipāda); I have not developed the five faculties (indriya); I have not developed the five powers (bala); I have not developed the seven factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga); I have not developed the noble eightfold path (magga). I have not fully understood the truth of suffering (dukkha-sacca); I have not yet abandoned the truth of the cause of suffering (samudaya-sacca); I have not yet developed the truth of the path (magga-sacca); I have not yet realized the truth of the cessation of suffering (nirodha-sacca)—thus one reproaches oneself. One reproaches oneself because of what has been done and what has not been done. Thus, one is a self-reproacher. One who does not perform this act of self-reproach, does not produce it, does not generate it, does not bring it into being, does not manifest it, is one who does not reproach oneself—such a person is not smeared (not attached) in the world.

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
'Having abandoned former taints (āsavas) and not creating new ones, he does not follow desire, nor is he a proponent of fixed views. That wise one is completely released from views; he is not smeared in the world, being one who does not reproach himself.'

He stands having dismantled the army of Māra in all things (dhamma); he is not attached to whatever is seen, heard, or sensed (smelled, tasted, touched). That sage (muni) has laid down the burden, is released from defilements, is not conditioned (by views), has no delight (like worldlings), and has no craving.

'He stands having dismantled the army of Māra in all things; he is not attached to whatever is seen, heard, or sensed' means: It is called the army (senā) of Māra. Bodily misconduct is Māra's army; verbal misconduct is Māra's army; mental misconduct is Māra's army. Lust, hatred, delusion, anger, enmity, disparaging, rivalry, envy, stinginess, deceit, craftiness, obstinacy, impetuosity, conceit, arrogance, intoxication, negligence—all defilements, all misconducts, all distresses, all fevers, all torments, all unwholesome volitional formations (akusala-abhisaṅkhāra) are Māra's army.

As the Blessed One has said:
'Sensual pleasures are your first army; the second is called discontent (arati)... (and so on), the coward cannot conquer that army; only after conquering it does one obtain the happiness (of the Path and Fruit).'

When all Māra's armies and all opposing defilements have been conquered, defeated, broken, crushed, and turned away by the four Noble Paths, such a person is called 'one who has dismantled the army' (visenibhūto). He has dismantled the army regarding what is seen, heard, sensed, and cognized. Thus, 'He stands having dismantled the army of Māra in all things; he is not attached to whatever is seen, heard, or sensed.'
260:
That person is a sage (muni) who has laid down the burden and is released from defilements. As for burdens, there are three: the burden of the aggregates (khandhabhāra), the burden of defilements (kilesabhāra), and the burden of volitional formations (abhisaṅkhārabhāra). What is the burden of the aggregates? Materiality, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness at rebirth—these are the burden of the aggregates. What is the burden of defilements? Lust, hatred, delusion... all unwholesome volitional formations—these are the burden of defilements. What is the burden of volitional formations? Meritorious volitional formations (puññābhisaṅkhāra), demeritorious volitional formations (apuññābhisaṅkhāra), and imperturbable volitional formations (āneñjābhisaṅkhāra)—these are the burden of volitional formations. When the burden of the aggregates, the burden of defilements, and the burden of volitional formations are abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm-tree stump, made non-existent, and are of a nature not to arise in the future, that person is called one who has laid down the burden, one whose burden has fallen, one who has put down the burden, one who has well-deposited the burden, one who has relinquished the burden, one whose burden is stilled.

'Muni' refers to 'mona', and 'mona' is indeed knowledge (ñāṇa). That wisdom which is knowing in various ways, selecting, selecting in various ways, investigation of states (dhamma-vicaya), well-noting, close-noting, repeated close-noting, the state of being wise, the state of being skilled, the state of being subtle, wisdom that analyzes, thinking, examination, wisdom like the earth, weighing wisdom, wisdom that leads beings to their welfare, wisdom of insight, wisdom of clear comprehension, wisdom that goads, wisdom, the faculty of wisdom, the power of wisdom, the sword of wisdom, the palace of wisdom, the light of wisdom, the radiance of wisdom, the lamp of wisdom, the jewel of wisdom, non-delusion, investigation of states, right view. One endowed with such knowledge is a sage (muni), one who has attained sagehood (mona).

There are three types of sagehood (moneyya): bodily sagehood, verbal sagehood, and mental sagehood. What is bodily sagehood? The abandoning of the three kinds of bodily misconduct is bodily sagehood; the three kinds of bodily good conduct is bodily sagehood; knowledge having the body as its object is bodily sagehood; the full understanding of the body is bodily sagehood; the Path accompanied by full understanding is bodily sagehood; the abandoning of desire and lust for the body is bodily sagehood; the cessation of bodily formations and the attainment of the fourth jhāna is bodily sagehood. This is bodily sagehood.

What is verbal sagehood? The abandoning of the four kinds of verbal misconduct is verbal sagehood; the four kinds of verbal good conduct is verbal sagehood; knowledge having speech as its object is verbal sagehood; the full understanding of speech is verbal sagehood; the Path accompanied by full understanding is verbal sagehood; the abandoning of desire and lust for speech is verbal sagehood; the cessation of verbal formations and the attainment of the second jhāna is verbal sagehood. This is verbal sagehood.

What is mental sagehood? The abandoning of the three kinds of mental misconduct is mental sagehood; the three kinds of mental good conduct is mental sagehood; knowledge having the mind as its object is...
261:
What is mental sagacity (manomoneyya)? The knowledge that fully understands the mind is called mental sagacity. The Path accompanied by full understanding (pariññā) is called mental sagacity. The abandoning of desire and lust in the mind is called mental sagacity. The attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling (saññāvedayitanirodhasamāpatti), which is the cessation of mental formations (cittasaṅkhāra), is called mental sagacity. This is mental sagacity.

“One who is a sage in body (kāyamuni) because of abandoning bodily misconduct, a sage in speech (vācāmuni) because of abandoning verbal misconduct, a sage in mind (manomuni) because of abandoning mental misconduct, who is taintless (anāsava), endowed with sagacity, and has abandoned all unwholesome states—him they call a sage.

One who is a sage in body because of relinquishing bodily misconduct, a sage in speech because of relinquishing verbal misconduct, a sage in mind because of relinquishing mental misconduct, who is taintless, endowed with sagacity, and has washed away evil states through the Path-knowledge—him they call a sage.”

There are six types of sages endowed with these three qualities of sagacity: the householder sage (agāramuni), the homeless sage (anagāramuni), the sage in training (sekhamuni), the sage beyond training (asekhamuni), the Pacceka sage (paccekamuni), and the sage of sages (munimuni). What is a householder sage? Those householders who have seen the state (Nibbāna) and understood the Teaching—these are called householder sages. What is a homeless sage? Those who have gone forth (monks) who have seen the state and understood the Teaching—these are called homeless sages. The seven types of persons in training are called sages in training. Arahants are called sages beyond training. Paccekabuddhas are called Pacceka sages. The Tathāgatas, Arahants, the Fully Enlightened Buddhas, are called the sages of sages.

“Not by silence alone does one become a sage, if one is foolish and ignorant. But the wise man, as if holding a pair of scales, takes what is excellent and avoids evils. Because he avoids them, he is a sage. He who understands both worlds is therefore called a sage.

That sage who, having known the unrighteous and the righteous dhammas internally and externally in the whole world, and having crossed over the net of attachment such as lust, is honored by devas and humans.”

“Vippamutto” (Fully released) means the sage's mind is released from lust, especially released, well and especially released. From hatred... from delusion, the mind is released, especially released, well and especially released... from all unwholesome volitional formations (akusalābhisaṅkhāra), the mind is released, especially released, well and especially released. Thus, that sage who has laid down the burden (pannabhāro) is one who is fully released.

In the phrase “Na kappiyo nūparato na patthiyo,” “kappa” (construction/conceptualization) is of two kinds: the construction of craving (taṇhākappa) and the construction of views (diṭṭhikappa). That sage has abandoned the construction of craving and relinquished the construction of views. Because the construction of craving is abandoned and the construction of views is relinquished, he does not construct, produce, well-produce, or manifest either the construction of craving or the construction of views. This is the meaning of “Na kappiyo nūparato na patthiyo.” “Patthiyo” (longing/desiring) means all blind worldlings long for things. From the virtuous worldling up to the seven types of persons in training, they long and desire to reach the fruit of Arahantship not yet reached, to attain the Dhamma not yet attained, and to realize the Dhamma not yet realized. Arahants, however, have far avoided, especially avoided, and escaped from those longings.
262: Because the construction of views has been abandoned, and because the construction of craving or the construction of views has been relinquished, he does not construct, does not generate, does not fully generate, does not produce, and does not manifest the construction of craving or the construction of views; thus he is 'na kappiyo' (one who does not construct). 'Nūparato' means: all foolish worldlings are attached (to defilements). Starting from the noble worldlings (kalyāṇa-puthujjana), the seven trainees (sekha) delight in, especially delight in, and repeatedly delight in the Dhamma for the sake of reaching the unreached fruit of Arahantship, for the sake of attaining the unattained Dhamma, and for the sake of realizing the unrealized Dhamma. The Arahant is far removed from defilements, especially removed, and repeatedly removed; he has emerged, is relinquished, is fully liberated, is detached, and dwells with a mind that has made an end to boundaries. Therefore, he is 'na kappiyo nūparato'. 'Na patthiyo' means: longing (patthanā) is called craving (taṇhā). Whatever lust, intense passion... covetousness, greed, and unwholesome root exists—for whom this longing called craving is abandoned, cut off, calmed, stilled, and burnt by the fire of knowledge so that it is incapable of arising again, he is called 'na patthiyo' (one who has no longing). 'Bhagavā' is a title of respect. Furthermore, he is Bhagavā because he has broken greed; he is Bhagavā because he has broken hatred; he is Bhagavā because he has broken delusion; he is Bhagavā because he has broken conceit; he is Bhagavā because he has broken views; he is Bhagavā because he has broken the thorns of defilements; he is Bhagavā because he has broken all defilements. He is Bhagavā because he associates with, especially associates with, and extensively associates with the Jewel of Dhamma. He is Bhagavā because he has made an end to the three types of existence. He is Bhagavā because he has a developed body, developed virtue, developed mind, and developed wisdom. Or, he is Bhagavā because he associates with lodgings in forests and remote jungles that are quiet, with little noise, little sound, free from the movement of people, suitable for human seclusion, and appropriate for retreat. Or, he is Bhagavā because he receives the group of requisites such as robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicines for the sick. Or, he is Bhagavā because he possesses the taste of meaning (attha-rasa), the taste of Dhamma (dhamma-rasa), the taste of liberation (vimutti-rasa), higher virtue (adhisīla), higher mind (adhicitta), and higher wisdom (adhipaññā). Or, he is Bhagavā because he possesses the four jhanas, the four immeasurables (appamaññā), and the four formless attainments (arūpa-samāpatti). Or, he is Bhagavā because he possesses the eight deliverances (vimokkha), the eight bases of mastery (abhibhāyatana), and the nine successive attainments (anupubba-vihāra-samāpatti). Or, he is Bhagavā because he associates with the ten developments of perception (saññā-bhāvanā), the ten kasina attainments, the concentration of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānassati-samādhi), and the attainments of foulness (asubha-samāpatti). Or, he is Bhagavā because he possesses the four foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna), the four right efforts (sammappadhāna), the four bases of power (iddhipāda), the five faculties (indriya), the five powers (bala), the seven factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga), and the Noble Eightfold Path. Or, he is Bhagavā because he receives the group of the ten powers of a Tathāgata (tathāgata-bala), the four kinds of intrepidity (vesārajja), the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā), the six higher powers (abhiññā), and the six Buddha-dhammas. This name 'Bhagavā' was not given by his mother, nor by his father, nor by his brother, nor by his sister, nor by his friends and colleagues...
263:
It was not given by relatives, nor by recluses and brahmins, nor by deities. This name “Bhagavā” is a designation realized by the Blessed Buddhas at the foot of the Bodhi tree along with the attainment of omniscience (sabbaññutañāṇa); it is a designation signifying the end of liberation from defilements. Thus, “Bhagavā” means one who is not associated with defilements, one whose defilements have been stilled, and one who is without longing.

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
“That sage has broken the army in all dhammas, whatever is seen, heard, or sensed (muta);
That sage has laid down the burden, is fully released;
He is not associated with defilements, his defilements are stilled, and he is without longing.”

## The Exposition of the Mahāviyūha Sutta, the thirteenth, is finished.

## 14. Exposition of the Tuvaṭṭaka Sutta

Furthermore, I shall now speak the exposition of the Tuvaṭṭaka Sutta which follows in sequence:

“I ask you, Kinsman of the Sun (Ādiccabandhu), about seclusion and the state of peace, O Great Seer (Mahesi). Seeing what does a bhikkhu become extinguished (nibbāti), not clinging to anything in the world?”

In the phrase “I ask you, Kinsman of the Sun,” there are three types of questions (pucchā): the question for illuminating the unseen (adiṭṭhajotanā pucchā), the question for comparing the seen (diṭṭhasaṃsandanā pucchā), and the question for cutting off doubt (vimaticchedanā pucchā).

What is the question for illuminating the unseen? When a characteristic is naturally unknown, unseen, unweighed, undecided, unmanifested, and not analyzed, one asks a question for the sake of knowing, seeing, weighing, deciding, and manifesting that characteristic. This is called the question for illuminating the unseen.

What is the question for comparing the seen? When a characteristic is naturally known, seen, weighed, decided, manifested, and analyzed, one asks a question for the sake of comparing it with other wise people. This is called the question for comparing the seen.

What is the question for cutting off doubt? When one naturally falls into doubt, falls into uncertainty, and becomes double-minded, thinking, “Is it thus? Is it not thus? What could it be? How could it be?” he asks a question for the sake of cutting off that doubt. This is called the question for cutting off doubt. These are the three types of questions.

There are also another three types of questions: questions asked by humans (manussa pucchā), questions asked by non-humans such as Nāgas and Garuḷas (amanussa pucchā), and questions asked by a created Buddha (nimmita pucchā). What is the question asked by humans? Humans approach the Blessed One and ask questions. Monks, nuns, laymen, laywomen, kings, nobles, brahmins, merchants, and commoners ask questions.
264:
There are another three types of questions (pucchā): questions asked by humans, questions asked by non-humans, and questions asked by a created Buddha-form. What are the questions asked by humans? Humans approach the Blessed One and ask a question. Monks ask, nuns ask, male lay followers ask, female lay followers ask, kings ask, nobles ask, brahmins ask, merchants ask, workers ask, householders ask, and renunciants ask. This is called 'questions asked by humans' (manussa-pucchā).

What are the questions asked by non-humans? Non-humans approach the Blessed One and ask a question. Nagas ask, Supannas ask, Yakkhas ask, Asuras ask, Gandhabba deities ask, the Four Great Kings ask, Indras ask, Brahmas ask, and goddesses ask. This is called 'questions asked by non-humans' (amanussa-pucchā).

What are the questions asked by a created Buddha-form? The Blessed One creates a mind-made form, complete in all its limbs and parts, with no faculty missing. That created form approaches the Blessed One and asks a question, and the Blessed One answers that created form. This is called 'questions asked by a created Buddha-form' (nimmita-pucchā). These are the three types of questions.

There are another three types of questions: questions asked for one's own benefit, questions asked for the benefit of others, and questions asked for the benefit of both. There are another three types of questions: questions asked for benefit in the present life, questions asked for benefit in the future life, and questions asked for the ultimate benefit. There are another three types of questions: questions asked for blameless benefit, questions asked for benefit free from defilements, and questions asked for pure benefit. There are another three types of questions: questions concerning the past, questions concerning the future, and questions concerning the present. There are another three types of questions: questions concerning internal states, questions concerning external states, and questions concerning both internal and external states. There are another three types of questions: questions concerning wholesome states, questions concerning unwholesome states, and questions concerning indeterminate states. There are another three types of questions: questions concerning the aggregates, questions concerning the elements, and questions concerning the bases. There are another three types of questions: questions concerning the foundations of mindfulness, questions concerning the right efforts, and questions concerning the bases of power. There are another three types of questions: questions concerning the faculties, questions concerning the powers, and questions concerning the factors of enlightenment. There are another three types of questions: questions concerning the path, questions concerning the fruit, and questions concerning Nibbāna.

'I ask you' (pucchāmi taṃ) means: I ask you, I entreat you, I invite you, I show devotion to you, [saying] 'Please tell me.' 'Kinsman of the Sun' (ādiccabandhu): The sun is called Ādicca. The sun is of the Gotama lineage, and the Blessed One is also of the Gotama lineage. The Blessed One is a kinsman of the sun by lineage. Therefore, the Buddha is called 'Kinsman of the Sun.' 'I ask you, O Kinsman of the Sun' (pucchāmi taṃ ādiccabandhu) means: I ask you, the Blessed One, who is a kinsman of the sun.

In the phrase 'Seclusion, the state of peace, and the Great Seeker' (vivekaṃ santipadañca mahesī), there are three types of seclusion: physical seclusion (kāya-viveka), mental seclusion (citta-viveka), and seclusion from acquisitions (upadhi-viveka). What is physical seclusion?
265:
In this Dispensation, a monk resorts to a secluded dwelling: a forest, the foot of a tree, a mountain, a glen, a hillside cave, a cemetery, a woodland grove, the open air, or a heap of straw; he dwells with a secluded body. That monk goes alone, stands alone, sits alone, lies down alone, enters the village for alms alone, returns alone, sits in private alone, practices walking meditation alone, and wanders, dwells, moves, proceeds, protects, maintains, and supports himself alone—this is called physical seclusion (kāya-viveka).

What is mental seclusion (citta-viveka)? For one who has attained the first jhāna, the mind is secluded from the hindrances. For one who has attained the second jhāna, the mind is secluded from applied and sustained thought. For one who has attained the third jhāna, the mind is secluded from rapture. For one who has attained the fourth jhāna, the mind is secluded from pleasure and pain. For one who has attained the sphere of infinite space, the mind is secluded from the perception of form, the perception of sensory impact, and the perception of diversity. For one who has attained the sphere of infinite consciousness, the mind is secluded from the perception of the sphere of infinite space. For one who has attained the sphere of nothingness, the mind is secluded from the perception of the sphere of infinite consciousness. For one who has attained the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the mind is secluded from the perception of the sphere of nothingness.

For a Stream-enterer, the mind is secluded from self-identity view, doubt, attachment to rites and rituals, the latent tendency of views, the latent tendency of doubt, and from the defilements associated with them. For a Once-returner, the mind is secluded from the gross fetters of sensual lust and aversion, the gross latent tendencies of sensual lust and aversion, and from the defilements associated with them. For a Non-returner, the mind is secluded from the subtle fetters of sensual lust and aversion, the subtle latent tendencies of sensual lust and aversion, and from the defilements associated with them. For an Arahant, the mind is secluded from lust for form, lust for the formless, conceit, restlessness, ignorance, the latent tendency of conceit, the latent tendency of lust for existence, the latent tendency of ignorance, from the defilements associated with them, and from all external signs—this is called mental seclusion (citta-viveka).

What is seclusion from acquisitions (upadhi-viveka)? Defilements, aggregates, and volitional formations are called acquisitions (upadhi). The deathless Nibbāna is called seclusion from acquisitions. That Nibbāna which is the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, and cessation—this is called seclusion from acquisitions. Physical seclusion is for those with secluded bodies who delight in renunciation; mental seclusion is for those with purified minds who have reached supreme purity; seclusion from acquisitions...
266:
...is for those persons who are free from acquisitions and have reached the unconditioned. Peace (santi) is, in one sense, that very deathless Nibbāna which has the characteristic of peace and is the cause of peace. That which is the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, and the escape from craving is Nibbāna. For this was said by the Blessed One: 'This is peaceful, this is sublime, namely, the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna.' In another sense, there are the states that lead to the attainment of peace, to the touch of peace, and to the realization of peace. They are as follows: the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the Noble Eightfold Path. These are called the cause of peace, the place of protection, the place of shelter, the place of refuge, the place of safety, the unshakable state, the deathless state, and the state of Nibbāna.

'Great Seeker' (Mahesī) refers to the Blessed One. He is called Mahesī because he sought, searched for, and thoroughly investigated the great aggregate of virtue, the great aggregate of concentration, the great aggregate of wisdom, the great aggregate of liberation, and the great aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation. He is called Mahesī because he sought, searched for, and thoroughly investigated the piercing of the great mass of darkness (ignorance), the breaking of the great perversion, the pulling out of the great dart of craving, the untying of the great knot of views, the lowering of the great banner of conceit, the stilling of the great volitional formations, the crossing of the great flood, the laying down of the great burden, the cutting off of the great round of rebirth, the extinguishing of the great fever, the calming of the great heat, and the raising of the great banner of the Dhamma. He is called Mahesī because he sought, searched for, and thoroughly investigated the great foundations of mindfulness, the great right efforts, the great bases of power, the great faculties, the great powers, the great factors of enlightenment, the great Noble Eightfold Path, and the great ultimate goal, the deathless Nibbāna. Alternatively, he is called Mahesī because he is sought, searched for, and thoroughly investigated by beings of great power, asking: 'Where is the Buddha? Where is the Blessed One? Where is the God of gods? Where is the Bull among men?' This is the meaning of the term Mahesī, who seeks seclusion and the state of peace.

'How, having seen, does a monk attain peace?' means: how, having seen, having observed, having weighed, having investigated, and having made clear, does he extinguish his own greed, extinguish hatred, extinguish delusion, anger... resentment, disparaging, domineering, envy, stinginess, deceit, craftiness, obstinacy, impetuosity, conceit, arrogance, intoxication, heedlessness, all defilements, all misconduct, all distress, all fever, all...
267:
...He extinguishes all defilements, all misconduct, all anxieties, all fevers, and all unwholesome volitional formations; he calms them, settles them, specifically extinguishes them, and cools them. A 'bhikkhu' refers to either a noble worldling (puthujjana-kalyāṇaka) or a trainee (sekha). This is the explanation of the phrase: 'Having seen what does a bhikkhu become cooled?'

'Without clinging to anything in the world' means living without clinging, without grasping, without misapprehending, and without being intent upon [anything] by way of the four types of clinging. 'In the world' refers to the world of misery, the human world, the deva world, the world of aggregates, the world of elements, and the world of bases. 'Anything' refers to any form, feeling, perception, volitional formations, or consciousness. This is the meaning of 'without clinging to anything in the world.'

Therefore, that created Buddha (nimmitabuddha) asked:
'I ask you, O Kinsman of the Sun, Great Seer, about seclusion and the state of peace. Having seen what does a bhikkhu become cooled, not clinging to anything in the world?'

[The Blessed One said:] 'Having understood the root of conceptual proliferation, let him suppress the entire conceit of "I am" with wisdom. Whatever cravings there are within, he should always train mindfully to remove them.'

'Having understood the root of conceptual proliferation... let him suppress the entire conceit of "I am" with wisdom' means: Conceptual proliferations (papañca) themselves are called 'conceptual proliferation-reckonings' (papañca-saṅkhā). They are the conceptual proliferation-reckonings of craving and the conceptual proliferation-reckonings of views. What is the root of the conceptual proliferation of craving? Ignorance is the root, unwise attention is the root, 'I am' conceit is the root, shamelessness is the root, fearlessness of wrongdoing is the root, and restlessness is the root—this is the root of the conceptual proliferation of craving. What is the root of the conceptual proliferation of views? Ignorance is the root, unwise attention is the root, 'I am' conceit is the root, shamelessness (ahirika) is the root, fearlessness of wrongdoing (anottappa) is the root, and restlessness (uddhacca) is the root—this is the root of the conceptual proliferation of views.

'Bhagavā' (Blessed One) is a designation of respect. Furthermore, he is called 'Bhagavā' because he has broken greed (bhaggarāga), he has broken hatred (bhaggadosa), he has broken delusion (bhaggamoha), he has broken conceit (bhaggamāna), he has broken views (bhaggadiṭṭhi), he has broken the thorns [of defilements] (bhaggakaṇṭaka), and he has broken all defilements (bhaggakilesa). He is called 'Bhagavā' because he associates with, distinguishes, and classifies the Dhamma-treasure. He is called 'Bhagavā' because he is the ender of existences. He is called 'Bhagavā' because he has a developed body, developed virtue, developed mind, and developed wisdom. Or else, he is called 'Bhagavā' because he is the possessor [of qualities or requisites].
268:
The Blessed One is called 'Bhagavā' because he frequents secluded forest-thickets and lodgings that are quiet, free from noise, free from the wind of human traffic, suitable for human secrecy, and appropriate for seclusion. Alternatively, he is called 'Bhagavā' because he possesses the requisites of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal supports for the sick. Alternatively, he is called 'Bhagavā' because he possesses the taste of the meaning, the taste of the Dhamma, the taste of liberation, higher virtue, higher mind, and higher wisdom. Alternatively, he is called 'Bhagavā' because he distinguishes the four jhānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments. Alternatively, he is called 'Bhagavā' because he distinguishes the eight liberations, the eight bases of transcendence, and the nine successive attainments. Alternatively, he is called 'Bhagavā' because he distinguishes the ten perceptions, the ten kasina attainments, mindfulness of breathing concentration, and the foulness attainments. Alternatively, he is called 'Bhagavā' because he distinguishes the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the Noble Eightfold Path. Alternatively, he is called 'Bhagavā' because he is the master of the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four intrepidities, the four analytical insights, the six superknowledges, and the six Buddha-dhamma.

This name 'Bhagavā' was not given by his mother, nor by his father, nor by his brothers, nor by his sisters, nor by his friends and colleagues, nor by his relatives and kinsmen, nor by recluses and brahmins, nor by deities. This name 'Bhagavā' is a realized designation (sacchikā paññatti) of the Blessed Buddhas, attained at the root of the Bodhi tree along with the acquisition of omniscience at the end of the path of Arahantship. 'Having understood the root of conceptual proliferation, the Blessed One suppresses the entire conceit of "I am" with wisdom.'

What is called 'mantā' is wisdom (paññā). That wisdom, knowing... (etc.) ... non-delusion, investigation of states, right view. 'Asmi' (I am) refers to the conceit 'I am,' the desire 'I am,' and the underlying tendency 'I am' regarding form... regarding feeling... regarding perception... regarding volitional formations... regarding consciousness. 'Having understood the root of conceptual proliferation, the Blessed One suppresses the entire conceit of "I am" with wisdom.' Having understood the root of conceptual proliferation and the 'I am' conceit with wisdom, one should suppress, specifically suppress, cease, calm, bring to an end, and settle everything. Therefore, it is said: 'Having understood the root of conceptual proliferation, the Blessed One suppresses the entire conceit of "I am" with wisdom.'

'Whatever cravings there are within'—'Whatever' (yā kāci) is an inclusive term for everything in every way, without exception, without remainder. 'Craving' (taṇhā) refers to craving for forms... (etc.) ... craving for mental objects. 'Within' (ajjhattaṃ) refers to that craving arising within one's own continuity.
269:
It is called 'internal' (ajjhatta) because it arises within one's own continuity, or because the mind is called 'internal' (ajjhattika). There is that mind (citta), mentation (mano), ideation (mānasa), heart (hadaya), luminosity (paṇḍara), mind (mano), mind-base (manāyatana), mind-faculty (manindriya), consciousness (viññāṇa), the aggregate of consciousness (viññāṇakkhandha), and the corresponding mind-consciousness element (manoviññāṇadhātu). That craving is also called 'internal' because it arises with the mind, is born with the mind, is blended with the mind, is associated with the mind, has the same arising, the same cessation, the same physical basis, and the same object as the mind. Thus it is said: "Whatever craving is internal" (yā kāci taṇhā ajjhattaṃ).

In the passage, "For the removal of those cravings, one should always train being mindful," the word "always" (sadā) means at all times, at all times, for all time, every day, perpetually, constantly, continuously, without interruption, in succession, like the waves of water, together with an uninterrupted continuity, touching, before the meal, after the meal, in the first watch, in the middle watch, in the last watch, during the dark fortnight, during the bright fortnight, in the rainy season, in the winter, in the summer, in the first stage of life, in the middle stage of life, and in the last stage of life.

"Mindful" (sato) means being mindful through four reasons: one is mindful while developing the foundation of mindfulness of contemplation of the body in the body; one is mindful while developing... [pe] ...in feelings... [pe] ...in the mind... [pe] ...one is mindful while developing the foundation of mindfulness of contemplation of phenomena in phenomena. One is also mindful through another four reasons: one is mindful because of avoiding the lack of mindfulness, one is mindful because of having performed the states to be performed with mindfulness, one is mindful because of having destroyed the states that are the opposites of mindfulness, and one is mindful because of not being confused regarding the objects of meditation which are the causes of mindfulness. One is also mindful through another four reasons: because of being endowed with mindfulness, because of having mastery over mindfulness, because of proficiency in mindfulness, and because of non-regression from mindfulness. One is also mindful through another four reasons: because of being steadfast, because of being peaceful, because of being unified, and because of being endowed with the peaceful Dhamma. One is mindful through the recollection of the Buddha (buddhānussati), the recollection of the Dhamma, the recollection of the Saṅgha, the recollection of virtue, the recollection of generosity, the recollection of devas, mindfulness of breathing, mindfulness of death, mindfulness of the body, and the recollection of peace. That which is mindfulness, constant recollection, repeated recollection, mindfulness, the state of bearing in mind, the state of non-drifting, the state of non-forgetfulness, mindfulness, the faculty of mindfulness, the power of mindfulness, right mindfulness, the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness, the one-way path—this is called mindfulness (sati). One who is possessed of, fully possessed of, attained to, fully attained to, endowed with, fully endowed with, and complete with this mindfulness is called "mindful" (sato).

"Should train" (sikkhe) refers to the three trainings: the training in higher virtue (adhisīla-sikkhā), the training in higher mind (adhicitta-sikkhā), and the training in higher wisdom (adhipaññā-sikkhā). What is the training in higher virtue? Here, a monk is virtuous, he dwells restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha, he is possessed of proper conduct and resort, and in the slightest faults...
270:
...seeing danger in the slightest faults, he trains by undertaking the rules of training. The small group of virtue, the large group of virtue, the foundation, the beginning, the conduct, the restraint, the control, the entrance, the foremost of all wholesome states for the sake of attainment—this is called the training in higher virtue (adhisīla-sikkhā).

What is the training in higher mind (adhicitta-sikkhā)? Here, a monk, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and evaluation, with joy and happiness born of seclusion. With the subsiding of thought and evaluation, he enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and singleness of mind, is without thought and evaluation, and has joy and happiness born of concentration. With the fading away as well of joy, he dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending, and experiences happiness with the body; he enters and dwells in the third jhāna of which the Noble Ones declare: 'He is equanimous, mindful, and dwells happily.' With the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, he enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which has neither-pain-nor-pleasure and has purity of mindfulness due to equanimity. This is called the training in higher mind.

What is the training in higher wisdom (adhipaññā-sikkhā)? Here, a monk is wise, possessed of wisdom regarding the arising and passing away [of phenomena], which is noble and penetrative, and leads to the complete destruction of suffering. He understands as it really is: 'This is suffering'; he understands as it really is: 'This is the origin of suffering'; he understands as it really is: 'This is the cessation of suffering'; he understands as it really is: 'This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering.' He understands as it really is: 'These are the taints (āsavas)'; he understands as it really is: 'This is the origin of the taints'; he understands as it really is: 'This is the cessation of the taints'; he understands as it really is: 'This is the way leading to the cessation of the taints.' This is called the training in higher wisdom.

"For the removal of those cravings, one should always train being mindful" means that for the sake of the removal, the total removal, the abandoning, the subsiding, the relinquishing, and the further calming of those cravings, one should train in higher virtue, one should train in higher mind, and one should train in higher wisdom. One should train while reflecting on these three trainings, while knowing them, while seeing them, while reviewing them, while resolving the mind, while being convinced through faith, while exerting energy, while establishing mindfulness, while concentrating the mind, while knowing through wisdom, while fully knowing what is to be fully known, while comprehending what is to be comprehended, while abandoning what is to be abandoned, and while developing what is to be developed.
271: One should train, practice, conduct oneself well, and undertake the practice while realizing the Dhamma that should be realized. One should train with constant mindfulness to abandon those cravings. Therefore, the Blessed One said: 'Having discerned with wisdom the conceit "I am," which is the root of conceptual proliferation (pappañca), one should restrain all such conceit. One should train with constant mindfulness to abandon all cravings that arise within.' Whether internally or externally, whatever Dhamma one may specially know, one should not make a stronghold of pride because of that knowledge; for such pride is not called peace by the virtuous. 'Whatever Dhamma one may specially know internally' means: one should know one's own qualities, whether they are wholesome (kusala) or indeterminate (abyākata). What are one's own qualities? If one is a monk ordained from a noble family, or from a family of great wealth, or from a family of excellent wealth; if one is famous and renowned among householders and monastics; if one is a recipient of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites; if one is a Suttantika (expert in Suttas), a Vinayadhara (expert in Vinaya), a Dhammakathika (teacher of Dhamma), a forest-dweller (āraññika), an alms-food eater (piṇḍapātika), a rag-robe wearer (paṃsukūlika), a triple-robe wearer (tecīvarika), a house-to-house alms-seeker (sapadānacārika), one who eats at one sitting (khalupacchābhattika), a sitter (nesajjika), one who uses whatever seat is assigned (yathāsanthatika); if one is an attainer of the first jhāna, the second jhāna, the third jhāna, or the fourth jhāna; if one is an attainer of the sphere of infinite space (ākāsānañcāyatana), the sphere of infinite consciousness (viññāṇañcāyatana), the sphere of nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatana), or the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (nevasaññānāsaññāyatana)—these are called one's own qualities. One should know, fully know, distinctly know, repeatedly know, and penetrate with knowledge one's own qualities. This is the meaning of 'Whatever Dhamma one may specially know internally.' 'Or externally' means: if those qualities belong to one's preceptor (upajjhāya) or teacher (ācariya). This is the meaning of 'Or externally.'
272: 'Na tena thāmaṃ kubbetha' means: one should not make a stronghold of pride, should not be stubborn, should not be arrogant, should not be haughty, and should not be conceited because of one's own qualities or the qualities of others. One should not let pride arise because of those qualities, nor should one become stiff, obstinate, or hold one's head high because of them. This is the meaning of 'Na tena thāmaṃ kubbetha.' 'Na hi sā nibbuti sataṃ vuttā' means: the peaceful ones, the virtuous ones whose defilements are extinguished—the Buddhas, the disciples of the Buddha, and the Paccekabuddhas—do not call that (pride) peace (Nibbāna). They do not declare, teach, prescribe, establish, open, analyze, clarify, or manifest it as such. This is the meaning of 'Na hi sā nibbuti sataṃ vuttā.' Therefore, the Blessed One said: 'Whether internally or externally, whatever Dhamma one may know, one should not make a stronghold of pride because of that; for such pride is not called peace by the virtuous. One should not think oneself superior because of that, nor should one think oneself inferior or equal. Though touched by many conditions, one should not remain thinking of oneself in various ways.' 'Seyyo na tena maññeyya' means: one should not give rise to excessive pride thinking 'I am superior' due to birth (jāti), lineage (gotta), family status (kolaputtiya), beauty (vaṇṇapokkharatā), wealth (dhana), study (ajjhayana), occupation (kammāyatana), craft (sippāyatana), science (vijjāṭṭhāna), knowledge (suta), eloquence (paṭibhāna), or any other grounds. This is the meaning of 'Seyyo na tena maññeyya.' 'Nīceyya atha vāpi sarikkho' means: one should not give rise to the conceit of inferiority thinking 'I am low' due to birth, lineage, etc. Nor should one give rise to pride thinking 'I am equal' due to birth, lineage, family status, beauty, wealth, study, occupation, craft, science, knowledge, eloquence, or any other grounds. This is the meaning of 'Nīceyya atha vāpi sarikkho.' 'Phuṭṭho anekarūpehi' means: one who is touched, oppressed, beset, or endowed with various and diverse conditions. This is the meaning of 'Phuṭṭho anekarūpehi.'
273:
One's self is called 'ātuma' (attā). 'One should not stand imagining oneself, bringing oneself into discrimination' is the meaning of 'nātumaṃ vikappayaṃ tiṭṭhe'.

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
'Though touched by various objects, one should not think "I am superior" because of that touch, nor should one think "I am inferior," nor should one think "I am equal." One should not stand imagining oneself.'

A bhikkhu should calm [defilements] only within himself; he should not seek peace from another source. For one who is calmed within himself, there is no self-view; how then could there be a view of annihilation?

'He should calm only within himself' means: he should calm lust (rāga) within himself, he should calm hatred (dosa), he should calm delusion (moha), anger (kodha), ill-will (upanāha), disparaging (makkha), domineering (paḷāsa), envy (issā), stinginess (macchariya), deceit (māyā), fraud (sāṭheyya), obstinacy (thambha), impetuosity (sārambha), conceit (māna), arrogance (atimāna), intoxication (mada), and negligence (pamāda). He should calm, settle, quieten, extinguish, and allay all defilements, all misconduct, all distress, all fever, all torment, and all unwholesome volitional formations (akusala-abhisaṅkhāra). This is the meaning of 'ajjhattamevūpasame'.

'A bhikkhu should not seek peace from another source' means: he should not seek, search for, or look for peace, tranquility, quietude, liberation (nibbāna), or stillness through other impure practices, through wrong practice, through a path that does not lead out of saṃsāra, or by excluding the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna), excluding the right efforts (sammappadhāna), excluding the bases of power (iddhipāda), excluding the faculties (indriya), excluding the powers (bala), excluding the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga), or excluding the Noble Eightfold Path. This is the meaning of 'na aññato bhikkhu santimeseyya'.

'For one who is calmed within himself' means: for one whose lust is calmed within himself, whose hatred is calmed, whose delusion is calmed... for one whose all unwholesome volitional formations are calmed, settled, quietened, extinguished, and allayed. This is the meaning of 'ajjhattaṃ upasantassa'.

'There is no self-view; how then could there be a view of annihilation?' means: 'natthi' (there is not) is a term of rejection. 'Attā' means there is no self-view (attadiṭṭhi). 'Nirattā' means there is no annihilation-view (ucchedadiṭṭhi). 'Attā' means there is nothing to be grasped. 'Nirattā' means there is nothing to be discarded. For whom there is something to be grasped, for him there is something to be discarded. That Arahant, who has well transcended both grasping and discarding, and has transcended both increase and decrease, has lived the noble life and has completed the training. For that Arahant, there is no further rebirth, which is called the saṃsāra of birth and death. This is the meaning of the phrase 'natthi attā kuto nirattā vā'. Therefore, the Blessed One said: 'A bhikkhu should calm only within himself; he should not seek peace from another source. For one who is calmed within himself, there is no self-view; how then could there be a view of annihilation?'

Just as in the middle of the ocean no wave arises and it stays still and unmoving, so too the bhikkhu who is free from the dust of defilements should stay still and unmoving. The bhikkhu should not create any proliferation (ussada) such as lust in any object.

'In the middle of the ocean no wave arises and it stays still' means: the ocean is eighty-four thousand yojanas deep. The water in the lower forty thousand yojanas is stirred by fish and turtles. The water in the upper forty thousand yojanas is stirred by winds. But the water in the middle forty thousand yojanas is not stirred, is especially not stirred, does not move, and being unmoving, it is repeatedly not stirred, well-unstirred...
274:
The Arahant, who has fully transcended grasping, clinging, and letting go, and has surpassed growth and decay, has nothing left to abandon (as there is no self to be taken). That Arahant has lived the noble life (ariyavāsa), has practiced the conduct... (pe)... the cycle of birth and death called saṃsāra, and rebirth no longer exists for him. Therefore, it means: "There is no self; how could there be anything to be discarded (nirattā)?"

For this reason, the Blessed One said:
"A bhikkhu should still the defilements within himself; he should not seek peace from any other external source. For one who is stilled within, there is no self; how could there be anything to be discarded (nirattā)? Just as in the middle of the ocean, no wave arises and it remains still; so too, the bhikkhu who is still and free from craving (aneja) should not create any protuberance (ussada) anywhere."

"Just as in the middle of the ocean, no wave arises and it remains still" means: The ocean is eighty-four thousand yojanas deep. The water in the lower forty thousand yojanas is agitated by fish and turtles. The water in the upper forty thousand yojanas is agitated by winds. But the water in the middle forty thousand yojanas does not shake, does not tremble, does not move, does not quiver, does not vibrate, does not stir. It is unmoving, untouched, unshaken, undisturbed, unwavering, and stilled; there, no wave arises, and the ocean remains still. Thus, it means "Just as in the middle of the ocean, no wave arises and it remains still."

Alternatively, between the seven mountains such as Mount Yugandhara, there are the seven Sīdantara Great Oceans. There, the water does not shake, does not tremble, does not move, does not quiver, does not vibrate, does not stir. It is unmoving, untouched, unshaken, undisturbed, unwavering, and stilled; there, no wave arises, and the ocean remains still. Thus also, it means "Just as in the middle of the ocean, no wave arises and it remains still."

In the phrase "so too, the bhikkhu who is still and free from craving (aneja)": "So too" (evaṃ) completes the simile. "Still" (ṭhito) means he does not shake in the face of gain, nor in the face of loss; he does not shake in the face of fame, nor in the face of obscurity; he does not shake in the face of praise, nor in the face of blame; he does not shake in the face of pleasure, nor in the face of pain; he does not move, does not shake, does not quiver, does not vibrate, does not stir—thus he is "still."

Regarding "free from craving" (anejassa): "Ejā" is a term for craving (taṇhā). For whom that craving called ejā—which is lust (rāga), intense lust... (pe)... covetousness (abhijjhā), the unwholesome root of greed (lobha)—has been abandoned, cut off, stilled, repeatedly stilled, made incapable of arising again, and burnt by the fire of knowledge (ñāṇa), he is called "aneja" (one free from craving). Because craving has been abandoned, he is called aneja. That person called aneja does not shake, move, or tremble in the face of gain, loss, fame, obscurity, praise, blame, pleasure, or pain.

In the phrase "the bhikkhu should not create any protuberance (ussada) anywhere": "Protuberance" (ussada) refers to the seven protuberances (sattussada)—the protuberance of lust, the protuberance of hatred, the protuberance of delusion, the protuberance of conceit, the protuberance of views, the protuberance of defilements, and the protuberance of kamma. He should not create, generate, produce, bring into being, or manifest these.
275:
Lust (rāga), intense lust... (pe)... covetousness (abhijjhā), greed (lobha) is the unwholesome root. For whom that craving called ejā has been abandoned, cut off at the root, stilled, repeatedly stilled, made incapable of arising again, and burnt by the fire of knowledge, he is called "aneja" (one without craving). Because craving has been abandoned, that person called aneja does not shake in the face of gain, nor in the face of loss; he does not shake in the face of fame, nor in the face of obscurity; he does not shake in the face of praise, nor in the face of blame; he does not shake in the face of pleasure, nor in the face of pain; he does not move, does not shake, does not quiver, does not vibrate. Such is the state of the aneja individual.

In the phrase "the bhikkhu should not create any protuberance (ussada) anywhere": "Protuberance" (ussada) refers to the seven protuberances (sattussada)—the protuberance of lust, the protuberance of hatred, the protuberance of delusion, the protuberance of conceit, the protuberance of views, the protuberance of defilements, and the protuberance of kamma. He should not create, generate, produce, bring into being, or manifest these. "Anywhere" (kuhiñci) means in any internal (ajjhatta), external (bahiddhā), or both internal and external (ajjhatta-bahiddhā) sense. Thus, the bhikkhu should not create any protuberance anywhere.

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
"Just as in the middle of the ocean, no wave arises and it remains still;
So too, the bhikkhu who is still and free from craving should not create any protuberance anywhere."

"O Blessed One with open eyes, you have proclaimed the Dhamma that is self-realized and leads to the removal of dangers.
Venerable Sir, please tell us the practice (paṭipadā), the Pātimokkha restraint, or else concentration (samādhi)."

In the phrase "akittayī vivaṭacakkhu": "Akittayī" means proclaimed, explained in detail, taught, designated, made manifest, opened up, analyzed, clarified, and shown. "Vivaṭacakkhu" means the Blessed One has eyes that are unobstructed by the five types of vision: he has unobstructed vision through the physical eye (maṃsacakkhu), the divine eye (dibbacakkhu), the wisdom eye (paññācakkhu), the Buddha eye (buddhacakkhu), and the all-seeing eye (samantacakkhu).

How does the Blessed One have unobstructed vision through the physical eye (maṃsacakkhu)? In the Blessed One's physical eye, there are five colors. They are: blue, yellow, red...
276: The Blessed One possesses five colors: blue, yellow, red, black, and white. The eyelashes of the Blessed One also possess these five colors. The place where the eyelashes are situated is like the umā flower, beautifully blue, pleasing, and lovely to behold. Beside those eyelashes, it is like the kaṇṇikāra flower, beautifully yellow, like the color of gold, pleasing, and lovely to behold. The two corners of the Blessed One's eyes are like the indagopaka, beautifully red, pleasing, and lovely to behold. In the middle, it is like collyrium, not coarse but smooth, beautifully black, pleasing, and lovely to behold. Around that black part, it is like the morning star (osadhī-tārakā), beautifully white, pure, and bright, pleasing, and lovely to behold. With this natural physical eye (māṃsacakkhu), which is part of his physical form and produced by the fruit of his previous meritorious deeds, the Blessed One sees for a league (yojana) all around, both by day and by night. Even in the fourfold darkness—when the sun has set, on the Uposatha day of the dark fortnight, in a dense forest, and when a great dark rain cloud (kāḷamegha) has risen—even in such fourfold darkness, he sees for a league all around. There are no walls, doors, ramparts, mountains, bushes, or creepers that can obstruct his vision of forms. If one were to mark a single sesame seed and throw it into a cartload of sesame, he could pick out that very same sesame seed. Thus is the Blessed One's natural physical eye pure. In this way, the Blessed One is one with 'opened eyes' (vivaṭacakkhu) even with the physical eye. How is the Blessed One one with 'opened eyes' through the divine eye (dibbacakkhu)? With the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, the Blessed One sees beings passing away and being reborn—lowly and excellent, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate. He understands how beings pass on according to their kamma: 'Friends, these beings were endowed with misconduct of body, speech, and mind; they were revilers of the Noble Ones, held wrong views, and undertook actions based on wrong views. With the breakup of the body, after death, they have been reborn in a state of loss, a bad destination, the nether world, even in hell. But these beings were endowed with good conduct of body, speech, and mind; they did not revile the Noble Ones, held right views, and undertook actions based on right views. With the breakup of the body, after death, they have been reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world...'
277: '...they have been reborn.' Thus, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, he sees beings passing away and being reborn—lowly and excellent, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate. He understands how beings pass on according to their kamma. If the Blessed One so desires, he can see one world system (lokadhātu), two world systems, three world systems, four world systems, five world systems, ten world systems, twenty world systems, thirty world systems, forty world systems, fifty world systems, or a hundred world systems. He can see the small thousandfold world system (cūḷanika-lokadhātu), the middle twice-thousandfold world system (majjhimika-lokadhātu), or the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world system (mahasahassī-lokadhātu). Or he can see as far as he wishes. Thus is the Blessed One's divine eye extremely pure. In this way, the Blessed One is one with 'opened eyes' (vivaṭacakkhu) even with the divine eye. How is the Blessed One one with 'opened eyes' through the wisdom eye (paññācakkhu)? The Blessed One possesses great wisdom, wide wisdom, joyful wisdom, swift wisdom, sharp wisdom, and penetrative wisdom. He is skilled in the various types of wisdom. He possesses vast knowledge. He has attained the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā). He has reached the four kinds of intrepidity (vesārajja). He possesses the ten powers (dasabala). He is the bull among men (purisāsabha), the lion among men (purisasīha), the elephant among men (purisanāga), the noble thoroughbred among men (purisājañña), the bearer of the burden for all beings (purisadhoreyya). He possesses infinite knowledge, infinite power, and infinite fame. He is rich, possessing the great wealth of wisdom. He is the leader, the trainer, the guide, the one who makes others understand, the one who removes doubt, the one who makes others see the practice, the one who sees what is to be seen, and the one who inspires faith. Indeed, that Blessed One is the producer of the path that had not arisen, the bringer-to-birth of the path that had not been born, the declarer of the path that had not been declared. He is the knower of the path, the one who understands the path, the one who is expert in the path. And now his disciples live following that path, becoming endowed with it afterwards. Indeed, that Blessed One knows what is to be known and sees what is to be seen. He has become vision, become knowledge, become Dhamma, become Brahma. He is the teacher, the proclaimer, the one who brings out the meaning, the giver of the Deathless (amata), the Lord of the Dhamma, the Tathāgata. There is nothing that is not known, not seen, not perceived, not realized, or not touched by the Blessed One's wisdom. All things—past, future, and present—in every aspect, come clearly into the range of the Buddha's knowledge. Whatever is knowable (neyyadhamma) exists, he has known it. Whether it be one's own benefit, the benefit of others, or the benefit of both...
278:
Whether it be the benefit for the present life, the benefit for the future life, the obvious meaning, the profound meaning, the hidden meaning, the concealed meaning, the meaning to be inferred, the explicit meaning, the blameless meaning, the defilement-free meaning, the pure meaning, or the ultimate meaning—all such meanings revolve within the Buddha's knowledge. All bodily actions, all verbal actions, and all mental actions of the Buddha follow his knowledge. The Buddha possesses unimpeded knowledge regarding the past, the future, and the present. As far as there is the knowable (ñeyya), so far extends his knowledge (ñāṇa). As far as there is knowledge, so far extends the knowable. Knowledge has the knowable as its limit; the knowable has knowledge as its limit. Knowledge does not proceed beyond the knowable, nor is there any path of the knowable (ñeyyapatha) beyond knowledge. These things stand at each other's limits. Just as with two well-fitted lids of a basket, the bottom lid does not exceed the top lid, and the top lid does not exceed the bottom lid, but they stand at each other's limits; even so, the knowable and the knowledge of the Buddha stand at each other's limits. As far as there is the knowable, so far extends his knowledge. As far as there is knowledge, so far extends the knowable. Knowledge has the knowable as its limit; the knowable has knowledge as its limit. Knowledge does not proceed beyond the knowable, nor is there any path of the knowable beyond knowledge. These things stand at each other's limits.

The Buddha's knowledge proceeds in all things (dhamma). All things are connected to the Buddha's reflection, his wish, his attention, and the arising of his thought. The Buddha's knowledge proceeds in all beings. The Blessed One knows the dispositions (āsaya) of all beings, knows their latent tendencies (anusaya), knows their temperaments (carita), and knows their inclinations (adhimutti). He knows distinctly those beings with little dust in their eyes and those with much dust, those with sharp faculties and those with dull faculties, those with good qualities and those with bad qualities, those easy to teach and those difficult to teach, and those capable of liberation and those incapable. The world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, this generation with its recluses and brahmins, its devas and humans, revolves within the Buddha's knowledge.

Just as all fish and turtles, including even the Timi and Timingala, revolve within the great ocean; even so, the world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, this generation with its recluses and brahmins, its devas and humans, revolves within the Buddha's knowledge. Just as all birds, including even the Garuda, the son of Vinatā, revolve in a portion of the sky; even so...
279:
Those wise ones who are equal to the Venerable Sāriputta in wisdom also revolve only within a portion of the Buddha's knowledge. The Buddha's knowledge stands overwhelming and surpassing the wisdom of devas and humans. There are wise kshatriyas, wise brahmins, wise householders, and wise recluses who are subtle, skilled in the debates of others, and who wander about like hair-splitters, destroying wrong views with their sharp wisdom. They prepare difficult and profound questions and approach the Tathāgata to ask these hidden and concealed questions. The Blessed One explains and answers those questions with their causes and reasons. Then, those wise ones become disciples of the Blessed One. At that time, the Blessed One shines and is most beautiful with his wisdom in the midst of those wise ones.
