In this way, the Blessed One is called 'one with opened eyes' (vivaṭacakkhu) also by means of the eye of wisdom (paññā-cakkhu).

How is the Blessed One called 'one with opened eyes' also by means of the Buddha-eye (buddha-cakkhu)? When the Blessed One surveys the world with the Buddha-eye, he sees beings with little dust in their eyes and those with much dust, those with sharp faculties and those with dull faculties, those with good qualities and those with bad qualities, those easy to teach and those difficult to teach, some who live seeing the danger and fault in the next world, and some who live without seeing the danger and fault in the next world. For example, in a pond of blue lotuses, red lotuses, or white lotuses, some lotuses are born in the water, grow in the water, and remain submerged beneath the water. Some lotuses stand level with the water. Some lotuses rise above the water and stand unsullied by the water. Even so, when the Blessed One surveys the world with the Buddha-eye, he sees beings with little dust, those with much dust, those with sharp faculties, those with dull faculties, those with good qualities, those with bad qualities, those easy to teach, those difficult to teach, those who see the danger of the next world, and those who do not.

The Blessed One knows: "This person is of a lustful temperament; this person is of a hating temperament; this person is of a deluded temperament; this person is of a speculative temperament; this person is of a faithful temperament; this person is of an intellectual temperament." To a person of lustful temperament, the Blessed One preaches the meditation on loathsomeness (asubha). To a person of hating temperament, the Blessed One instructs in the meditation on loving-kindness (mettā-bhāvanā). To a person of deluded temperament, the Blessed One establishes them in learning, questioning, hearing the Dhamma at the right time, discussing the Dhamma at the right time, and living in the company of teachers. To a person of speculative temperament, the Blessed One instructs in mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasati). To a person of faithful temperament, the Blessed One instructs in an inspiring sign (pasādanīya nimitta).
280:
The Blessed One explains to a person of intellectual temperament the state of the Buddha's well-penetrated enlightenment, the excellence of the Dhamma, the good conduct and virtue of the Saṅgha, as well as the aspects of impermanence, suffering, and non-self, which are the signs of insight (vipassanā-nimitta).

'As one standing on a rocky mountain peak might behold the people all around, even so, O Wise One, O All-seeing One, having ascended the palace of Dhamma made of wisdom, look down, free from sorrow, upon the people immersed in sorrow, overcome by birth and old age.'

In this way, the Blessed One is also known as the 'One with Opened Eyes' (vivaṭa-cakkhu) through the 'Buddha-eye' (buddha-cakkhu).

How is the Blessed One also known as the 'One with Opened Eyes' through the 'All-seeing Eye' (samanta-cakkhu)? The 'All-seeing Eye' refers to the knowledge of omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa). The Blessed One is endowed with, fully endowed with, attained to, fully attained to, possessed of, and fully possessed of the knowledge of omniscience.

'There is nothing in this world unseen by Him, nor is there anything unknown that should be known. He has fully known everything that can be known; therefore, the Tathāgata is called the All-seeing One.'

In this way, the Blessed One is also known as the 'One with Opened Eyes' through the 'All-seeing Eye'—thus He praised the 'One with Opened Eyes.'

Regarding the phrase 'sakkhi-dhammaṃ parissayavinayaṃ': 'Sakkhi-dhamma' means the Dhamma realized by oneself, through one's own direct experience, not by hearsay, not by tradition, not by lineage, not by the authority of scriptures, not by logical reasoning, not by inferential method, not by reflecting on appearances, and not by acceptance of a view after pondering it.

Regarding the phrase 'parissayavinayaṃ': 'Parissaya' (dangers) are of two kinds—manifest dangers (pākaṭa-parissaya) and concealed dangers (paṭicchanna-parissaya). 

What are the manifest dangers? They are lions, tigers, leopards, bears, hyenas, wolves, buffaloes, elephants, snakes, scorpions, centipedes; or they may be thieves, or violent men, or those who have committed crimes, or those who have set out to commit crimes. They may also be eye-disease, ear-disease, nose-disease, tongue-disease, body-disease, head-disease, ear-ache, mouth-disease, tooth-disease, cough, asthma, catarrh, burning sensation, fever, stomach-ache, fainting, dysentery, sharp pain, cholera, leprosy, boils, eczema, or consumption.
281:
Epilepsy, ringworm, itch, scabies, scratches from nails, skin eruptions on palms or soles, vomiting of blood, diabetes, piles, abscesses, fistula; afflictions arising from bile, afflictions arising from phlegm, afflictions arising from wind, afflictions arising from the conflict of the humors (sannipāta), afflictions produced by change of season, afflictions produced by improper care, afflictions produced by external exertion, afflictions produced by the result of kamma; cold, heat, hunger, thirst, excrement, urine, and contact with gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and creeping things—these are called manifest dangers.

What are the concealed dangers? Misconduct of body, misconduct of speech, misconduct of mind; the hindrance of sensual desire (kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa), the hindrance of ill-will (byāpāda-nīvaraṇa), the hindrance of sloth and torpor (thina-middha-nīvaraṇa), the hindrance of restlessness and remorse (uddhacca-kukkucca-nīvaraṇa), the hindrance of doubt (vicikicchā-nīvaraṇa); lust (rāga), hatred (dosa), delusion (moha), anger (kodha), enmity (upanāha), disparaging (makkha), domineering (paḷāsa), envy (issā), stinginess (macchariya), deceit (māyā), treachery (sāṭheyya), obstinacy (thambha), impetuosity (sārambha), conceit (māna), arrogance (atimāna), intoxication (mada), and negligence (pamāda); all defilements, all misconduct, all distress (daratha), all burning (pariḷāha), all fever (santāpa), and all unwholesome formations (akusalābhisaṅkhāra)—these are called concealed dangers.

In what sense are they 'dangers' (parissaya)? They are called dangers because they oppress (pari-sahanti); they are called dangers because they lead to decline (parihānāya saṃvattanti); they are called dangers because they reside therein (tatrāsaya). 

How are they called dangers because they oppress? Those dangers oppress, repeatedly oppress, overcome, overwhelm, exhaust, and harass that person. In this way, they are called dangers because they oppress.

How are they called dangers because they lead to decline? Those dangers lead to the obstruction and decline of wholesome states. Of which wholesome states? They lead to the obstruction and decline of: right practice, conformable practice, non-hostile practice, non-opposing practice, practice according to the goal, practice in accordance with the Dhamma; the fulfillment of virtue, guarding the doors of the senses, moderation in eating, devotion to wakefulness, mindfulness and clear comprehension, devotion to the development of the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the Noble Eightfold Path. In this way, they are called dangers because they lead to decline.
282:
In what way are they dangers because they reside there? In that body, these evil unwholesome states arise depending on the individual existence (attabhāva). Just as creatures residing in a hole sleep in a hole, just as creatures residing in water sleep in water, just as creatures residing in a forest sleep in a forest, and just as creatures residing in a tree sleep in a tree; even so, these evil unwholesome states arise in that body depending on the individual existence. In this way also, they are called dangers (parissaya) because they reside there.

Indeed, this was said by the Blessed One: "Monks, a monk who has a resident pupil and a teacher lives in suffering and not in comfort. And how, monks, does a monk who has a resident pupil and a teacher live in suffering and not in comfort? Here, monks, when a monk sees a form with the eye, evil unwholesome states consisting of thoughts and fetters arise. Those evil unwholesome states dwell within him and flow within him. Therefore, he is called 'one who has a resident pupil.' Those evil unwholesome states harass him. Therefore, he is called 'one who has a teacher.'"

"Furthermore, monks, when a monk hears a sound with the ear... smells an odor with the nose... tastes a flavor with the tongue... touches a tangible object with the body... cognizes a mental phenomenon with the mind, evil unwholesome states consisting of thoughts and fetters arise. Those evil unwholesome states dwell within him and flow within him. Therefore, he is called 'one who has a resident pupil.' Those evil unwholesome states harass him. Therefore, he is called 'one who has a teacher.' Thus, monks, a monk who has a resident pupil and a teacher lives in suffering and not in comfort." In this way also, they are called dangers because they reside there.

Indeed, this was said by the Blessed One: "Monks, there are these three internal stains, internal enemies, internal foes, internal killers, and internal adversaries. What are the three? Greed, monks, is an internal stain, an internal enemy, an internal foe, an internal killer, and an internal adversary. Hatred, monks... Delusion, monks, is an internal stain, an internal enemy, an internal foe, an internal killer, and an internal adversary. These, monks, are the three internal stains, internal enemies, internal foes, internal killers, and internal adversaries."
283:
Greed produces misfortune; greed disturbs the mind.
A person does not notice the danger born from within.
A greedy person does not know the benefit; a greedy person does not see the Dhamma.
When greed overcomes a man, there is then utter darkness.

Hatred produces misfortune; hatred disturbs the mind.
A person does not notice the danger born from within.
An angry person does not know the benefit; an angry person does not see the Dhamma.
When hatred overcomes a man, there is then utter darkness.

Delusion produces misfortune; delusion disturbs the mind.
A person does not notice the danger born from within.
A deluded person does not know the benefit; a deluded person does not see the Dhamma.
When delusion overcomes a man, there is then utter darkness.

In this way also, they arise in that body; therefore, they are called dangers (parissaya).

Indeed, this was said by the Blessed One: "Great King, there are these three things arising within a man that arise for his harm, for his suffering, and for his uncomfortable living. What are the three? Great King, greed is a thing arising within a man that arises for his harm, for his suffering, and for his uncomfortable living. Great King, hatred... Great King, delusion is a thing arising within a man that arises for his harm, for his suffering, and for his uncomfortable living. Great King, these three things, when they arise within a man, arise for his harm, for his suffering, and for his uncomfortable living."

Greed, hatred, and delusion,
Harm the man of evil mind, having arisen within himself,
Just as its own fruit destroys the bamboo.

In this way also, they arise in that body; therefore, they are called dangers (parissaya).
284:
The Blessed One said this:

"Lust and hatred have this individual existence as their origin; boredom, delight, and horripilation are born from this. Arising from this, thoughts of the mind release [and harass the mind], just as boys release a crow."

Thus, because they arise depending on that body, they are called 'tatrāsaya' (perils).

'Parissayavinaya' refers to the deathless Nibbāna, which is the destruction of perils, the abandonment of perils, the stilling of perils, the relinquishment of perils, and the subsiding of perils. It is the very 'parissayavinaya' which is the Dhamma to be realized.

'Venerable Sir, tell me the practice' means: tell me the right practice, the conforming practice, the non-hostile practice, the practice in accordance with the goal, the practice in accordance with the Dhamma; the fulfillment of moral virtue, the guarding of the sense doors, moderation in eating, devotion to wakefulness, mindfulness and clear comprehension, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the noble eightfold path, Nibbāna, and the practice leading to Nibbāna. Tell, explain, teach, prescribe, establish, open, analyze, clarify, and manifest it—this is what 'tell me the practice' means. By the word 'Bhaddante' (Venerable Sir), that created Buddha addresses the Blessed One. Alternatively, it means: 'Venerable Sir, whatever Dhamma you explain, teach, prescribe, establish, open, analyze, clarify, and manifest, all that is excellent, good, beautiful, blameless, and to be followed.' Thus, he requests, 'Venerable Sir, tell me the practice.'

In the phrase 'Pātimokkha or concentration': 'Pātimokkha' refers to virtue (sīla), which is the foundation, the beginning, the conduct, the restraint, the control, the mouth, and the foremost entrance for the attainment of wholesome states. 'Concentration' (samādhi) refers to the steadiness, stability, and fixedness of the mind; non-distraction, non-wavering, an unperturbed mental state, serenity, the faculty of concentration, the power of concentration, and right concentration.

Therefore, that created Buddha said:
"The one with vision opened has described the removal of perils (Nibbāna), the Dhamma to be realized. Venerable Sir, tell me the practice, the Pātimokkha, and also concentration."
285:
One should not be fickle with the eyes; one should close one's ears to village-talk. One should not be greedy for tastes, and one should not regard anything in the world as 'mine'.

'Cakkhūhi neva lolassa' (not fickle with the eyes): How is one fickle with the eyes? In this Dispensation, some person is possessed of fickleness of the eyes, thinking, 'I must see what I have not seen; I must go beyond what I have seen.' He is constantly devoted to wandering for long distances, from monastery to monastery, park to park, village to village, town to town, city to city, kingdom to kingdom, and province to province, for the sake of seeing forms. In this way, one is fickle with the eyes.

Furthermore, a monk enters a village and, while walking on the street, goes without restraint, looking at elephants, looking at horses, looking at chariots, looking at infantry, looking at women, looking at men, looking at boys, looking at girls, looking at shops, looking at the doors of houses, looking up, looking down, and looking all around the various quarters. In this way, too, one is fickle with the eyes.

Furthermore, a monk, seeing a form with the eye, grasps its signs and features. Since covetousness and displeasure, evil unwholesome states, might flow in upon one who dwells with the eye-faculty unrestrained, he does not practice for its restraint, he does not guard the eye-faculty, and he does not achieve restraint over the eye-faculty. In this way, too, one is fickle with the eyes.

Or else, some venerable recluses and brahmins, having eaten the food given in faith, remain devoted to witnessing unseemly shows (visūkadassana) which are like thorns to the Dispensation. These include: dancing, singing, music, theatrical shows, storytelling, hand-clapping, cymbals, jar-drums, art exhibitions, acrobatic shows, playing with iron balls, bamboo-climbing, bone-washing, elephant fights, horse fights, buffalo fights, bull fights, goat fights, ram fights, cock fights, quail fights, staff-fights, boxing, wrestling, sham battles, counting of troops, battle arrays, and witnessing military reviews. In this way, too, one is fickle with the eyes.
286:
How is one not eye-fickle? Here, in this Dispensation, a monk, when entering a village or walking along a street, goes with eyes restrained. He does not go looking at elephants, he does not go looking at horses, he does not go looking at chariots, he does not go looking at infantry. He does not go looking at women, he does not go looking at men, he does not go looking at boys, he does not go looking at girls. He does not go looking at shops, he does not go looking at the doorways of houses. He does not look up, he does not look down, and he goes without looking all around in every direction. In this way, too, he is not eye-fickle.

Alternatively, a monk, seeing a form with the eye, does not grasp at its signs (such as being a woman or a man) nor does he grasp at its features (such as hands, feet, smiles, or laughter). Since unwholesome states of covetousness and grief might flow in upon one who dwells with the eye faculty unrestrained, he practices for its restraint; he guards the eye faculty; he achieves restraint of the eye faculty. In this way, too, he is not eye-fickle.

Furthermore, whereas some recluses and brahmins, after eating food given in faith, remain addicted to such unseemly shows (visūkadassana) which are contrary to the Dispensation, such as: dancing, singing, music, theatrical performances, storytelling ... and looking at armies; he refrains from such unseemly shows. In this way, too, he is not eye-fickle.

"He should not be fickle with his eyes" (cakkhūhi neva lolassa) means he should abandon, dispel, destroy, and bring to non-existence eye-fickleness. He should be far removed from eye-fickleness, specially refrained, repeatedly refrained, emerged, released, delivered, and detached from it, and should dwell with a mind that has no boundaries.

"He should shut his ear to village talk" (gāmakathāya āvaraye sotaṃ) means the thirty-two types of low talk (tiracchānakathā) which are contrary to the path to Nibbāna are called village talk. These are: talk about kings, talk about thieves, talk about ministers, talk about armies, talk about dangers, talk about battles, talk about food, talk about drink, talk about clothing, talk about vehicles, talk about beds, talk about garlands, talk about perfumes, talk about relatives, talk about villages, talk about market towns, talk about cities, talk about districts, talk about women, talk about men, talk about heroes, talk about streets, talk about watering places, talk about ancestors, miscellaneous talk, talk about the world, talk about the ocean, and talk about existence and non-existence. From such village talk, he should shut his ear.
287:
"Ear" means he should shut, block, restrain, guard, protect, close, and cut off the ear from village talk. In this way, he should shut his ear to village talk.

"He should not be greedy for tastes" means tastes are: the juice of roots, the juice of stems, the juice of bark, the juice of leaves, the juice of flowers, the juice of fruits, sour, sweet, bitter, pungent, salty, alkaline, oily, astringent, delicious tastes, non-delicious tastes, cold, and hot. Some recluses and brahmins are greedy for tastes; they wander about seeking excellent tastes with the tip of their tongue. If they get sour, they seek non-sour; if they get non-sour, they seek sour... (p)... if they get cold, they seek hot; if they get hot, they seek cold. Whatever they get, they are not satisfied with it and seek other tastes. They are attached, greedy, infatuated, intoxicated, deeply absorbed, stuck, entangled, and fettered by pleasant tastes. For one in whom this craving for taste (rasataṇhā) is abandoned, cut off at the root... (p)... burnt by the fire of knowledge, that monk reflects wisely and partakes of food, not for amusement... (p)... but only for the sake of being blameless and living in comfort.

Just as one would apply ointment to a wound only for the sake of healing, or just as one would grease an axle only for the sake of carrying a load, or just as one would eat the flesh of one's son only for the sake of crossing a desert; even so, a monk reflects wisely and partakes of food, not for amusement... (p)... reflecting, "Thus I shall be blameless and live in comfort," he should abandon, dispel, remove, and bring to non-existence the craving for taste. He should be one who is far removed from craving for taste, specially refrained, repeatedly refrained, emerged, delivered, specially delivered, and detached, and should dwell with a mind that has no boundaries. In this way, he should not be greedy for tastes.

"He should not regard anything in the world as mine" (na ca mamāyetha kiñci lokasmiṃ) means there are two types of mineness (mamatta): mineness through craving (taṇhā-mamatta) and mineness through views (diṭṭhi-mamatta). ... (p) ... This is mineness through craving. ... (p) ... This is mineness through views. Having abandoned mineness through craving and relinquished mineness through views, he should not regard the eye as "mine," should not grasp it, should not handle it, should not be attached to it. The ear... the nose... the tongue... the body... forms... sounds... smells... tastes... tangibles... family... group... dwelling... gain... fame... praise... happiness... robe... almsfood... lodging... medicinal requisites for the sick... the sense element... the fine-material element... the immaterial element... the sense-sphere existence... the fine-material existence... the immaterial existence... the percipient existence... the non-percipient existence... the neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient existence... the one-constituent existence... the four-constituent existence...
288:
Existence with perception, existence without perception, existence with neither-perception-nor-non-perception, existence with one constituent, existence with four constituents, existence with five constituents; things past, future, or present, seen, heard, sensed, or cognized—one should not regard them as 'mine', should not grasp them as 'mine', should not handle them as 'mine', and should not focus on them as 'mine'.

'Anything' refers to any form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. 'In the world' means in the world from the realms of misery to the world of the sense bases—the meaning is that one should not regard anything as 'mine' in the world.

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
'One should not be fickle with the eyes, one should block the ear from village-talk,
One should not be greedy for tastes, and one should not regard anything in the world as "mine".'

When touched by contact, a bhikkhu should not lament anywhere,
He should not long for existence, and he should not tremble in the face of terrors.

'When touched by contact' (phassena yadā phuṭṭhassa): 'Contact' refers to the contact of disease. One may be touched, oppressed, afflicted, and beset by the contact of disease. One may be touched, oppressed, afflicted, and beset by eye disease, ear disease... nose disease, tongue disease, body disease, head disease, ear-lobe disease, mouth disease, tooth disease, cough, asthma, catarrh, burning sensation, fever, stomach ailment, fainting, dysentery, sharp pain, cholera, leprosy, boils, eczema, consumption, epilepsy, ringworm, itch, scabies, nail-scratch, skin-eruption, blood-disorder, bile-disorder, diabetes, hemorrhoids, pustules, fistula; afflictions arising from bile, phlegm, wind, or a combination; afflictions produced by change of climate, improper behavior, assault, or the result of kamma; cold, heat, hunger, thirst, excrement, urine; or touched, oppressed, beset, and filled with the contact of gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and creeping things.

'A bhikkhu should not lament anywhere' (paridevaṃ bhikkhu na kareyya kuhiñci): He should not perform, produce, or generate wailing, lamenting, the state of wailing, the state of lamenting, babbling, talk, chatter, prattle, the state of prattling, or the state of chattering.
289:
He should not cause it to arise, nor cause it to arise intensely. 'Anywhere' (kuhiñci) means in any place, in some place, in any location, internally, externally, or both internally and externally. A bhikkhu should not perform lamentation anywhere.

'He should not long for existence' (bhavañca nābhijappeyya) means he should not long for, intensely long for, or excessively long for sensual existence, fine-material existence, or immaterial existence.

'He should not tremble in the face of terrors' (bheravesu ca na sampavedheyya) means he should not shake in the face of frightening dangers. 'Terror' (bherava) is, in one sense, the same as fear and dread. For it was said by the Blessed One: 'Indeed, this fear and terror comes to one who has not abandoned it.' To speak of external objects of fear, they are: lions, tigers, leopards, bears, hyenas, wolves, buffaloes, horses, elephants, snakes, scorpions, centipedes; or they may be robbers, or violent youths, those who have committed crimes or those who have not. Again, in another sense, fear is said to be internal, arising from the mind: fear, dread, trembling, hair-standing-on-end, agitation of the mind, and alarm. These include the fear of birth, aging, sickness, death, kings, thieves, fire, water, self-reproach, reproach by others, punishment, unfortunate destinations, waves, crocodiles, whirlpools, sharks, fear regarding livelihood, ill-repute, stage-fright in assemblies, intoxication, and the fear of falling into the four woeful states. These are fear, dread, trembling, hair-standing-on-end, agitation of the mind, and alarm. 'He should not tremble in the face of terrors' means that upon seeing or hearing terrors, he should not shake, should not tremble, should not be greatly shaken, should not be terrified, should not be intensely terrified, should not be terrified all around, should not be afraid, and should not fall into distress. He should be one who is fearless, not trembling, not alarmed, and not fleeing. He should dwell having abandoned fear and terror, and with hair-standing-on-end gone.

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
'When touched by contact, a bhikkhu should not lament anywhere,
He should not long for existence, and he should not tremble in the face of terrors.'

Having obtained almsfood, and also drinks, snacks, and also clothing,
He should not make a hoard, nor should he be anxious if he does not obtain them.

'Almsfood' (anna) refers to boiled rice and meat. 'Drinks' (pāna) refers to the eight kinds of juices: mango juice, rose-apple juice, seeded-banana juice, seedless-banana juice, honey-tree juice, grape juice, water-lily root juice, and phaggumaka juice. Furthermore, there are eight other kinds of drinks: jujube juice, wild jujube juice (badara), ghee, oil, milk, gruel, and broth. 'Snacks' (khādanīya) should be understood as edible roots, bark, leaves, flowers, and fruits. 'Clothing' (vattha) refers to the six kinds of robes: linen, cotton, silk, wool, hemp, and cloth mixed with these five materials. In the phrase 'having obtained, he should not make a hoard', 'having obtained' means obtaining without greed, without deception, without flattery, without hinting, and without giving to others for the sake of gain.
290:
## 'Annānamatho pānānaṃ khādanīyānamatho pi vatthānaṃ' means foods and drinks, snacks and clothing. 'Annānaṃ' refers to cooked rice, barley meal, flour, fish, and meat. 'Pānānaṃ' refers to the eight kinds of drinks: mango drink, rose-apple drink, banana drink, wild banana drink, madhuka drink, grape drink, water-lily root drink, and phārushaka fruit drink. There are also eight other drinks: jujube drink, plum drink, badara-plum drink, ghee drink, oil drink, milk drink, gruel drink, and broth drink. 'Khādanīyānaṃ' refers to flour-snacks, cakes, root-snacks, bark-snacks, leaf-snacks, flower-snacks, and fruit-snacks. 'Vatthānaṃ' refers to the six kinds of robes: linen, cotton, silk, wool, hemp, and robes made of a mixture of these five. This is the meaning of 'Annānamatho pānānaṃ khādanīyānamatho pi vatthānaṃ'.

In the phrase 'Laddhā na sannidhiṃ kayirā', 'laddhā' means having obtained, having acquired, having reached, having found, or having received. In such obtaining, it is not through hypocrisy (kuhanā), not through flattery (lapanā), not through hinting (nemittikatā), not through belittling (nippesikatā), not through pursuing gain with gain, not by giving firewood, not by giving bamboo, not by giving leaves, not by giving flowers, not by giving fruit, not by giving bath-water, not by giving scented powder, not by giving clay, not by giving tooth-sticks, not by giving face-water, not through the desire for endearing speech, not through 'bean-soup' talk (muggasūpyatā - falsehood), not by nursing children, not by entering houses and sitting on chairs, not through the art of sites (vatthuvijjā), not through low arts (tiracchānavijjā), not through the art of marks (aṅgavijjā), not through the art of stars (nakkhattavijjā), not by going as a messenger, not by going as an emissary, not by serving as a foot-messenger, not through medical practice, not through construction work, not by reciprocating alms with alms, and not by reciprocating gifts; rather, it means having obtained righteously and fairly. 'Na sannidhiṃ kayirā' means one should not make, should not produce, should not generate, should not bring into being, and should not manifest the hoarding of food, the hoarding of drinks, the hoarding of clothes, the hoarding of vehicles, the hoarding of beds and seats, the hoarding of perfumes, or the hoarding of material things.

'Na ca parittase tāni alabhamāno' means when not receiving food, or not receiving drinks, or not receiving clothes, or not receiving a family, or not receiving a group, or not receiving a dwelling, or not receiving gain, or not receiving fame, or not receiving praise, or not receiving happiness, or not receiving robes, or not receiving alms-food, or not receiving lodging, or not receiving medicinal requisites for the sick, or not receiving an attendant for the sick, one should not be anxious, should not be terrified, should not be agitated, should not be afraid, and should not fall into distress, thinking 'I am unknown.' One should be fearless, unshakable, unalarmed, and not prone to flight. One should dwell with fear and danger abandoned, and with horripilation (bristling of hair) removed. This is the meaning of 'Na ca parittase tāni alabhamāno'. Therefore, the Blessed One said: 'Annānamatho pānānaṃ, khādanīyānamatho pi vatthānaṃ. Laddhā na sannidhiṃ kayirā, na ca parittase tāni alabhamāno.' A person who meditates should not be restless and should abstain from remorse (kukkucca).
291:
One should not fall into anxiety; one should be fearless, unshaken, not terrified, and not prone to flee, dwelling with fear and dread abandoned and with horripilation gone. This is the meaning of 'nor be anxious when not receiving them.'

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
'Foods, drinks, edibles, and clothes;
Having received, one should not store up, nor be anxious when not receiving them.'

'A meditator should not be restless of foot, should abstain from remorse, should not be negligent; moreover, in seats and beds that are quiet, a bhikkhu should dwell.'

'A meditator should not be restless of foot' (jhāyī na pādalolassa). 'A meditator' (jhāyī) refers to one who meditates with the first jhāna, the second jhāna, the third jhāna, or the fourth jhāna. It refers to one who meditates with jhāna accompanied by initial and sustained thought; with jhāna without initial thought but with sustained thought only; with jhāna without both initial and sustained thought. It refers to one who meditates with jhāna accompanied by rapture; with jhāna without rapture; with jhāna associated with rapture; with jhāna associated with pleasure; with jhāna associated with happiness; or with jhāna associated with equanimity. It refers to one who meditates with the emptiness jhāna, the signless jhāna, or the undirected jhāna. It refers to one who meditates with mundane jhāna or supramundane jhāna. One who delights in jhāna, is devoted to one-pointedness of mind, and values the ultimate truth is called 'a meditator.'

'Not restless of foot' (na pādalolassa). How is one restless of foot? Here, someone is possessed of restlessness of foot and dwells devoted to wandering long and aimlessly from park to park, from garden to garden, from village to village, from town to town, from city to city, from country to country, and from province to province. In this way, one is restless of foot.

Alternatively, a bhikkhu is possessed of restlessness of foot even within the monastery (saṅghārāma). Without purpose or reason, with a mind that is agitated and unpeaceful, he goes from one enclosure to another, and from one dwelling to another.
292:
He goes from a lean-to to a lean-to, from a mansion to a mansion, from a flat-roofed house to a flat-roofed house, from a cave to a cave, from a grotto to a grotto, from a hut to a hut, from a gabled house to a gabled house, from a watchtower to a watchtower, from a hall to a hall, from a high-roofed house to a high-roofed house, from an assembly hall to an assembly hall, from a circular pavilion to a circular pavilion, and from the foot of one tree to the foot of another tree. Or else, he goes to where monks are sitting; there he becomes a second to one, a third to two, or a fourth to three. In going thus, he indulges in much low talk, namely: talk about kings, thieves, ministers, armies, dangers, battles, food, drink, clothing, vehicles, beds, garlands, perfumes, relatives, villages, market towns, cities, districts, women, men, streets, water-fetching places, the departed, miscellaneous topics, speculations about the world and the sea, and talk about becoming and non-becoming. In this way, he is one who is restless of foot.

"He should not be restless of foot" means: he should abandon foot-restlessness, dispel it, put an end to it, and make it non-existent. He should be one who stays far from foot-restlessness, especially abstaining, repeatedly abstaining, escaped, released, particularly released, and detached. He should dwell, practice, especially practice, move about, proceed, guard, maintain, and support himself with a mind that has no boundaries. He should be one who delights in seclusion, enjoys seclusion, is devoted to internal mental tranquility, does not neglect jhāna, is possessed of insight, increases it, frequents empty huts, is a meditator, delights in jhāna, is devoted to solitude, and values the ultimate goal. This is the meaning of "A meditator should not be restless of foot."

"He should abstain from remorse (kukkucca) and should not be negligent" means: fidgeting with the hands is remorse, fidgeting with the feet is remorse, and fidgeting with both hands and feet is remorse. Perceiving what is unallowable as allowable, perceiving what is allowable as unallowable, perceiving what is faultless as faulty, and perceiving what is faulty as faultless—such remorse, the act of being remorseful, the state of being remorseful, mental regret, and mental irritation is called remorse.

Furthermore, remorse, which is mental regret and mental irritation, arises from two causes: because of what has been done and because of what has not been done. How does remorse, mental regret, and mental irritation arise from what has been done and what has not been done? Remorse, mental regret, and mental irritation arise thinking, "I have committed bodily misconduct, I have not performed bodily good conduct."
293:
The occurrence of mental dissatisfaction and mental scratching is as follows: "I have committed vocal misconduct; I have not performed vocal good conduct." Thus, remorse (kukkucca), mental dissatisfaction, and mental scratching arise. "I have committed mental misconduct; I have not performed mental good conduct..." (pe) ... "I have committed the taking of life (pāṇātipāta); I have not performed the abstention from taking life." Thus, remorse arises... (pe) ... The occurrence of mental scratching is: "I have committed the taking of what is not given... I have committed sexual misconduct... I have committed false speech... I have committed malicious speech... I have committed harsh speech... I have committed frivolous chatter... I have committed covetousness... I have committed ill will... I have committed wrong view; I have not performed right view." Thus, remorse, mental dissatisfaction, and mental scratching arise. Remorse, mental dissatisfaction, and mental scratching arise due to what has been done and what has not been done.

Alternatively, remorse, mental dissatisfaction, and mental scratching arise as follows: "I am one who does not fully practice the virtues (sīla)." "I am one whose sense-doors are unguarded..." (pe) ... "I am one who does not know moderation in eating..." "I am one who is not devoted to wakefulness..." "I am not endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension..." "I have not developed the four foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna)." "I have not developed the four right efforts (sammappadhāna)." "I have not developed the four bases of power (iddhipāda)." "I have not developed the five faculties (indriya)." "I have not developed the five powers (bala)." "I have not developed the seven factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga)." "I have not developed the Noble Eightfold Path." "I have not fully understood the Truth of Suffering (dukkha)." "I have not abandoned the Truth of Origin (samudaya)." "I have not developed the Truth of the Path (magga)." "I have not realized the Truth of Cessation (nirodha)." Thus, remorse, mental dissatisfaction, and mental scratching arise.

"Viramē kukkuccā" means one should abstain from remorse, should especially abstain, should repeatedly abstain; one should abandon remorse, dispel it, put an end to it, and make it non-existent. One who abstains from remorse, especially abstains, repeatedly abstains, has emerged from it, is released from it, is specially liberated, and is disengaged from it, should dwell with a mind that is free from boundaries—this is the meaning of the phrase "Viramē kukkuccā."

"Nappamajjeyya" means one should be one who acts with respect, acts constantly, acts continuously, whose behavior is not sluggish, whose desire is not discarded, and whose burden is not laid down; thus, non-negligence (appamāda) should occur in wholesome states. One should reflect: "When shall I fulfill the aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha) that is not yet fulfilled? When shall I contemplate with wisdom the aggregate of virtue that is already fulfilled in various instances?" The desire (chanda), effort (vāyāma), exertion (ussāha), intense effort (ussoḷhī), strength (thāma), persistence (appaṭivānī), mindfulness (sati), clear comprehension (sampajañña), ardor (ātappa), striving (padhāna), determination (adhiṭṭhāna), devotion (anuyoga), and non-negligence (appamāda) that occur therein are in wholesome states.
294:
In regard to wholesome states, one should reflect: "When shall I fulfill the aggregate of virtue that is not yet fulfilled? When shall I contemplate with wisdom the aggregate of virtue that is already fulfilled in various instances? When shall I fully understand the aggregate of concentration (samādhikkhandha), the aggregate of wisdom (paññākkhandha), the aggregate of liberation (vimuttikkhandha), and the aggregate of knowledge and vision of liberation (vimuttiñāṇadassanakkhandha)? When shall I fully understand the Truth of Suffering (dukkha-sacca) which is not yet fully understood? When shall I abandon the defilements (kilesa) which are not yet abandoned? When shall I develop the Path (magga) which is not yet developed? When shall I realize the Truth of Cessation (nirodha-sacca) which is not yet realized?" The desire, effort, exertion, intense effort, strength, persistence, mindfulness, clear comprehension, ardor, striving, determination in wholesome states, devotion, and non-negligence that exist therein—this is the meaning of "Viramē kukkuccā nappamajjeyya."

"Then, in seats and beds, in places with little noise, the monk should dwell." "Atha" (Then) is a conjunction... (pe) ... Where one sits is called a seat (āsana). These include a couch, a chair, a rug, a mat, a skin-mat, a grass-mat, a leaf-mat, and a straw-mat. A bed (sayana) refers to a lodging (senāsana) such as a monastery, a lean-to, a mansion, a gabled house, or a cave—this is the meaning of "Athāsanesu sayanesu."

"In places with little noise, the monk should dwell" means he should practice, especially practice, dwell, move about, behave, protect, and maintain himself in lodgings that have little noise, little sound, are secluded from people, are suitable for secret acts, and are appropriate for seclusion. This is the meaning of "Athāsanesu sayanesu appasaddesu bhikkhu vihareyya."

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
"The meditative monk should not be unsteady of foot; he should abstain from remorse and should not be negligent.
Then, in seats and beds, in places with little noise, the monk should dwell."

One should not indulge in much sleep; being ardent, one should devote oneself to wakefulness.
One should abandon laziness, deceit, laughter, play, and sexual intercourse along with adornment.

"One should not indulge in much sleep" means that having divided the day and night into six parts, one should remain awake for five parts, excluding the middle watch (majjhima-yāma), and sleep for only one part. This is the meaning of "Niddaṃ na bahulīkareyya."

"Being ardent, one should devote oneself to wakefulness" means that in this Dispensation, a monk should purify his mind from the hindering states (nīvaraṇa) by walking and sitting throughout the day. He should purify his mind from the hindering states by walking and sitting throughout the first watch of the night. In the middle watch of the night...
295:
At midnight, one should lie down on the right side in the lion's posture (sīhaseyya), placing one foot on the other, mindful and clearly comprehending, keeping in mind the thought of rising. Having risen in the last watch of the night, one should purify the mind of the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) by walking and sitting.

"One should cultivate wakefulness" (jāgariyaṃ bhajeyya) means one should associate with, well associate with, frequent, especially frequent, well frequent, and repeatedly frequent wakefulness.

"Ardent" (ātāpī) refers to one endowed with energy (vīriya) called ātāpa. The mental arousal of energy, exertion, endeavor, striving, effort, zeal, vigor, strength, persistence, the state of unfaltering endeavor, the state of not laying down the desire, the state of not laying down the burden, the upholding of the burden, energy, the faculty of energy, the power of energy, right effort—one who is endowed with, fully endowed with, possessed of, fully possessed of, and attained to this burning energy is called "ardent" (ātāpī). Therefore, it is said: "One should cultivate wakefulness, being ardent."

In the passage "One should abandon laziness, deceit, laughter, play, sexual intercourse, along with adornment" (tandīṃ māyaṃ hassaṃ khiḍḍaṃ, methunaṃ vippajahe savibhūsaṃ), "laziness" (tandī) means laziness, the manner of being lazy, the state of being lazy, the state of having a lazy mind, sloth, the manner of sloth, and the state of being slothful. "Deceit" (māyā) refers to a deceptive practice. Here, someone having committed misconduct by body... by speech, or by mind, entertains an evil desire for the sake of concealing that misconduct. He desires: "May others not know me"; he intends: "May others not know me"; he speaks: "May others not know me"; he exerts himself physically: "May others not know me." Such deceit, concealment of faults, hiding of evil, trickery, fraud, covering up, evasion, guarding and concealing, covering with a roof, making non-apparent, making non-manifest, complete concealment, and the repetition of evil—this is called "deceit." "Laughter" (hassa) means here someone laughs excessively, showing the teeth. For it was said by the Blessed One: "Monks, in the discipline of the Noble Ones, this excessive laughter showing the teeth is like the behavior of children."

"Play" (khiḍḍā) is of two kinds: physical play and verbal play. What is physical play? They play with elephants, with horses, with chariots, with bows, with eight-squared boards, with ten-squared boards, in the sky, on paths, with hand-clapping, with throwing up, with hitting sticks, with bamboo splints, with cowrie shells, with blowing through leaf-trumpets...
296:
...they play; they play with toy plows, they play with turning somersaults, they play with windmills, they play with leaf-cups, they play with toy chariots, they play with toy bows, they play with guessing letters, they play with guessing thoughts, they play with mimicking deformities (such as hunchbacked or crooked-limbed). This is called physical play (kāyika-khiḍḍā). What is verbal play (vācasika-khiḍḍā)? Beating the mouth-drum, making drum sounds with the mouth, showing drum sounds only with the mouth, making sounds by closing the lips, making the sound of a wheel with the mouth, beating a drum with the mouth, dancing, playing music, singing, and joking. This is called verbal play (vācasika-khiḍḍā).

Sexual intercourse (methunadhamma) is that which is the ignoble practice (asaddhamma), the village practice (gāmadhamma), the low practice (vasaladhamma), the practice of worldlings (pothujjanika), the practice ending in washing (odakantika), the practice to be done in secret (rahassa), the union of a pair (dvayaṃdvayasamāpatti). Why is it called sexual intercourse? Because it is the practice of two persons of similar nature whose minds are lustful, strongly lustful, wet with the sap of defilements, pierced by defilements, and overwhelmed by defilements; for that reason, it is called sexual intercourse. Just as two people who quarrel are called "a pair" (methunaka), two who fight... two who talk... two who cause a legal issue... two who dispute... two who hold a view... two who converse are called "a pair" (methunaka); even so, because it is the practice of two persons of similar nature whose minds are lustful, strongly lustful, wet with the sap of defilements, pierced by defilements, and overwhelmed by defilements, for that reason, it is called sexual intercourse.

Adornment (vibhūsā) is of two kinds: the adornment of a householder and the adornment of a renunciant. What is the adornment of a householder? Hair, beard, flowers, scents, ointments, ornaments, decorations, clothes, beds and seats, turbans, breast-ornaments, massaging, bathing, rubbing with oil, looking in a mirror, applying eye-liner, wearing flowers, applying scents, applying face powder, applying face cream, bracelets, tying the topknot, decorated sticks, swords, umbrellas, variegated sandals, headbands, gems, yak-tail fans, white clothes with long fringes, and so on. This is called the adornment of a householder (agāriyassa vibhūsā). What is the adornment of a renunciant? Adorning the robes, adorning the bowl, adorning the dwelling, or adorning this foul body or external requisites, special adornment, beautifying, excessive desire, and vanity. This is called the adornment of a renunciant (pabbajitassa vibhūsā).

One should abandon laziness, deceit, laughter, play, and sexual intercourse, along with adornment. One should abandon, dispel, destroy, and bring to non-existence laziness, deceit, laughter, play, sexual intercourse, along with adornment, retinue, equipment, and requisites. Therefore, it is said: "One should abandon laziness, deceit, laughter, play, and sexual intercourse, along with adornment."

## Therefore, the Blessed One said:
297:
One should not indulge in sleep; the energetic one should practice wakefulness. One should especially abandon laziness, deceit, laughter, play, sexual intercourse, and adornment (and its accompaniments).

One should not practice Athabbaṇa spells, the science of dreams, or the science of signs (physiognomy); furthermore, one should not practice the science of constellations (astrology). My disciple (māmaka) should not resort to listening to the cries of animals, inducing pregnancy, or medical treatment.

One should not practice Athabbaṇa spells, the science of dreams, or the science of signs; furthermore, one should not practice the science of constellations. Those skilled in Athabbaṇa spells perform Athabbaṇa spells. When a city is besieged or when a war is occurring, they cause calamity, danger, disease, fever, piercing pain, cholera, and dysentery among the enemy forces. In this way, those skilled in Athabbaṇa spells perform Athabbaṇa spells.

Dream interpreters interpret dreams. They predict: 'If someone sees a dream in the morning, such will be the result.' If someone sees a dream at noon, such will be the result. If someone sees a dream in the evening, such will be the result. If someone sees a dream in the first watch... [p]... in the middle watch... in the last watch... lying on the right side... lying on the left side... lying on the back... lying prone... sees the moon... the sun... the great ocean... Sineru, the king of mountains... an elephant... a horse... a chariot... infantry... an army formation... a delightful garden... a delightful forest... a delightful land... a delightful lotus pond, such will be the result. In this way, dream interpreters interpret dreams.

Physiognomists interpret signs—the signs of gems, sticks, clothes, swords, arrows, bows, weapons, women, men, girls, boys, female slaves, male slaves, elephants, horses, buffaloes, and bulls.
298:
...the signs of cows, goats, sheep, cocks, quails, iguanas, earrings, tortoises, and deer. In this way, physiognomists interpret signs.

Astrologers interpret the constellations. There are twenty-eight constellations. They predict: 'Under this constellation, one should enter a house; under this constellation, one should wear a crown; under this constellation, one should give a daughter in marriage; under this constellation, one should sow seeds; under this constellation, one should engage in cohabitation.' In this way, astrologers interpret the constellations.

'One should not practice Athabbaṇa spells, dreams, signs, and constellations' means one should not perform, practice, well-practice, or undertake Athabbaṇa spells, dreams, signs, or constellations. Alternatively, one should not take them up, learn them, bear them, hold them, mark them, or apply them in various ways; this is the meaning of 'One should not practice Athabbaṇa spells, dreams, signs, and constellations'.

'My disciple should not resort to the cries of animals, inducing pregnancy, or medical treatment' means: The cries of animals are called 'viruta'. Interpreters of animal cries interpret the cries of animals. They know the cries or calls of birds or four-footed animals. In this way, interpreters of animal cries interpret the cries of animals. Those who induce pregnancy stabilize the pregnancy. Pregnancy may fail for two reasons—due to parasites or due to wind disorders. They give medicine to counteract parasites or wind disorders. In this way, those who induce pregnancy stabilize the pregnancy. Medical treatment (tikicchā) consists of five types: ophthalmology (sālākiya), surgery (sallakattiya), general medicine (kāyatikicchā), demonology (bhūtiya), and pediatrics (komārabhacca). 'Māmaka' refers to one who cherishes the Buddha, one who cherishes the Dhamma, and one who cherishes the Saṅgha. Such a person cherishes the Blessed One as their own, and the Blessed One also accepts that person. This was spoken by the Blessed One: 'Monks, those monks who are deceitful, stubborn, talkative regarding requisites, fraudulent, arrogant, and uncomposed—monks, those monks are not my disciples (māmaka); they have gone away from this Dhamma-Vinaya, and they do not achieve growth, increase, or fulfillment in this Dhamma-Vinaya. But monks, those monks who are not deceitful, not talkative regarding requisites, who are wise, not stubborn, and well-composed—monks, those monks are indeed my disciples (māmaka); they have not gone away from this Dhamma-Vinaya, and they achieve growth, increase, and fulfillment in this Dhamma-Vinaya.'
299:
"Those who are deceitful, stubborn, talkative regarding requisites, given to ornamentation, arrogant, and unconcentrated do not flourish in the Dhamma taught by the Fully Enlightened One. Those who are not deceitful, not talkative, who are wise, not stubborn, and well-concentrated, they indeed flourish in the Dhamma taught by the Fully Enlightened One."

"The cries of birds (omens), the practice of inducing pregnancy, and medical treatment—my disciple (māmaka) should not resort to these." This means: my disciple should not resort to, especially not resort to, not frequent, not repeat, not practice, not excessively practice, not undertake and practice the cries of birds, the practice of inducing pregnancy, and medical treatment. Alternatively, he should not take up, not learn, not carry, not keep near, not mark, and not apply them. Therefore, it is said: "The cries of birds, the practice of inducing pregnancy, and medical treatment—my disciple should not resort to these."

Therefore, the Blessed One said:

"He should not practice Atharvana spells, dreams, signs, or astrology. Nor should he practice the cries of birds, inducing pregnancy, or medical treatment—my disciple should not resort to these."

"A bhikkhu should not tremble because of blame, nor should he be elated when praised. He should dispel greed along with stinginess, anger, and slander."

"He should not tremble because of blame" means: In this Dispensation, some bhikkhus are blamed, censured, or accused based on birth, lineage, family status, beauty of complexion, wealth, learning, occupation, craft, science, knowledge, wisdom, or any other grounds. Even when blamed, censured, or accused, he should not tremble, especially not tremble, not be shaken here and there, not be terrified, especially not be terrified, not be terrified from all sides, not be afraid, and not fall into terror because of that blame, censure, accusation, ill-repute, or detraction. He should be fearless, unshakable, undaunted, and not one who flees; he should live with fear and dread abandoned, and with hair not standing on end. Therefore, it is said: "He should not tremble because of blame."

"A bhikkhu should not be elated when praised" means: In this Dispensation, some bhikkhus are praised based on birth, lineage, family status, beauty of complexion, wealth, learning, occupation, craft, science...
300:
...knowledge, wisdom, or any other grounds. They are praised, lauded, extolled, and commended. When thus praised, lauded, extolled, and commended, he should not be elated, should not be uplifted, should not be conceited, and should not be stubborn because of that praise, laudation, fame, or commendation. He should not generate pride because of it; he should not be stubborn, very stubborn, or one who holds his head high because of that praise. This is the meaning of "A bhikkhu should not be elated when praised."

"He should dispel greed along with stinginess, anger, and slander" means: Greed (lobha) is the act of longing, the state of longing, intense lust, the act of intense lust, the state of intense lust, covetousness, and the unwholesome root of greed. Stinginess (macchariya) refers to the five types of stinginess: stinginess regarding dwellings, families, gains, beauty, and the Dhamma. Stinginess is also called "grasping" (gāha). Anger (kodha) is the resentment of the mind, hostility, enmity, opposition, anger, fury, intense fury, hatred, intense hatred, pervasive hatred, corruption of the mind, mental ill-will, the act of being angry, the state of being angry, the act of hating, the state of hating, the act of corruption, the state of corruption, opposition, repeated opposition, harshness, speaking ill, and the mind's dissatisfaction. Slander (pesuñña) means: In this Dispensation, a certain person is one of divisive speech; hearing from these people, he tells those people to divide them; or hearing from those people, he tells these people to divide them. Thus, he divides those who are united and encourages those who are divided. He delights in factions, enjoys factions, rejoices in factions, and speaks words that create factions. This is called slander.

Furthermore, one conveys slander for two reasons: out of a desire to be loved or with the intention to divide. How does one convey slander out of a desire to be loved? Thinking, "I will be dear to this person, I will be pleasing, I will be an intimate, I will be an insider, I will be a close friend," one conveys slander out of a desire to be loved. How does one convey slander with the intention to divide? Thinking, "How can these people be separated, be apart, be in factions, be divided in two, be of two minds, be in two parties, be split, not come together, and live in suffering and discomfort?" one conveys slander with the intention to divide. "He should dispel greed along with stinginess, anger, and slander" means he should dispel, especially dispel, abandon, remove, destroy, and bring to non-existence greed, stinginess, anger, and slander.

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
301:
## 

A bhikkhu should not tremble because of blame, nor should he be elated when praised. He should dispel greed along with stinginess, and also anger and slander. He should not engage in buying and selling; a bhikkhu should not make any accusation anywhere; he should not be attached to the village; he should not speak flatteringly to people with a desire for gain.

'He should not engage in buying and selling' means: Those types of buying and selling prohibited in the Vinaya are not what is intended in this context. How does one engage in buying and selling? One exchanges a bowl, a robe, or any other requisite with the five classes of fellow practitioners while practicing deception or desiring profit. In this way, one engages in buying and selling. How does one not engage in buying and selling? One exchanges a bowl, a robe, or any other requisite with the five classes of fellow practitioners without practicing deception and without desiring profit. In this way, one does not engage in buying and selling. 'He should not engage in buying and selling' means: He should not engage in buying and selling, he should not persist in it; he should abandon buying and selling, dispel it, put an end to it, and lead it to non-existence. He should be far removed from buying and selling, abstain from it, refrain from it, emerge from it, be released from it, be liberated from it, be disconnected from it, and dwell with a mind that has no boundaries. This is the meaning of 'He should not engage in buying and selling.'

'A bhikkhu should not make any accusation anywhere' means: What are the defilements that cause accusations? There are certain ascetics and brahmins who possess psychic powers, the divine eye, and the ability to know the minds of others. They see even from afar, they are not seen even when near, and they know the minds of others with their own minds. There are also deities who possess psychic powers, the divine eye, and the ability to know the minds of others. They see even from afar, they are not seen even when near, and they know the minds of others with their own minds. They might accuse one based on gross defilements, medium defilements, or subtle defilements.

What are the gross defilements? Bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct—these are called gross defilements. What are the medium defilements? Thoughts of sensual desire, thoughts of ill-will, and thoughts of cruelty—these are called medium defilements. What are the subtle defilements? Thoughts related to relatives, thoughts related to the country, thoughts of immortality (amara-vitakka), thoughts connected with compassion for others...
302:
...thoughts related to relatives, thoughts related to the country, thoughts of immortality, thoughts connected with compassion for others, thoughts connected with gain, honor, and fame, and thoughts connected with the desire not to be despised—these are called subtle defilements. One should not be accused by those [beings] with gross defilements, medium defilements, or subtle defilements; one should not make an accusation. One should not perform, generate, produce, give rise to, or manifest the defilements that cause accusations. One should abandon the defilements that cause accusations, dispel them, put an end to them, and lead them to non-existence. Being far removed from the defilements that cause accusations, abstaining from them, refraining from them, emerging from them, being released from them, being liberated from it, being disconnected from them, one should dwell with a mind that has no boundaries. 'Anywhere' (kuhinci) means in any place, whether internally, externally, or both internally and externally. This is the meaning of 'a bhikkhu should not make any accusation anywhere.'

'He should not be attached to the village' means: How is one attached to the village? Here, a bhikkhu dwells in association with laypeople, sharing their joys and sorrows, being happy when they are happy and sad when they are sad; when their affairs and duties arise, he personally exerts effort and carries them out. In this way, he is attached to the village.

Furthermore, a bhikkhu, having dressed in the morning and taking his bowl and robe, enters a village or town for alms with an unguarded body, unguarded speech, and unguarded mind, without established mindfulness and with unrestrained senses. He gets attached to various objects there, clings to them, becomes bound by them, and falls into ruin. In this way, too, he is attached to the village.

How is one not attached to the village? Here, a bhikkhu dwells in the village without associating with laypeople, not sharing their joys and sorrows, not being happy when they are happy and not being sad when they are sad; when their affairs and duties arise, he does not personally exert effort to carry them out. In this way, he is not attached to the village.

Furthermore, a bhikkhu, having dressed in the morning and taking his bowl and robe, enters a village or town for alms with a guarded body, guarded speech, and guarded mind, with established mindfulness and restrained senses. He does not get attached to various objects there, does not cling to them, does not become bound by them, and does not fall into ruin. In this way, too, he is not attached to the village. 'He should not be attached to the village' means he should not be attached, should not cling, should not be bound, and should not be entangled in the village.
303:
One who is without greed, unattached, not infatuated, not engrossed, with greed gone, with greed vanished, with greed abandoned... should dwell with a mind that has become sublime—he should not be attached even in the village.

One should not speak flatteringly to people out of desire for gain—what is flattery (lapana)? For one who is dependent on gain, honor, and fame, who has evil desires, who is overcome by longing, who has an eye for material things, who regards worldly conditions as important, it is the talking to others, prattling, whispering, flattering, high-flattery, extolling, great-extolling, praising, special praising, showing off, special showing off, speaking pleasant words for the sake of the four requisites, speaking to gain affection, speaking in a broken way like bean soup (muggasūpyatā), acting like a nursemaid, speaking ill of others behind their backs, and the smooth talk, gentle talk, soft talk, and non-harsh talk towards them—this is called flattery (lapana).

Furthermore, one speaks flatteringly to people for two reasons: either by putting oneself low and exalting others, or by putting oneself high and lowering others. How does one speak flatteringly to people by putting oneself low and exalting others? "You are of great help to me; depending on you, I receive robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites. Even when others think of giving to me or serving me, it is only because they depend on you and look up to you. Even my old name given by my parents has disappeared. Because of you, I am known as the family-priest of such-and-such a person, or the family-priest of such-and-such a lady." In this way, one speaks flatteringly to people by putting oneself low and exalting others.

How does one speak flatteringly to people by putting oneself high and lowering others? "I am of great help to you; because of me, you have gone to the Buddha for refuge, gone to the Dhamma for refuge, gone to the Saṅgha for refuge. You abstain from taking life, from taking what is not given, from sexual misconduct, from false speech, and from the use of intoxicants which cause heedlessness. I give you the recitation of the texts, I give you the explanations, I inform you of the Uposatha day, I supervise the new constructions. Yet, you disregard me and show respect, honor, esteem, and veneration only to others." In this way, one speaks flatteringly to people by putting oneself high and lowering others.
304:
One should not speak to people out of desire for gain—this means that for the sake of gain, by reason of gain, because of gain, for the production of gain, while ripening gain, one should not speak to people. One should abandon flattery, dispel it, make an end of it, and bring it to non-existence. One should be far from flattery, abstain from it, refrain from it, be withdrawn from it, be released from it, be specially released from it, be detached from defilements, and dwell with a mind that is without boundaries. Therefore, it is said: "One should not speak flatteringly to people out of desire for gain."

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
"He should not stand in buying and selling; a monk should not utter blame anywhere;
He should not be attached in the village; he should not speak flatteringly to people out of desire for gain."

A monk should not be a boaster, nor should he speak words that are calculated;
He should not train in impudence, nor should he speak wrangling speech.

"A monk should not be a boaster"—here, a certain monk is a boaster, an excessive boaster. He boasts and brags, "I am accomplished in virtue," or "I am accomplished in practices," or "I am accomplished in virtue and practices." He boasts and brags by way of birth, or lineage, or being a son of a good family, or beauty of complexion, or wealth, or study, or work, or craft, or science, or learning, or ready wit, or some other thing. Or he boasts and brags, "I am one who went forth from a high family," or "I am one who went forth from a family of great wealth," or "I am one who went forth from a family of noble wealth," or "I am a reciter of the Suttas," or "I am a bearer of the Vinaya," or "I am a Dhamma-teacher," or "I am a forest-dweller"... or "I am an attainer of the meditative attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception." He should not boast in this way, he should not brag excessively. He should abandon boasting, dispel it, make an end of it, and bring it to non-existence. He should be far from boasting, abstain from it, refrain from it, be withdrawn from it, be released from it, be specially released from it, be detached from defilements, and dwell with a mind that is without boundaries. Therefore, it is said: "A monk should not be a boaster."
305:
One should not speak calculated speech (speech with an intended benefit). What is calculated speech? Here, someone speaks speech connected with robes, speaks speech connected with alms-food, speaks speech connected with lodgings, or speaks speech connected with medicinal requisites for the sick. This is called calculated speech.

Alternatively, for the sake of robes, for the sake of alms-food, for the sake of lodgings, or for the sake of medicinal requisites for the sick, one speaks what is true and what is false, speaks slander and what is not slander, speaks harsh words and what is not harsh, speaks frivolous talk and what is not frivolous, or speaks in a slow, hesitant manner. This also is called calculated speech. Alternatively, with a devout mind, one teaches the Dhamma to others, thinking: 'Oh, if only they would listen to my Dhamma! Having heard it, if only they would gain faith in the Dhamma! Having gained faith, if only they would show gestures of devotion towards me!' This is called calculated speech.

'One should not speak calculated speech' means that, starting from speech connected even with teaching the Dhamma, one should not say, speak, recite, show, or express calculated speech. One should abandon, dispel, destroy, and bring to an end calculated speech. One should be one who keeps far from calculated speech, especially abstaining, repeatedly abstaining, escaped, released, fully liberated, and detached from it. One should dwell with a mind that is free from boundaries. Thus, one should not speak calculated speech.

'One should not practice impudence of body, speech, and mind' means there are three kinds of impudence (pāgabbhiya): bodily impudence, verbal impudence, and mental impudence. What is bodily impudence? Here, a certain monk shows bodily impudence even when in the midst of the Saṅgha, even when in a group, even in the dining hall, even in the sauna, even at the water ghat, even when entering a village, and even when inside a village.

How does one show bodily impudence in the midst of the Saṅgha? Here, a certain monk, when in the midst of the Saṅgha, acting without respect, stands jostling the elder monks, sits jostling them, stands in front of them, sits in front of them, sits on a high seat, sits with his head covered, speaks while standing, or speaks while waving his arms. Thus, he shows bodily impudence in the midst of the Saṅgha.
306:
How does one show bodily impudence in a group? Here, a certain monk, when in a group, acting without respect, walks with sandals on while elder monks are walking unshod on the ambulatory; he walks on a higher ambulatory while they are walking on a lower one; he walks on the ambulatory while they are walking on the ground; he stands jostling them, sits jostling them, stands in front of them, sits in front of them, sits on a high seat, sits with his head covered, speaks while standing, or speaks while waving his arms. Thus, he shows bodily impudence in a group.

How does one show bodily impudence in the dining hall? Here, a certain monk, in the dining hall, acting without respect, sits crowding the elder monks, prevents junior monks from their seats, stands jostling them, sits jostling them, stands in front of them, sits in front of them, sits on a high seat, sits with his head covered, speaks while standing, or speaks while waving his arms. Thus, he shows bodily impudence in the dining hall.

How does one show bodily impudence in the sauna? Here, a certain monk, in the sauna, acting without respect, stands jostling the elder monks, sits jostling them, stands in front of them, sits in front of them, sits on a high seat, adds wood without asking permission, or closes the door without asking permission. Thus, he shows bodily impudence in the sauna.

How does one show bodily impudence at the water ghat? Here, a certain monk, at the water ghat, acting without respect, descends jostling the elder monks, descends in front of them, bathes jostling them, bathes in front of them, bathes upstream from them, ascends jostling them, or ascends in front of them. Thus, he shows bodily impudence at the water ghat.

How does one show bodily impudence when entering a village? Here, a certain monk, when entering a village, acting without respect, walks jostling the elder monks, walks in front of them, or overtakes the elder monks to walk in front of them. Thus, he shows bodily impudence when entering a village.

How does one show bodily impudence when inside a village? Here, a certain monk, when inside a village, enters even when told, 'Venerable sir, do not enter,' or stands even when told, 'Venerable sir, do not stand'...
307:
Even when told, "Venerable sir, do not stand," he stands. Even when told, "Venerable sir, do not sit," he sits. He enters an inappropriate place, stands in an inappropriate place, and sits in an inappropriate place. He forcibly enters the private, hidden, and secluded chambers of families where women, girls, daughters-in-law, and young maidens reside. He even strokes the head of a child. Thus, having entered a house, he displays bodily impudence. This is called bodily impudence (kāyika pāgabbhiya).

What is verbal impudence? In this Dispensation, a certain monk displays verbal impudence when in the midst of the Saṅgha, when in the midst of a group, or when having entered a house. How does he display verbal impudence in the midst of the Saṅgha? In this Dispensation, a certain monk, acting without respect in the midst of the Saṅgha, without asking the senior monks or without being invited, teaches the Dhamma to the monks in the monastery, answers questions, or recites the Pātimokkha. He recites while standing or while waving his arms. Thus, he displays verbal impudence in the midst of the Saṅgha.

How does he display verbal impudence in the midst of a group? In this Dispensation, a certain monk, acting without respect in the midst of a group, without asking the senior monks or without being invited, teaches the Dhamma to the monks in the monastery, answers questions, recites while standing, or recites while waving his arms. He teaches the Dhamma to the bhikkhunīs, laymen, and laywomen in the monastery, answers questions, recites while standing, or recites while waving his arms. Thus, he displays verbal impudence in the midst of a group.

How does he display verbal impudence when having entered a house? In this Dispensation, a certain monk, having entered a house, says this to a woman or a girl: "Woman of such-and-such a name, of such-and-such a clan, what is there? Is there gruel? Is there rice? Is there food? What shall we drink? What shall we eat? What shall we chew? Or what is there? Or what will you give me?" Thus he prattles. In this way, he displays verbal impudence when having entered a house. This is called verbal impudence (vācasika pāgabbhiya).

What is mental impudence? In this Dispensation, a certain monk, though not one gone forth from a high-born family, makes himself equal in mind to one gone forth from a high-born family. Though not one gone forth from a family of great wealth, he makes himself equal in mind to one gone forth from a family of great wealth. Though not one gone forth from a family of magnificent possessions...
308:
...though not one gone forth from a family of magnificent possessions, he makes himself equal in mind to one gone forth from a family of magnificent possessions. Though not a reciter of the Suttas (suttantika), he makes himself equal in mind to a reciter of the Suttas. Though not a master of the Vinaya (vinayadhara)... though not a Dhamma-speaker (dhammakathika)... though not a forest-dweller (āraññika)... though not an alms-food eater (piṇḍapātika)... though not a rag-robe wearer (paṃsukūlika)... though not a three-robe wearer (tecīvarika)... though not a consecutive-house walker (sapadānacārika)... though not one who refuses later food (khalupacchābhattika)... though not a sitter-up (nesajjika)... though not one who uses whatever seat is offered (yathāsanthatika), he makes himself equal in mind to one who uses whatever seat is offered. Though not an attainer of the first jhāna, he makes himself equal in mind to an attainer of the first jhāna. Though not an attainer of the second jhāna... the third jhāna... the fourth jhāna... the attainment of the base of infinite space... the attainment of the base of infinite consciousness... the attainment of the base of nothingness... though not an attainer of the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he makes himself equal in mind to an attainer of the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. This is called mental impudence (cetasika pāgabbhiya). "One should not train in impudence" means one should not learn impudence, should not practice it, should not frequent it, should not perform it well, and should not undertake and practice it. One should abandon impudence, dispel it, eliminate it, and bring it to non-existence. One should be one who keeps far from impudence, especially abstaining, repeatedly abstaining, escaped, released, fully liberated, and detached. One should dwell with a mind that has no boundaries. This is the meaning of the phrase "One should not train in impudence."

How should one not speak contentious words? What is contentious speech (viggāhikā kathā)? In this Dispensation, a certain person is a speaker of such words as: "You do not understand this Dhamma and Vinaya... if you are able, explain yourself to be free from the fault I have pointed out." For this was said by the Blessed One: "Moggallāna, when there is contentious speech, much talk is to be expected. When there is much talk, there is restlessness. For one who is restless, there is no restraint. For one who is unrestrained, the mind is far from concentration."

How should one not speak contentious words? One should not speak, utter, show, or use contentious speech. One should abandon contentious speech, dispel it, eliminate it, and bring it to non-existence. One should be one who keeps far from contentious speech, especially abstaining, repeatedly abstaining, escaped, released, fully liberated, and detached. One should dwell with a mind that has no boundaries. This is the meaning of the phrase "How should one not speak contentious words."

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
309:
A monk should not be boastful, nor should he speak words that are connected with what is useless. He should not practice impudence (pāgabbhiya) of body, speech, or mind, nor should he speak words that lead to contention.

He should not be attached to lying, nor should he knowingly practice deceit. Furthermore, he should not despise others on account of his livelihood, wisdom, or virtue and practices.

'Mosavajje na niyyetha' means: Falsehood is called mosavajja. In this Dispensation, some person, whether in the midst of an assembly or in the midst of a gathering... for the sake of some small worldly gain, knowingly speaks a lie; this is called mosavajja. In another way, false speech occurs through three aspects: the prior intention 'I will lie', the awareness while speaking 'I am lying', and the awareness after speaking 'I have lied'. Furthermore, false speech occurs through four, five, six, seven, or eight aspects. By perverting one's view, perverting one's patience, perverting one's preference, perverting one's perception, and perverting one's intention, along with the prior intention 'I will lie', the awareness while speaking 'I am lying', and the awareness after speaking 'I have lied'—through these eight aspects, false speech occurs. 'Mosavajje na niyyetha' means one should not go towards, depart into, be carried by, or accumulate false speech. One should abandon, dispel, end, and bring to non-existence false speech. One should be one who is far from, particularly abstinent from, repeatedly abstinent from, emerged from, released from, particularly released from, and disconnected from false speech, and should dwell with a mind that has made no boundaries—this is 'mosavajje na niyyetha'.

'Sampajāno saṭhāni na kayirā' means: What is deceit (sāṭheyya)? In this Dispensation, some person is deceitful, thoroughly deceitful.
