They invite him again and again with robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites. That monk says: 'Due to the presence of three things, a son of good family who is endowed with faith accumulates much merit. Due to the presence of faith, a son of good family who is endowed with faith accumulates much merit; due to the presence of the gift (deyyadhamma), a son of good family who is endowed with faith accumulates much merit; due to the presence of the recipients (dakkhiṇeyya), a son of good family who is endowed with faith accumulates much merit. You have this faith, the gift is present, and I am the recipient. If I do not accept, and if I do not accept in this way, you will be excluded from merit. I have no need for this benefit, but I accept it solely out of compassion for you.' Based on that reason, he accepts many robes, many alms-food, many lodgings, and many medicinal requisites. Such deceit and the state of being a deceiver is...
368:
'I shall accept; if I do not accept, you will be excluded from merit. I have no need for this gift, but I accept it solely out of compassion for you.' Based on that reason, he accepts many robes, accepts much alms-food, accepts many lodgings, and accepts many medicinal requisites for the sick. Such frowning, the state of frowning, deceit, the act of deceiving, the state of being deceitful—this is the ground of deceit known as the use of requisites.

What is the ground of deceit known as postures? Here, someone has evil desires, is overcome by wrong ambition, and desires recognition. Thinking, 'Thus people will recognize me,' he regulates his walking, regulates his standing, regulates his sitting, and regulates his lying down. He walks with composure, stands with composure, sits with composure, and lies down with composure. He walks as if he were concentrated, stands as if he were concentrated, sits as if he were concentrated, and lies down as if he were concentrated. He becomes like one who meditates in the presence of others. Such regulating, maintaining, and well-maintaining of postures, frowning, the state of frowning, deceit, the act of deceiving, the state of being deceitful—this is the ground of deceit known as postures.

What is the ground of deceit known as talk related to [attainments like] jhāna and paths? Here, someone has evil desires, is overcome by wrong ambition, and desires recognition. Thinking, 'Thus people will recognize me,' he speaks words connected with the Dhamma of the Noble Ones. He says, 'The monk who wears such a robe is an influential monk.' He says, 'The monk who carries such an alms-bowl... carries a bronze bowl... carries a water-strainer... carries a filter... carries a key... carries sandals... carries a waist-band... carries a meditation strap (āyoga), that monk is an influential monk.' He says, 'The monk who has such a preceptor (upajjhāya) is an influential monk.' He says, 'The monk who has such a teacher (ācariya)... has such fellow-preceptor-students... fellow-teacher-students... friends... acquaintances... intimates... companions, that monk is an influential monk.' He says, 'The monk who lives in such a monastery (vihāra) is an influential monk.' He says, 'The monk who lives in such a lean-to (aḍḍhayoga)... lives in a mansion (pāsāda)... lives in a flat-roofed house (hammiya)... lives in a cave (guhā)... lives in a mountain cleft (leṇa)... lives in a hut (kuṭi)... lives in a gabled house (kūṭāგāra)... lives in a watchtower (aṭṭa)... lives in a pavilion (māḷa)... lives in a stilted house (uddaṇḍa)... lives in an attendance hall (upaṭṭhānasālā)...'
369: (That person) says, "This monk lives in a rest house, lives in a pavilion, lives at the foot of a tree; that monk is of great power." Alternatively, being one who frowns much, who is very deceitful, who speaks with flattery, and who puts on a certain facial expression, (he says), "This monk is a gainer of such attainments of the meditative abidings." He speaks such deep, secret, subtle, concealed, supramundane speech connected with emptiness. There is such frowning, the state of frowning, deceiving, the manner of deceiving, and the state of being a deceiver. This is called the ground of deceit (kuhana) known as talking about nearby attainments (sāmantajappana). For the Blessed Buddha, these three grounds of deceit have been abandoned, cut off at the root, calmed, quieted, made incapable of arising, and burnt by the fire of knowledge. Therefore, because the Buddha is without deceit, he is called "Akuha." "Gaṇimāgataṃ" means: The Buddha is called "Gaṇī" because he has a following. He is "Gaṇī" because he is a group teacher; he is "Gaṇī" because he is the master of a group; he is "Gaṇī" because he leads a group; he is "Gaṇī" because he advises a group; he is "Gaṇī" because he instructs a group; he is "Gaṇī" because he approaches a group confidently; he is "Gaṇī" because the members of the group listen to him respectfully, lend an ear, and apply their minds to understand; he is "Gaṇī" because he rouses the group from unwholesome states and establishes them in wholesome states. He is the Gaṇī, the leader of the group of monks, the group of nuns, the group of laymen, the group of laywomen, the group of kings, the group of Khattiyas, the group of Brahmins, the group of Vessas, the group of Suddas, the group of Brahmas, and the group of Devas. To the Blessed One who has a following and is a group teacher. "Āgataṃ" means approached, well-approached, or arrived. "Saṅkassanagaraṃ" means to the city of Saṅkassa. Thus, "Akuhaṃ gaṇimāgataṃ" (the undeceiving one, the group teacher, who has arrived). "Bahūnamidha baddhānaṃ" means: In this Dispensation, of many Khattiyas, Brahmins, Vessas, Suddas, householders, renunciants, devas, and humans. "Baddhānaṃ" means those who are bound, constant attendants, servants, or disciples (into the midst of whom). "Atthi pañhena āgamaṃ" means: They have come because they desire a question; they have come wishing to ask a question; they have come wishing to hear a question. In this way also, it means "Atthi pañhena āgamaṃ." Alternatively, there may be the coming, the approaching, the drawing near, and the attending of those who desire a question, who wish to ask a question, or who wish to hear a question. Alternatively, there is a coming to you for the purpose of asking a question.
370: You also are capable of speaking and answering the question I have asked. There is also a coming with a question that says, "Carry this burden." Therefore, the Elder Sāriputta said: "I pay homage to that Buddha, who is independent of craving, unshaken by the worldly conditions, free from deceit, the teacher of a group, who has arrived (at the city of Saṅkassa), to whom many disciples and attendants in this world, who are bound, come to ask questions." For a monk who is repelled (by the suffering of the round of rebirths), who resorts to a secluded seat, the foot of a tree, or a cemetery, or the caves of mountains (he should endure dangers). "Bhikkhuno vijigucchato" means: "Bhikkhuno" refers to a virtuous worldling monk or a monk who is a trainee (sekha). "Vijigucchato" means because of being repelled by birth; because of being repelled by aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, physical pain, mental grief, and despair; by the suffering in hell, the suffering in the animal realm, the suffering in the realm of hungry ghosts, the suffering in the human realm; the suffering rooted in entering the womb, the suffering rooted in staying in the womb, the suffering rooted in emerging from the womb; the suffering of a newborn being washed and cared for; the suffering of a newborn being oppressed by others; the suffering due to one's own effort, the suffering due to the effort of others; the suffering of pain (dukkha-dukkha), the suffering of formations (saṅkhāra-dukkha), the suffering due to change (vipariṇāma-dukkha); the suffering due to eye disease, ear disease, nose disease, tongue disease, body disease, head disease, ear-flap disease, mouth disease, tooth disease; the suffering due to cough, asthma, catarrh, internal heat, fever, stomach disease, fainting, vomiting blood, piercing pain, diarrhea, leprosy, boils, eczema, consumption, epilepsy, skin rash, itching, ringworm, scratches, sores on palms and soles, disorders of blood and bile, diabetes, hemorrhoids, pustules, fistula; illness arising from bile, illness arising from phlegm, illness arising from wind, illness arising from a conflict of humors, illness produced by change of season, illness produced by improper care, illness produced by external assault, illness produced by the result of kamma; cold, heat, hunger, thirst, defecation, urination; the suffering from the touch of gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and reptiles; the suffering from the death of a mother, the death of a father, the death of a brother, the death of a sister (it refers to a monk who is repelled and disgusted by these).
371:
For a monk who is disgusted, weary, ashamed, and repelled by the suffering of the death of a son, the death of a daughter, the loss of relatives, the loss of wealth, the occurrence of disease, the failure of virtue, or the failure of right view, it is said: "bhikkhuno vijigucchato" (for a monk who is disgusted).

"bhajato rittamāsanaṃ" (resorting to an empty seat) means: where one sits is called a seat (āsana). These are a couch, a bench, a cushion, a mat, a skin-rug, a grass-mat, a leaf-mat, or a straw-mat (or a branch-mat). That seat is empty, secluded, and quite secluded from seeing unsuitable forms; empty, secluded, and quite secluded from hearing unsuitable sounds; empty, secluded, and quite secluded from the five unsuitable cords of sensual pleasure. For a monk who resorts to, frequents, serves, uses, associates with, and makes use of such a quite secluded seat, it is said: "bhajato rittamāsanaṃ."

"rukkhamūlaṃ susānaṃ vā" (the root of a tree or a cemetery) means: the root of a tree is just the root of a tree; a cemetery is just a cemetery. "pabbatānaṃ guhāsu vā" (or in mountain caves) means: a mountain is just a mountain; a cleft is just a cleft; a cave in a mountain is just a mountain cave. Mountain valleys are called pabbatantarikā (mountain gaps).

Therefore, the Elder Sāriputta said:
"A monk who is disgusted should resort to an empty seat,
The root of a tree, or a cemetery,
Or in mountain caves."

In high and low lodgings, there are dreadful things making sounds.
Because of those [fears], a monk should not tremble in a silent lodging.

"uccāvacesu sayanesu" (in high and low lodgings) means: in high and low, inferior and superior, good and bad lodgings. A lodging (sayana) is called a dwelling (senāsana), such as a monastery (vihāra), a curved house (aḍḍhayoga), a long house (pāsāda), a mansion (hammiya), or a cave (guhā). "kivanto tattha bheravā" (how many are the dreadful things there) means: those fears that make sounds and cries. Alternatively, "kivanto" asks: how many, what amount, what extent, or how numerous are they? Dreadful things (bheravā) are lions, tigers, leopards, bears, hyenas, wolves, buffaloes, elephants, snakes, scorpions, and centipedes. Or they could be thieves, or men, or those who have committed crimes, or those who have not committed crimes.

"ye hi bhikkhu na vedheyya" (by which a monk should not tremble) means: seeing or hearing those dreadful things, a monk should not tremble, should not be shaken, should not be greatly shaken, should not be terrified, should not...
372: ...should not be startled, should not be especially startled, should not be terrified, should not be afraid, and should not fall into terror. He should dwell without fear, without trembling, without being terrified, without fleeing, having abandoned fear and dread, and with his hair not standing on end. This is the meaning of 'ye hi bhikkhu na vedheyya'. 'Nigghose sayanāsane' means in a bed and dwelling that is quiet, free from the noise of towns and villages, secluded from people, desired for its solitude, and suitable for seclusion. Therefore, the Elder Sāriputta said: 'How many terrors are there in high and low dwellings? A monk should not tremble in a noiseless dwelling.' For one who goes to the region of Nibbāna, which has not even been reached in dreams, how many dangers are there in the world? What dangers should a monk overcome in a secluded dwelling? In the phrase 'kati parissayā loke', 'kati' asks: how many, what amount, or what extent are they? 'Parissayā' (dangers) are of two kinds: manifest dangers and hidden dangers. What are the manifest dangers? They are lions, tigers, leopards, bears, hyenas, wolves, buffaloes, elephants, snakes, scorpions, centipedes, thieves, oppressors, those who have committed crimes, or those who have not yet committed crimes. Furthermore, they include eye-disease, ear-disease, nose-disease, tongue-disease, body-disease, head-disease, internal ear-disease, mouth-disease, tooth-disease, cough, asthma, catarrh, burning fever, fever, stomach-ache, fainting, dysentery, sharp pain, cholera, leprosy, boils, eczema, consumption, epilepsy, ringworm, scabies, itch, scratches, foot and hand sores, blood-disorders, bile-disorders, diabetes, shoulder-pain, abscesses, fistula; diseases arising from bile, phlegm, or wind; diseases caused by the union of humors, by change of season, by improper posture, by exertion, or by kamma; and the touch of cold, heat, hunger, thirst, excrement, urine, gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and creeping things. These are called manifest dangers. What are the hidden dangers? They are bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, mental misconduct, the hindrance of sensual desire, the hindrance of ill-will, the hindrance of sloth and torpor, the hindrance of restlessness and worry, the hindrance of doubt, greed, hatred, delusion, anger, enmity, disparaging, malice, envy, stinginess, deceit, craftiness, obstinacy, impetuosity, conceit, arrogance, intoxication, and negligence; all defilements, all misconduct, all distress, all fevers, all anxieties, and all unwholesome formations. These are called hidden dangers.
373:
What is the meaning of 'parissaya' (danger)? They are called 'parissaya' because they oppress; they are called 'parissaya' because they lead to decline; they are called 'parissaya' because they reside therein (within the individual existence).

How do they oppress, thus being called 'parissaya'? These dangers oppress, overcome, overwhelm, exhaust, and harass that person. Thus, they are called 'parissaya' because they oppress.

How do they lead to decline, thus being called 'parissaya'? These dangers lead to obstacles and the decline of wholesome states (kusala dhamma). What wholesome states? They lead to obstacles and the decline of: right practice, conformable practice, non-hostile practice, non-opposing practice, practice according to the meaning, practice according to the Dhamma, fulfillment of virtue (sīla), guarding the doors of the sense faculties, moderation in eating, devotion to wakefulness, mindfulness and clear comprehension, the development of the four foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna), the four right efforts (sammappadhāna), the four bases of power (iddhipāda), the five faculties (indriya), the five powers (bala), the seven factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga), and the development of the Noble Eightfold Path. Thus, they are called 'parissaya' because they lead to decline.

How do they reside therein, thus being called 'parissaya'? These evil unwholesome states arise depending on the individual existence (attabhāva). Just as creatures that dwell in holes reside in holes, creatures that dwell in water reside in water, creatures that dwell in the forest reside in the forest, and creatures that dwell in trees reside in trees; in the same way, these evil unwholesome states arise depending on the individual existence. Thus, they are called 'parissaya' because they reside therein.

The Blessed One said this: "Monks, a monk who is sāntevāsika (having an internal pupil) and sācariyaka (having an internal teacher) lives in suffering and discomfort. And how, monks, is a monk sāntevāsika and sācariyaka? Here, monks, when a monk sees a form with the eye, evil unwholesome states arise through various thoughts and as objects of the fetters. These evil unwholesome states dwell within him and flow along. Therefore, he is called 'sāntevāsika'. Those states oppress him; those evil unwholesome states arise by oppressing him. Therefore, he is called 'sācariyaka'.

Furthermore, monks, when a monk hears a sound with the ear... smells an odor with the nose... tastes a flavor with the tongue... touches a tangible object with the body... cognizes a mental phenomenon with the mind, evil unwholesome states arise through various thoughts and as objects of the fetters."
374:
These evil unwholesome states dwell within him and flow along. Therefore, he is called 'sāntevāsika' (one who has a co-resident within). Those states arise by oppressing him; those evil unwholesome states arise by oppressing him. Therefore, he is called 'sācariyaka' (one who has a teacher within). Monks, in this way, a monk who is sāntevāsika and sācariyaka lives in suffering and discomfort. In this way also, 'tatrāsaya' (residing therein) refers to these very dangers (parissaya).

The Blessed One said this: 'Monks, there are these three internal stains, internal enemies, internal adversaries, internal killers, and internal foes. What three? Monks, greed (lobha) is an internal stain, an internal enemy, an internal adversary, an internal killer, and an internal foe. Hatred (dosa) is... [as above]... Delusion (moha) is an internal stain, an internal enemy, an internal adversary, an internal killer, and an internal foe. Monks, these three are internal stains, enemies, adversaries, killers, and foes.'

Greed produces harm; greed agitates the mind.
Danger arises from within, but people do not realize it.
A greedy person does not know the benefit; a greedy person does not see the Dhamma.
When greed overcomes a man, then there is utter darkness.

Hatred produces harm; hatred agitates the mind.
Danger arises from within, but people do not realize it.
An angry person does not know the benefit; an angry person does not see the Dhamma.
When hatred overcomes a man, then there is utter darkness.

Delusion produces harm; delusion agitates the mind.
Danger arises from within, but people do not realize it.
A deluded person does not know the benefit; a deluded person does not see the Dhamma.
When delusion overcomes a man, then there is utter darkness.

In this way also, 'tatrāsaya' refers to these very dangers (parissaya). The Blessed One said this: 'Great King, three things arising within a man arise for his harm, for his suffering, and for his discomfort. What three?'
375:
“Great King, three things that arise within a man arise for his harm, for his suffering, and for his discomfort. Great King, greed, when it arises within a man, arises for his harm, for his suffering, and for his discomfort. Great King, hatred... (pe)... Great King, delusion, when it arises within a man, arises for his harm, for his suffering, and for his discomfort. Great King, these three things, when they arise within a man, arise for his harm, for his suffering, and for his discomfort.”

“Greed, hatred, and delusion,
Arising from within himself,
Harm the man of evil mind,
Just as its own fruit destroys the bamboo reed.”

In this way, the things resorted to therein are ‘perils’ (parissaya).
For this was said by the Blessed One:
‘Passion and hatred have this self as their cause; dislike, delight, and horripilation are born from this self. Arising from this self, unwholesome thoughts (disturb the mind), just as boys release a crow.’

In this way, the things resorted to therein are perils. ‘In the world’ means in the world of humans—how many perils are there in the world?

‘One who goes sees the unreached region.’ The ‘unreached region’ (agata disā) refers to the deathless Nibbāna. That Nibbāna is the stilling of all formations (saṅkhāra), the relinquishing of all acquisitions (upadhi), the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna. That region has not been reached before; it is a region not previously reached in this long period of time.

‘Just as one would carry a bowl of oil filled to the brim without spilling,
So should one who longs for the unreached region protect his own mind.’

One who goes, who proceeds, who advances towards the unreached region—this is meant by ‘one who goes to the unreached region.’

‘The monk who can overcome (perils).’ ‘Who’ means the person who can overcome, conquer, overwhelm, master, and crush the perils—this is meant by ‘the monk who can overcome.’
376:
‘In a remote lodging’ (pantaṃ sayanāsanaṃ) means—a lodging that is at the edge, distant, on the boundary, at the foot of a mountain, in a forest, by a river, or by the water; where there is no plowing or sowing, beyond the vicinity of people, and past the range of human travel—this is meant by ‘in a remote lodging.’

Therefore, the Elder Sāriputta said:

“How many are the perils in the world,
For a monk who goes to the unreached region (Nibbāna),
And stays in a remote lodging?

What would be his mode of speech?
What would be his resorts (gocara) here?
What would be the virtues and vows,
Of that monk who is resolute?”

‘What would be his mode of speech?’ (kyāssa byappathayo assu) means—with what kind of speech would he be endowed? Of what form, what variety, and what nature would it be? Thus, it asks about the purity of speech (vacīpārisuddhi). What is purity of speech? Here, a monk, having abandoned false speech, abstains from false speech; he speaks the truth, is devoted to truth, is reliable, trustworthy, and not a deceiver of the world. Having abandoned slanderous speech, he abstains from slanderous speech; what he hears here he does not tell there to cause division among these people, or what he hears there he does not tell here to cause division among those people; thus he is a reconciler of those who are divided and a promoter of those who are united; he loves concord, delights in concord, enjoys concord, and speaks words that create concord. Having abandoned harsh speech, he abstains from harsh speech; he speaks such words as are blameless, pleasant to the ear, lovely, reaching the heart, polite, pleasing to many, and agreeable to many. Having abandoned frivolous chatter, he abstains from frivolous chatter; he speaks at the right time, speaks what is factual, speaks what is beneficial, speaks what is Dhamma, speaks what is Vinaya; at the right time he speaks words worth treasuring, accompanied by reasons, defined, and connected with the goal.

Endowed with these four types of right speech and free from the four faults of speech, he speaks. He avoids, abstains, refrains, emerges from, is released from, and is detached from the thirty-two types of lowly talk (tiracchānakathā), and dwells with a mind that is boundless. He speaks on the ten subjects of talk (kathāvatthu), namely: talk on wanting little, talk on contentment, talk on seclusion, talk on non-association, talk on arousing energy, talk on virtue, talk on concentration, talk on wisdom, talk on liberation, and talk on the knowledge and vision of liberation. Furthermore, he speaks on the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna), the right efforts (sammappadhāna), the bases of power (iddhipāda), the faculties (indriya), the powers (bala), the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga), the path (magga), the fruits (phala), and Nibbāna.
377:
He speaks words connected with the bases of power (iddhipāda), the faculties (indriya), the powers (bala), the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga), the path (magga), the fruit (phala), and Nibbāna. This state, which is guarded, secure, and tranquil in speech, is called purification of speech (vacīpārisuddhi). To be endowed with such purification of speech is the meaning of the phrase 'kyāssa byappathayo assu' (What would his manner of speech be?).

'kyāssassu idha gocarā' (What would be his resort here?) is an inquiry into the resort (gocara): with what kind of resort should he be endowed in this Dispensation? In what form, in what variety, and in what manner? There is a proper resort (gocara) and an improper resort (agocara).

What is an improper resort? Here, a certain monk has as his resort courtesans (vesiyā), or widows (vidhavā), or mature maidens (thullakumārī), or eunuchs (paṇḍaka), or bhikkhunīs, or taverns (pānāgāra). He lives in improper association with kings, royal ministers, heretics, and disciples of heretics. Or else, he frequents, associates with, and attends upon such families that are faithless, without confidence, who are not like a source of refreshment (anopānabhūta), who are abusive and reviling, who wish for the harm, disadvantage, discomfort, and lack of security from bondage of monks, bhikkhunīs, laymen, and laywomen. This is called an improper resort.

Furthermore, when he has entered the village or is walking on the road, he goes without restraint, looking at elephants, horses, chariots, infantry, women, men, girls, boys, looking at shops and the doors of houses, looking upwards, looking downwards, and looking all around the various quarters. This also is called an improper resort.

Furthermore, having seen a form with the eye, he grasps at its signs (nimitta) and features (anubyañjana). Since, if he leaves the faculty of the mind unrestrained... for one who dwells with the mind faculty unrestrained, evil unwholesome states of covetousness and displeasure might flow in; he does not practice for its restraint, he does not guard the mind faculty, he does not achieve restraint over the mind faculty. This also is called an improper resort.
378:
Furthermore, some honorable recluses and brahmins, having eaten the food given in faith, remain addicted to visiting such unseemly shows (visūkadassana) which are like thorns to the Dispensation. Namely: dancing, singing, music, theatrical shows, storytelling, hand-clapping, cymbals, kettle-drums, dramatic performances, acrobatic displays, artful displays, bone-play, elephant fights, horse fights, buffalo fights, bull fights, goat fights, ram fights, cock fights, quail fights, fighting with sticks, boxing, wrestling, sham fights, roll-calls, battle arrays, and seeing troops. In this way, he is addicted to such unseemly shows. This also is called an improper resort (agocara).

The five cords of sensual pleasure are also called improper resorts. For this was said by the Blessed One: "Monks, do not wander in an improper resort, the range of another. Monks, for one wandering in an improper resort, the range of another, Māra will gain an opening, Māra will gain an object. And what, monks, is the improper resort, the range of another, for a monk? It is the five cords of sensual pleasure. What five? Forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust; sounds cognizable by the ear... odors cognizable by the nose... flavors cognizable by the tongue... tangibles cognizable by the body that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust. This, monks, is called the improper resort, the range of another, for a monk." This also is called an improper resort.

What is a proper resort (gocara)? Here, a monk does not have courtesans as his resort, does not have widows as his resort, does not have mature maidens as his resort, does not have eunuchs as his resort, does not have bhikkhunīs as his resort, and does not have taverns as his resort. He lives without improper association with kings, royal ministers, heretics, and disciples of heretics. Furthermore, he frequents, associates with, and attends upon such families that are faithful, full of confidence, who are like a well (opānabhūta), who are glowing with saffron robes, who are touched by the breeze of the sages, and who wish for the welfare, benefit, comfort, and security from bondage of monks, bhikkhunīs, laymen, and laywomen. This also is called a proper resort.

Furthermore, when a monk has entered the village or has reached the road, he goes with his senses restrained. He goes without looking at elephants, without looking at horses, without looking at chariots, without looking at infantry... without looking around at the quarters and intermediate quarters. This also is called a proper resort.
379:
Alternatively, a monk, having seen a form with the eye, does not grasp at its signs... he attains restraint in the faculty of the mind—this also is called 'resort' (gocara).

Alternatively, just as some honorable recluses and brahmins, having consumed food given in faith, remain addicted to such spectacles which are thorns to the dispensation, such as dancing, singing, music... watching armies; he is one who abstains from such spectacles—this also is called 'resort'.

The four foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) are also called 'resort'. For this was said by the Blessed One: "Monks, wander in your own resort, in your ancestral domain. Monks, for those wandering in their own resort, in their ancestral domain, Māra will not find an opening, Māra will not find an object. And what, monks, is a monk's own resort, his ancestral domain? It is the four foundations of mindfulness. What four? Here, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body... feelings... mind... dhammas, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and grief for the world. This, monks, is called a monk's own resort, his ancestral domain." This also is called 'resort'. He should be endowed with such a resort. "What are his resorts here?" refers to these aforementioned qualities.

Regarding the phrase "What are his virtues and vows?": With what kind of virtue and vow is he endowed? In what form, in what way, and in what likeness is he endowed? Thus, it asks about the purity of virtue and vows (sīlabbata-pārisuddhi). What is the purity of virtue and vows? There is that which is both virtue (sīla) and vow (vata), and there is that which is a vow but not virtue. What is both virtue and vow? Here, a monk is virtuous, dwelling restrained by the Pātimokkha restraint, endowed with conduct and resort, seeing danger in the slightest faults, and training in the rules of training he has undertaken. That restraint, control, and non-transgression therein is "virtue". That undertaking is "vow". It is virtue in the sense of restraint, and a vow in the sense of undertaking. This is called "both virtue and vow".

What is a vow but not virtue? The eight ascetic practices (dhutaṅga): the forest-dweller's practice, the alms-food-eater's practice, the refuse-rag-wearer's practice, the triple-robe-wearer's practice, the house-to-house-alms-seeker's practice, the one-session-eater's practice, the sitter's practice, and the any-available-seat-user's practice. This is called "a vow but not virtue". The undertaking of energy (vīriya-samādāna) is also called "a vow but not virtue". "Let only skin, sinews, and bones remain; let the flesh and blood in the body dry up; that which is attainable by manly strength, manly power, manly energy, and manly effort, without reaching it, the persistence of energy..."
380:
...will not [cease]," thus he exerts his mind and strives. This kind of undertaking of energy is also called "a vow but not virtue".

"I will not eat, I will not drink,
I will not leave the monastery,
As long as the thorn of craving is not pulled out,
I will not even lie down to sleep,"

thus he exerts his mind and strives. This kind of undertaking of energy is also called "a vow but not virtue".

"I will not break this cross-legged posture as long as my mind is not liberated from the taints (āsavas) through non-clinging," thus he exerts his mind and strives. This kind of undertaking of energy is also called "a vow but not virtue".

"I will not rise from this seat... I will not descend from this walkway... I will not leave the monastery... the aḍḍhayoga... the palace... the hammiya palace... the cave... the grotto... the hut... the peaked house... the watchtower... the pavilion... the house with pillars... the attendance hall... the pavilion... I will not leave the foot of the tree as long as my mind is not liberated from the taints through non-clinging," thus he exerts his mind and strives. This kind of undertaking of energy is also called "a vow but not virtue".

"In this very morning, I will bring, fully bring, attain, touch, and realize the Noble Dhamma," thus he exerts his mind and strives. This kind of undertaking of energy is also called "a vow but not virtue".

"In this very noon... evening... before the meal... after the meal... first watch... middle watch... last watch... during the dark fortnight... the bright fortnight... the rainy season... the winter... the summer... the first stage of life... the middle stage of life... the last stage of life, I will bring, fully bring, attain, touch, and realize the Noble Dhamma," thus he exerts his mind and strives. This kind of undertaking of energy is also called "a vow but not virtue"—this is called the purity of virtue and vows. He should be endowed with such purity of virtue and vows. "What are his virtues and vows?"

Regarding the phrase "pahitattassa bhikkhuno": "pahitattassa" means one who has aroused energy in wholesome states, who has reached strength, who has firm effort, who has unflagging desire, and who has not laid down the burden. Alternatively, "pesitattassa" means one whose self is directed for the sake of the goal, for one's own benefit (Arahatship), for the right path, for the characteristics, for the cause, and for what is or is not a cause. "All formations are impermanent"—thus his self is directed. "All formations are suffering"—thus his self is directed. "All dhammas are non-self"—thus his self is directed. "With ignorance as condition, formations come to be"—thus...
381:
... "With birth as condition, aging and death come to be"—for one who has directed the mind; "With the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease"—for one who has directed the mind; ... "With the cessation of birth, aging and death cease"—for one who has directed the mind; "This is suffering"—for one who has directed the mind; ... "This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering"—for one who has directed the mind; "These are the taints"—for one who has directed the mind; ... "This is the practice leading to the cessation of the taints"—for one who has directed the mind; "These things should be known with higher knowledge"—for one who has directed the mind; ... "These things should be realized"—for one who has directed the mind; regarding the arising, disappearance, gratification, danger, and escape of the six bases of contact—for one who has directed the mind; regarding the five aggregates of clinging ... regarding the arising, disappearance, gratification, danger, and escape of the four great elements—for one who has directed the mind; "Whatever is of the nature to arise, all that is of the nature to cease"—for one who has directed the mind. "Bhikkhuno" refers to either a virtuous worldling monk or a monk in higher training (sekha); this is the monk who has directed his mind.

Therefore, the Elder Sāriputta said this:
"What would be his modes of speech? What would be his resorts here?
What would be his virtues and vows, for a monk who has directed his mind?"
"Having taken up what training, unified, prudent, and mindful,
Should he blow away his own dross, as a smith blows away the dross of silver?"

"Kaṃ so sikkhaṃ samādāya" means: having taken, having undertaken, having grasped, having touched, and having applied the mind to what training (should he blow away the dross).

In the phrase "Ekodi nipako sato": "Ekodī" means having a unified mind, an undistracted mind, an unperturbed mind, serenity, the faculty of concentration, the power of concentration ... Right Concentration. "Nipako" means wise, prudent, intelligent, knowledgeable, discerning, and sagacious. "Sato" means mindful through four reasons: being mindful while developing the foundation of mindfulness of the body, ... of feelings, ... of the mind, ... being mindful while developing the foundation of mindfulness of mental objects. Such a person is called "sato." By "Kaṃ so sikkhaṃ samādāya," he asks about the training in higher virtue (adhisīla-sikkhā). By "Ekodi," he asks about the training in higher mind (adhicitta-sikkhā). By "Nipako," he asks about the training in higher wisdom (adhipaññā-sikkhā). By "Sato," he asks about the purity of mindfulness.
382:
As a goldsmith blows away the dross of gold, so should he blow away his own dross. A smith is called "kammāra," and gold is called "jātarūpa." Just as a goldsmith blows, thoroughly blows, and repeatedly blows away the gross dross of gold; blows, thoroughly blows, and repeatedly blows away the middle dross; and blows, thoroughly blows, and repeatedly blows away the subtle dross; in the same way, a monk blows, thoroughly blows, and repeatedly blows away his own gross defilements, abandons them, dispels them, brings them to an end, and leads them to non-arising. He blows away the middle defilements ... and the subtle defilements, abandons them, dispels them, brings them to an end, and leads them to non-arising.

Alternatively, a monk blows, thoroughly blows, and repeatedly blows away his own dross of lust, dross of hatred, dross of delusion, dross of conceit, dross of views, dross of defilements, and dross of misconduct; as well as those things that cause darkness, cause lack of vision, cause lack of knowledge, stifle wisdom, are associated with distress, and do not lead to Nibbāna; he abandons them, dispels them, brings them to an end, and leads them to non-arising.

Alternatively, through Right View, he blows, thoroughly blows, and repeatedly blows away Wrong View, abandons it, dispels it, brings it to an end, and leads it to non-arising. Through Right Intention, he blows away Wrong Intention ... through Right Speech, Wrong Speech ... through Right Action, Wrong Action ... through Right Livelihood, Wrong Livelihood ... through Right Effort, Wrong Effort ... through Right Mindfulness, Wrong Mindfulness ... through Right Concentration, Wrong Concentration ... through Right Knowledge, Wrong Knowledge ... through Right Liberation, he blows, thoroughly blows, and repeatedly blows away Wrong Liberation, abandons it, dispels it, brings it to an end, and leads it to non-arising.

Alternatively, through the Noble Eightfold Path, he blows, thoroughly blows, and repeatedly blows away all defilements, all misconduct, all distress, all fevers, all torments, and all unwholesome volitional formations, abandons them, dispels them, brings them to an end, and leads them to non-arising. This is the meaning of the words: "As a smith blows away the dross of silver, so should he blow away his own dross." Therefore, the Elder Sāriputta said: "Having taken up what training, unified, prudent, and mindful, should he blow away his own dross, as a smith blows away the dross of silver?"

(The Blessed One, addressing Sāriputta, said:)
"Sāriputta, for the monk who loathes (birth, aging, etc.), who frequents a secluded seat and bed, and who desires enlightenment—I shall explain to you the Dhamma as I know it, the way of living comfortably according to the Dhamma."
383:
In the phrase “vijigucchamānassa yadidaṃ phāsu,” “vijigucchamānassa” means for one who is repelled by being reborn, by aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, despair... for one who is repelled, weary, and ashamed of the suffering caused by the ruin of views. “Yadidaṃ phāsu” means “I shall speak of that comfortable living.” What is comfortable living (phāsuvihāra)? It is the right practice, the practice in accordance with the goal, the non-opposing practice, the non-conflicting practice, the practice in accordance with the benefit, the practice in accordance with the Dhamma, being one who fulfills the virtues (sīla), having guarded doors in the senses, knowing moderation in eating, being devoted to wakefulness, mindfulness and clear comprehension, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the Noble Eightfold Path, Nibbāna, and the practice leading to Nibbāna. This is the comfortable living meant by “vijigucchamānassa yadidaṃ phāsu.”

“Sāriputta”—the Blessed One addresses the Elder by name. “Bhagavā” (the Blessed One) is a title of respect. Furthermore, He is “Bhagavā” because He has broken (bhagga) lust; He is “Bhagavā” because He has broken hatred; He is “Bhagavā” because He has broken delusion; He is “Bhagavā” because He has broken pride; He is “Bhagavā” because He has broken views; He is “Bhagavā” because He has broken the thorns of defilements; He is “Bhagavā” because He has broken all defilements. He is “Bhagavā” because He frequents (bhaji), specially frequents, and extensively frequents the gem of the Dhamma. He is “Bhagavā” because He has made an end to existences. He is “Bhagavā” because He has a developed body, developed virtue, developed mind, and developed wisdom.

Or else, He is “Bhagavā” because He frequents (bhaji) remote lodgings (senāsana) in the great forest, which are secluded, quiet, free from noise, away from the crowd, hidden from people, and suitable for retreat. Or else, He is “Bhagavā” because He shares (bhāgī) the robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick. Or else, He is “Bhagavā” because He is a partaker (bhāgī) of the taste of the meaning, the taste of the Dhamma, the taste of liberation, higher virtue, higher mind, and higher wisdom. Or else, He is “Bhagavā” because He is a partaker of the four jhānas, the four immeasurables (appamaññā), and the four formless attainments. Or else, He is “Bhagavā” because He is a partaker of the eight deliverances (vimokkha), the eight bases of mastery (abhibhāyatana), and the nine successive attainments. Or else, He is “Bhagavā” because He is a partaker of the ten perceptions, the ten kasina attainments, the concentration on mindfulness of breathing, and the attainment of foulness (asubha). Or else, He is “Bhagavā” because He is a partaker of the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the Noble Eightfold Path. Or else, He is “Bhagavā” because He is a partaker of the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four kinds of intrepidity (vesārajja), the four kinds of analytical knowledge (paṭisambhidā), the six higher powers (abhiññā), and the six qualities of a Buddha (buddhadhamma).
384:
This name “Bhagavā” was not given by His mother, nor by His father, nor by His brothers, nor by His sisters, nor by His friends and colleagues, nor by His relatives and kin, nor by ascetics and brahmins, nor by deities. This name “Bhagavā” is a designation (paññatti) based on realization, attained by the Blessed Buddhas at the foot of the Bodhi tree along with the acquisition of omniscience at the end of the path of Arahantship. “Sāriputta, the Blessed One...” (thus the word “Bhagavā” is explained).

In the phrase “to one who resorts to a secluded seat and bed” (rittāsanaṃ sayanaṃ sevatovē), “āsana” (seat) refers to where one sits—a couch, a chair, a cushion, a mat, a piece of skin, a grass mat, a leaf mat, or a straw mat. “Sayana” (bed/dwelling) refers to a lodging (senāsana)—a monastery, a lean-to, a palace, a mansion, or a cave. That seat and bed is empty (ritta), secluded, and solitary from the sight of unsuitable forms, from the hearing of unsuitable sounds... (pe)... and from the five unsuitable cords of sensual pleasure. To one who resorts to, frequents, associates with, and makes use of that secluded seat and bed—this is the meaning of “to one who resorts to a secluded seat and bed.”

In the phrase “for one desiring enlightenment in accordance with the Dhamma” (sambodhikāmassa yathānudhamman), “bodhi” (enlightenment) refers to the knowledge, wisdom, faculty of wisdom, power of wisdom... (pe)... the enlightenment factor of investigation of states (dhammavicaya-sambojjhaṅga), inquiry, insight (vipassanā), and right view in the four paths. For one desiring to know, to follow in knowing, to penetrate, to fully awaken to, to attain, to touch, and to realize that enlightenment—this is the meaning of “for one desiring enlightenment.”

Regarding “in accordance with the Dhamma” (yathānudhamman), what are the conforming dhammas (anudhamma) of enlightenment? They are the right practice, the practice in accordance with the goal, the non-opposing practice, the practice in accordance with the meaning, the practice in accordance with the Dhamma, being one who fulfills the virtues, having guarded doors in the senses, knowing moderation in eating, being devoted to wakefulness, and mindfulness and clear comprehension. These are called the conforming dhammas of enlightenment. Alternatively, the insights (vipassanā) occurring in the preliminary stage of the four paths are the conforming dhammas of enlightenment. This is the meaning of “for one desiring enlightenment in accordance with the Dhamma.”

In the phrase “I shall declare that to you as I know it” (taṃ tē pavakkhāmi yathā pajānaṃ), “taṃ” refers to the conforming dhamma of enlightenment. “Pavakkhāmi” (I shall declare) means I will tell, I will announce, I will teach, I will point out, I will establish, I will reveal, I will analyze, I will clarify, and I will manifest. “As I know it” (yathā pajānaṃ) means as it is known, being one who knows well, who knows specially, who knows repeatedly, who knows by penetration; not by hearsay, not by tradition, not by lineage of transmission, not by conformity with scripture, not by mere logic, not by mere inference, not by reflecting on reasons, not by acceptance of a view after pondering it, but a Dhamma known by oneself, through one's own higher knowledge, personally realized. This is the meaning of “I shall declare that to you as I know it.”

Therefore, the Blessed One (said this):
385:
Sāriputta, for one who loathes defilements,
who frequents a secluded dwelling,
and who desires the knowledge of the path to Arahantship, I shall preach the appropriate Dhamma as I know it, in its various aspects.

A wise and mindful monk, who practices within limits,
should not fear the five dangers:
the danger of gadflies and flies, the danger of snakes, scorpions, and lice,
the danger of human contact, and the danger of four-legged beasts.

"A wise one should not fear the five dangers" means: A wise one (dhīra) is one who is wise, learned, intelligent, sagacious, possessed of knowledge, discerning, and prudent. A wise one should not fear the five dangers, should not tremble, should not be agitated, should not be terrified, should not be struck with terror from all sides, and should not fall into anxiety. He should dwell without fear, being unshakable, undaunted, not fleeing, with fear and dread abandoned, and with hair not standing on end.

"A mindful monk who practices within limits" means: A monk (bhikkhu) is either a virtuous ordinary person or a trainee (sekha). A mindful one (sato) is mindful through four causes: one who develops the foundation of mindfulness of contemplation of the body in the body is mindful; ... in feelings ... in the mind ... one who develops the foundation of mindfulness of contemplation of phenomena in phenomena is mindful—such a person is called mindful. One who practices within limits (sapariyantacārī) has four limits: the limit of restraint of virtue, the limit of restraint of the sense faculties, the limit of moderation in eating, and the limit of devotion to wakefulness.

What is the limit of restraint of virtue? Here, a monk is virtuous; he dwells restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha, possessed of proper conduct and resort; seeing danger in the slightest faults, he trains himself by undertaking the rules of training. Reflecting on internal impurity, he practices within the internal limit of restraint of virtue and does not break the boundary. This is the limit of restraint of virtue.

What is the limit of restraint of the sense faculties? Here, a monk, having seen a form with the eye, does not grasp at its signs or its features. Since, if he were to leave the eye faculty unguarded...
386:
...he attains restraint. Having heard a sound with the ear... having smelled an odor with the nose... having tasted a flavor with the tongue... having touched a tangible object with the body... having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, he does not grasp at signs such as 'man' or 'woman', nor does he grasp at features such as hands, feet, smiles, or laughter. Since, if he were to leave the mind faculty unguarded, evil unwholesome states of covetousness and distress might follow him, he practices for the restraint of the mind faculty, guards the mind faculty, and attains restraint over the mind faculty. Reflecting on the Ādittapariyāya Sutta, he practices within the limit of restraint of the sense faculties and does not break the boundary. This is called the limit of restraint of the sense faculties.

What is the limit of moderation in eating? Here, a monk, reflecting wisely, partakes of food neither for amusement, nor for intoxication, nor for physical beauty, nor for beautification, but only for the endurance and continuance of this body, for ending discomfort, and for assisting the holy life. He eats reflecting: 'Thus I shall terminate old feelings and not arouse new feelings, and I shall have maintenance, blamelessness, and a comfortable abiding.' Reflecting on the similes of greasing an axle, dressing a wound, and eating the flesh of one's own son, he practices within the limit of moderation in eating and does not break the boundary. This is called the limit of moderation in eating.

What is the limit of devotion to wakefulness? Here, a monk, during the day, while walking and sitting, purifies his mind of obstructive states (hindrances). During the first watch of the night, while walking and sitting, he purifies his mind of obstructive states. During the middle watch of the night, he lies down on his right side in the lion's posture, with one foot overlapping the other, mindful and clearly comprehending, after noting in his mind the time for rising. During the last watch of the night, having risen, while walking and sitting, he purifies his mind of obstructive states. Reflecting on the abiding mentioned in the Bhaddekaratta Sutta, he practices within the limit of devotion to wakefulness and does not break the boundary. This is called the limit of devotion to wakefulness. Thus, a monk is mindful and practices within limits.

Regarding 'gadflies, flies, and snakes': 'Gadflies' (ḍaṃsa) refers to yellow flies. All kinds of flies are called 'adhipāta'. For what reason are all flies called 'adhipāta'? Because they fly up again and again to bite; for that reason, all flies are called 'adhipāta'. 'Snakes' (sarīsapa) refers to serpents. This is the meaning of the phrase 'ḍaṃsādhipātānaṃ sarīsapānaṃ'.
387:
The extent of repeated effort in mindfulness is the meaning of the phrase 'bhikkhu sato sapariyantacārī' (a monk, mindful, wandering within limits). Ḍaṃsa (gadflies), adhipāta (flies), and sarīsapa (reptiles/snakes) are referred to. Ḍaṃsa refers to gadflies. All kinds of flies are called adhipāta because they fly up again and again to bite. Sarīsapa refers to snakes. This is the meaning of the phrase 'ḍaṃsādhipātānaṃ sarīsapānaṃ'.

'Manussaphassānaṃ catuppadānaṃ' refers to the contact of humans and the dangers of four-footed animals. What is called 'human contact' (manussaphassa) may include thieves, or violent youths, or those who have committed crimes, or those who have not yet committed crimes. They may question a monk, present a doctrine, abuse, threaten, offend, especially offend, harass, especially harass, oppress, especially oppress, kill, murder, or attempt to murder. Any absolute assault caused by humans is called manussaphassa (human contact). 'Four-footed animals' (catuppadānaṃ) refers to lions, tigers, leopards, bears, hyenas, wolves, buffaloes, and elephants. These wild animals may trample, bite, harass, especially harass, oppress, especially oppress, kill, murder, or attempt to murder a monk. Any assault caused by four-footed animals or any danger from four-footed animals is called 'manussaphassānaṃ catuppadānaṃ'.

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
'A wise monk, mindful and wandering within limits, should not fear the five fears: gadflies, flies, reptiles, human contact, and quadrupeds.'
'Even seeing many terrors of those of other faiths, he should not be terrified; moreover, the seeker of merit should overcome other dangers.'

'Even seeing many terrors of those of other faiths, he should not be terrified' means: excluding the seven types of fellow practitioners, all those who do not have faith in the Buddha, Dhamma, and Saṅgha are called those of other faiths (paradhammika). They may question a monk, present a doctrine, abuse, threaten, offend, especially offend, harass, especially harass, oppress, especially oppress, kill, murder, or attempt to murder. Even seeing or hearing many of their terrors, he should not tremble, should not be shaken, should not be greatly shaken, should not be terrified, should not be greatly terrified, should not be especially terrified, should not be terrified in any manner, should not be afraid, and should not fall into a state of terror. He should dwell as one who is fearless, undaunted, not terrified, not fleeing, one who has abandoned fear and dread, and one whose hair does not stand on end.

'Moreover, the seeker of merit should overcome other dangers' means: there are also other dangers that must be thoroughly subdued, overcome, mastered, and crushed. 'Dangers' (parissaya) are of two kinds: manifest dangers and concealed dangers... Thus, because they arise in that body, they are called dangers (parissaya). 'Seeker of merit' (kusalānuesī) refers to one who seeks good practice and appropriate practice.
388:
(There are other dangers) that are mastered and crushed. 'Dangers' (parissaya) are of two kinds: manifest dangers and concealed dangers... In this way also, because they arise in that body, they are called dangers.

'Seeker of merit' (kusalānuesī) refers to one who seeks the good practice, the conforming practice, the non-opposing practice, the non-conflicting practice, the practice in accordance with the goal... the Noble Eightfold Path, Nibbāna, and the practice leading to Nibbāna. By one who is seeking, searching, and looking all around for these, the dangers should be thoroughly subdued, overcome, mastered, and crushed. This is the meaning of 'Moreover, the seeker of merit should overcome other dangers'.

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
'Even seeing many terrors of those of other faiths, he should not be terrified;
Moreover, the seeker of merit should overcome other dangers.'

'Afflicted by the touch of disease or by hunger, he should endure cold and heat;
Though afflicted by these in many ways, the homeless one should make his energy and effort firm.'

'Afflicted by the touch of disease or by hunger' means: the touch of disease (ātaṅkaphassa) is called ātaṅkaphassa. He may be touched, afflicted, beset, and possessed by the touch of disease. He may be touched, afflicted, beset, and possessed by eye disease. [The same applies to] ear disease, nose disease, tongue disease, body disease... [Note:] he may be touched, afflicted, beset, and possessed by the touch of gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, reptiles, scorpions, and lice. 'Hunger' (khudā) means starvation. He may be touched, afflicted, beset, and possessed by starvation. This is the meaning of the phrase 'afflicted by the touch of disease or by hunger'.

'He should endure cold and heat' means: 'cold' (sīta) occurs due to two causes—either due to the internal disturbance of elements or due to the external weather. 'Heat' (uṇha) also occurs due to two causes—either due to the internal disturbance of elements or due to the external weather. This is the meaning of the phrase 'cold and heat'. 'He should endure' (adhivāsayeyya) means he should be one who patiently endures cold, heat, hunger, thirst, and the touch of gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, reptiles, scorpions, and lice.
389:
One should be of a nature to endure paths of speech that are ill-spoken and ill-arrived, as well as painful bodily feelings that have arisen—sharp, harsh, bitter, unpleasant, disagreeable, and life-threatening. One should endure cold and heat.

'Touched by these in many ways, he is homeless (or one who gives no opportunity).' 'Touched by these' means he may be touched, oppressed, beset, or affected by the touch of illness, by hunger, by cold, or by heat. 'In many ways' means he may be touched, oppressed, beset, or affected in various ways and modes. 'Homeless (anoka)' means he is called 'anoka' because he does not give opportunity (okāsa) to consciousness accompanied by volitional formations (saṅkhāra), or because he does not give opportunity to bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, or mental misconduct. Thus, 'touched by these in many ways, he is homeless.'

'One should make firm one's energy and effort.' What is called 'energy and effort' (viriya-parakkama) is the mental arousal of energy, exertion, striving, endeavor, effort, zeal, persistence, vigor, fortitude, unfaltering effort, unflagging desire, unremitting duty, the firm grasping of the burden, energy, the faculty of energy, the power of energy, and right effort. 'One should make firm one's energy and effort' means one should make energy and effort firm, make it stable; one should be one of firm undertaking, one of steadfast undertaking.

Therefore, the Blessed One said:

'Touched by the touch of illness and hunger, one should endure cold and heat;
Touched by these in many ways, being homeless, one should make firm one's energy and effort.'

One should not commit theft, nor speak lies; one should touch (pervade) with loving-kindness the trembling and the steady.
When one knows the turbidity of the mind, one should dispel it, knowing, "This is the side of the Dark One (Kaṇha)."

## One should not commit theft, nor speak lies

'One should not commit theft' means: in this Dispensation, a monk, having abandoned the taking of what is not given, should be one who abstains from taking what is not given; he should be one who takes only what is given, one who expects only what is given.
390:
'By not stealing, he should live with a pure self'—this refers to 'one should not commit theft.' He should live as one with a pure mind who does not wish to steal. 'One should not speak lies' means: in this Dispensation, a monk, having abandoned false speech, should be one who abstains from false speech. He should be a speaker of truth, one linked to truth, steadfast, reliable, and not a deceiver of the world. Thus, 'one should not commit theft, nor speak lies.'

'One should touch the trembling and the steady with loving-kindness.' 'Loving-kindness' (mettā) is the love for beings, the way of loving, the state of loving, protection, the way of protecting, the state of protecting, desiring their welfare, compassion, non-enmity, non-oppression, faultlessness, and the wholesome root of non-hatred (adosa). 'The trembling' (tasa) refers to those in whom the trembling of craving has not been abandoned, and in whom fears and terrors have not been abandoned. Why are they called 'the trembling'? They tremble, are terrified, are intensely terrified, are afraid, and fall into consternation; for that reason, they are called 'the trembling.' 'The steady' (thāvara) refers to those in whom the trembling of craving has been abandoned, and in whom fears and terrors have been abandoned. Why are they called 'the steady'? They do not tremble, are not terrified, are not intensely terrified, are not afraid, and do not fall into consternation; for that reason, they are called 'the steady.' 'One should touch the trembling and the steady with loving-kindness' means: one should touch or pervade both the trembling and the steady with loving-kindness. One should dwell pervading them with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness—vast, exalted, immeasurable, without enmity, and without ill-will.

'When one knows the turbidity of the mind' means: at whatever time (one should know). 'Of the mind' (manaso) refers to the mind (citta), the intellect (mano), the mental faculty (mānasa), the heart (hadaya), the bright mind (paṇḍara), the mind-base (manāyatana), the faculty of mind (manindriya), consciousness (viññāṇa), the aggregate of consciousness (viññāṇakkhandha), and the appropriate mind-consciousness element (manoviññāṇadhātu). Through bodily misconduct, the mind becomes turbid, agitated, stirred, struck, shaken, wandering, and unpeaceful. Through verbal misconduct... through mental misconduct... through greed, hatred, delusion, anger, malice, hypocrisy, rivalry, envy, stinginess, deceit, craftiness, obstinacy, impetuosity, conceit, arrogance, intoxication, negligence, all defilements, all misconduct, all distress, all burning, all fever, and all unwholesome formations, the mind becomes turbid, agitated, stirred, struck, shaken, wandering, and unpeaceful. 'When one knows the turbidity of the mind' means one should know, fully know, specifically know, repeatedly know, and penetratingly know that state of turbidity of the mind.
391:
One should know the turbidity of the mind, know it well, know it specially, know it repeatedly, and know it through penetration. 'When one knows the turbidity of the mind' means at the time of knowing the mind's lack of clarity.

'One should dispel it as the side of the Dark One' means—the Dark One (Kaṇha) is that Mara who possesses unwholesome karma, who is a ruler, who brings about death, who is named Namuci, and who is the kinsman of the heedless. The side of the Dark One includes Mara’s faction, Mara’s snare, Mara’s hook, Mara’s bait, Mara’s domain, Mara’s dwelling, Mara’s pasture, and Mara’s bond; one should abandon, dispel, destroy, and bring them to non-existence. In this way also, it is said, 'One should dispel it as the side of the Dark One.' Alternatively, the side of the Dark One refers to Mara’s faction, the unwholesome side, which results in suffering, has painful consequences, and leads to hell, to the animal realm, or to the realm of hungry ghosts (petas); one should abandon, dispel, destroy, and bring them to non-existence. In this way also, it is said, 'One should dispel it as the side of the Dark One.'

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
'One should not cause theft, nor speak lies; one should touch with loving-kindness both the trembling and the firm. When one knows the turbidity of the mind, knowing it as the side of the Dark One, one should dispel it.'

One should not fall under the power of anger and excessive pride; one should stand having dug up their very root. Furthermore, whether it be the pleasant or the unpleasant, one should certainly overcome them.

'One should not fall under the power of anger and excessive pride' means—anger (kodha) is the mind's resentment, hostility... (pe) ...harshness, incomplete speech, and the mind's displeasure. Excessive pride (atimāna) means—here, a certain person looks down on another by way of birth, or by way of lineage... (pe) ...or by way of any other grounds. One should not fall under the power of anger and excessive pride; one should abandon, dispel, destroy, and bring to non-existence both anger and excessive pride. This is the meaning of the phrase 'One should not fall under the power of anger and excessive pride.'

'One should stand having dug up their very root' means—what is the root of anger? Ignorance is the root, unwise attention is the root, the conceit 'I am' is the root, lack of moral shame is the root, lack of moral dread is the root, and restlessness is the root. This is the root of anger. What is the root of excessive pride? Ignorance is the root, unwise attention is the root, the conceit 'I am' is the root, lack of moral shame is...
392:
...is also the root, lack of moral dread is the root, and restlessness is the root—this is the root of excessive pride. 'One should stand having dug up their very root' means—having dug up, extracted, uprooted, pulled out, abandoned, dispelled, and destroyed the root of both anger and excessive pride, one should stand, one should remain firm, while bringing them to non-existence. This is the meaning of 'One should stand having dug up their very root.'

In the sentence 'Furthermore, whether it be the pleasant or the unpleasant, one should certainly overcome them,' the word 'atha' (furthermore) is a term used for word-connection, word-combination, word-completion, the union of letters, the smoothness of consonants, and the sequence of words. Regarding 'piya' (the pleasant/dear), there are two kinds: beings and formations (saṅkhāras). What are dear beings? In this world, they are those who desire one's welfare, benefit, comfort, and security, such as one's mother, father, brother, sister, son, daughter, friends, ministers, relatives, and kinsmen. These beings are called dear beings. What are dear formations? They are pleasant sights, sounds, smells, tastes, and touches. These formations are called dear formations. Regarding 'appiya' (the unpleasant/undear), there are also two kinds: beings and formations. What are undear beings? In this world, they are those who desire one's harm, misfortune, discomfort, and insecurity, or those who wish to take one's life. These beings are called undear beings. What are undear formations? They are unpleasant sights, sounds, smells, tastes, and touches. These formations are called undear formations. 'Addhā' (certainly) is a word of certainty, a word of doubtlessness, a word of conviction, a word of singleness of purpose, a word of decisiveness, a word of deliverance, a word of truth, and a word of establishment. 'Whether it be the pleasant or the unpleasant, one should certainly overcome them' means that one should conquer and master the pleasant and unpleasant, the agreeable and disagreeable, pleasure and pain, joy and grief, and the desirable and undesirable.

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
'One should not fall under the power of anger and excessive pride,
One should stand having dug up their very root.
Furthermore, whether it be the pleasant or the unpleasant,
One should certainly overcome them.'
393:
Putting wisdom first and having wholesome joy, one should dispel and remove those dangers. One should endure discontent in a secluded lodging. One should endure the four things that are the causes of lamentation.

## Paññaṃ purakkhatvā kalyāṇapītīti.

Wisdom (paññā) means that which is wisdom, knowing, investigation, discernment, investigation of the Dhamma... non-delusion, and right view. "Putting wisdom first" (paññaṃ purakkhatvā) means that in this Dispensation, a certain person practices by placing wisdom in front. He has wisdom as his banner, wisdom as his crest, and wisdom as his governing authority. He is abundant in investigation, abundant in discernment, and abundant in observation. He dwells with clarity, is devoted to that wisdom, develops it much, honors it, leans towards it, inclines towards it, tends towards it, is resolved on it, and is governed by it. In this way, it is called "putting wisdom first."

Alternatively, when walking, he knows "I am walking"; when standing, he knows "I am standing"; when sitting, he knows "I am sitting"; when lying down, he knows "I am lying down." In whatever way his body is positioned, he knows it accordingly. In this way, too, it is called "putting wisdom first."

Alternatively, he is one who acts with clear comprehension in going forward and returning. He is one who acts with clear comprehension in looking ahead and looking aside. He is one who acts with clear comprehension in bending and stretching. He is one who acts with clear comprehension in wearing the outer robe, the bowl, and the robes. He is one who acts with clear comprehension in eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting. He is one who acts with clear comprehension in defecating and urinating. He is one who acts with clear comprehension in walking, standing, sitting, falling asleep, waking up, speaking, and keeping silent. In this way, too, it is called "putting wisdom first."

## Kalyāṇapītīti

The joy and gladness that arise through the recollection of the Buddha (buddhānussati) is called wholesome joy (kalyāṇapīti). The joy and gladness that arise through the recollection of the Dhamma, the recollection of the Saṅgha, the recollection of virtue, the recollection of generosity, the recollection of devas, mindfulness of breathing, the recollection of death, mindfulness directed to the body (such as hair, etc.), and the recollection of peace (Nibbāna) is called wholesome joy (kalyāṇapīti). Thus, it is "putting wisdom first and having wholesome joy."

## Vikkhambhaye tāni parissayānīti.

Dangers (parissaya) are of two kinds: manifest dangers and concealed dangers... These bodily misconducts and so forth are called manifest dangers...
394:
These (bodily misconducts, etc.) are called concealed dangers... Thus, they are called dangers (parissaya) because they reside in that person. "One should dispel those dangers" means one should dispel, overcome, overwhelm, exhaust, and crush those dangers.

"One should endure discontent in a secluded lodging" (aratiṃ sahetha sayanamhi pante): Discontent (arati) means that which is discontent, the state of being discontented, the condition of one who is not delighted, lack of delight, and longing with a dissatisfied mind. "In a secluded lodging" means one should endure, overcome, overwhelm, exhaust, and crush discontent in secluded dwellings or in any of the superior wholesome states.

"One should endure the four things that are the causes of lamentation" means one should endure, thoroughly endure, overcome, overwhelm, exhaust, and crush the four things that lead to lamentation.

For that reason, the Blessed One said:
"Putting wisdom first and having wholesome joy, one should dispel those dangers;
One should endure discontent in a secluded lodging, and endure the four things that cause lamentation."

"What shall I eat? Or where shall I eat? Alas, I slept poorly here; where shall I sleep today?
An home-less trainee (sekha) should remove these thoughts that lead to lamentation."

"What shall I eat? Or where shall I eat?": "What shall I eat?" means what kind of thing among rice, cakes, barley-balls, fish, or meat shall I eat? "Where shall I eat?" means in which of the families—Khattiya, Brāhmaṇa, Vessa, or Sudda—shall I eat?

"Alas, I slept poorly here; where shall I sleep today?": This means "I slept poorly this night on a plank, a mat, a skin, a grass-spread, a leaf-spread, or a straw-spread. In the coming night, in what place shall I sleep comfortably—on a couch, a chair, a mattress, a rug, a coverlet, in a mansion, a gabled house, a cave, or a grotto?"
395:
Whether on a mat, or on a pillow, or in a monastery, or in a half-roofed house, or in a mansion, or in a pinnacled house, or in a cave—this refers to the thought: 'I have slept miserably here; where shall I sleep today?'

These lamentable thoughts refer to the two thoughts connected with alms-food and the two thoughts connected with lodgings. Because they are particularly worthy of lamentation and surrounding lamentation, they are called 'these lamentable thoughts.'

The trainee (sekha) who is a homeless wanderer should remove (those thoughts). For what reason is one called a 'sekha'? One is called a 'sekha' because one trains. In what does one train? One trains in higher virtue (adhisīla), one trains in higher mind (adhicitta), and one trains in higher wisdom (adhipaññā). What is the training in higher virtue? ... (and so on) ... this is the training in higher wisdom. One trains while reflecting on these three trainings; one trains while knowing, seeing, contemplating with wisdom, and resolving the mind. One trains while being devoted through faith, while exerting energy, while establishing mindfulness, while concentrating the mind, and while understanding with wisdom. One trains while specially knowing what should be specially known, while fully understanding what should be fully understood, while abandoning what should be abandoned, while developing what should be developed, and while realizing what should be realized; one practices, one practices well, and one trains by undertaking them. For that reason, one is called a 'sekha.' For the sake of removal, for the sake of further removal, for the sake of abandoning, for the sake of calming, for the sake of relinquishment, and for the sake of tranquility, one should train in higher virtue, one should train in higher mind, and one should train in higher wisdom. One should train while reflecting on these three trainings, while knowing ... (and so on) ... one should train while realizing what should be realized, one should practice, one should practice well, and one should proceed by undertaking them. This is the meaning of the words: 'The trainee (sekha) should remove (those thoughts).'

How is one a person who lives with a fixed abode (niketasārī)? In this Dispensation, a certain person is possessed of the impediment of family (kulapalibodha), the impediment of a group, the impediment of a dwelling, the impediment of robes, the impediment of alms-food, the impediment of lodging, and the impediment of medicinal requisites for the sick. In this way, one is a person who lives with a fixed abode (dependent on craving and views). How is one a homeless wanderer (aniketasārī)? In this Dispensation, a monk is not possessed of the impediment of family, the impediment of a group, the impediment of a dwelling, the impediment of robes, the impediment of alms-food, the impediment of lodging, and the impediment of medicinal requisites for the sick. In this way, one is a homeless wanderer (independent of craving and views).
396:
“Some monks go from the Vajjī country to the Magadha country, and to the Kosala country. Those monks, who wander without companions like deer, live as homeless ones without a fixed abode (aniketa) through craving and views.

“The practice is excellent; the well-practiced conduct is excellent. Living at all times without a fixed abode is excellent. Inquiring about the benefit is a noble deed; for one who is without possessions, this practice is indeed the state of a recluse (sāmañña).”

The trainee (sekha) who is a homeless wanderer should discipline himself. Therefore, the Blessed One said:

‘“What shall I eat? Where shall I eat? Sleeping here was miserable; where shall I sleep tonight?” A trainee who is a homeless wanderer should remove such thoughts that are like lamentations.’

When food and clothing are easily obtained at the proper time, one should know the right measure in those food and clothing for the sake of contentment in this Dispensation. That monk, wandering in the village with guarded senses, being well-restrained in those requisites, should not speak harsh words even when provoked by others.

In the phrase ‘annañca laddhā vasanañca kāle,’ ‘anna’ (food) refers to boiled rice, bread/snacks, flour, fish, and meat. ‘Vasana’ (clothing) refers to the six types of robes: linen, cotton, silk, wool, coarse hemp, and robes woven with five kinds of fibers. Obtaining food and clothing at the proper time means: having obtained robes and having obtained alms-food, not through scheming (kuhanā), not through flattery (lapanā), not through hinting (nemittikatā), not through belittling (nippesikatā), and not through pursuing gain with gain (lābhena lābhaṃ nijigīsanatā); not by giving firewood, not by giving bamboo, not by giving leaves, not by giving flowers, not by giving fruits, not by giving medicinal powder, not by giving scented powder, not by giving clay, not by giving tooth-sticks, not by giving water for washing the face; not by flattering speech, not by inconsistent speech like bean soup (muggasūpyatā), not by acting as a nursemaid, not by sitting on a couch (to please laypeople), not by the art of sites (vatthuvijjā), not by low arts (tiracchānavijjā), not by the art of signs/limbs (aṅgavijjā), not by the art of stars (nakkhattavijjā); not by acting as a messenger, not by running errands, not by carrying news, not by practicing medicine, not by giving alms in return for alms, and not by giving gifts in return for gifts—but obtaining them in accordance with the Dhamma and with righteousness.
397:
In this Sāsana, one should know the measure for the sake of contentment. 'One should know the measure' means one should know the measure through two reasons: through receiving or through using. How does one know the measure through receiving? Even when a little is given, he accepts it out of compassion and protection for the families; even when much is given, he accepts only robes sufficient to cover the body and almsfood sufficient to sustain the stomach. Thus, he knows the measure through receiving. How does one know the measure through using?

Reflecting wisely, he uses the robe only for the sake of warding off cold, for warding off heat, for warding off the touch of gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and reptiles, and only for the purpose of covering the parts of the body that cause shame.

Reflecting wisely, he uses almsfood not for fun, not for intoxication, not for beautification, not for adornment, but only for the maintenance and endurance of this body, for ending discomfort, and for assisting the holy life. He uses it reflecting: 'Thus I shall ward off old feelings and not produce new feelings, and there will be for me maintenance, blamelessness, and living at ease.'

Reflecting wisely, he uses the lodging only for the sake of warding off cold, for warding off heat, for warding off the touch of gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and reptiles, and only for the purpose of removing the danger of the seasons and for the enjoyment of seclusion.

Reflecting wisely, he uses medicinal requisites for the sick only for the sake of warding off arisen painful feelings caused by illness and for the sake of maximum freedom from disease.

Thus, he knows the measure through using. 'One should know the measure' means through these two reasons, he should know, understand, specially know, and penetrate the measure.

'In this Sāsana, for the sake of contentment' means in this Sāsana, a bhikkhu is content with any kind of robe, and he speaks in praise of contentment with any kind of robe. He does not engage in improper and unsuitable seeking for the sake of robes. If he does not obtain a robe, he is not troubled; if he obtains one, he uses it without being greedy, infatuated, or obsessed, seeing the danger and possessing the wisdom of escape.
398:
Furthermore, through that contentment with any kind of robe, he does not exalt himself nor disparage others. That bhikkhu who is skillful, not lazy, clearly comprehending, and mindful in that regard is said to be one who stands in the ancient, primordial, noble lineage.

Furthermore, a bhikkhu is content with any kind of almsfood and speaks in praise of contentment with any kind of almsfood. He does not engage in improper and unsuitable seeking for the sake of almsfood. If he does not obtain almsfood, he is not troubled; if he obtains it, he uses it without being greedy, infatuated, or obsessed, seeing the danger and possessing the wisdom of escape.
