Furthermore, through that contentment with any kind of almsfood, he does not exalt himself nor disparage others. That bhikkhu who is skillful, not lazy, clearly comprehending, and mindful in that regard is said to be one who stands in the ancient, primordial, noble lineage.

Furthermore, a bhikkhu is content with any kind of lodging and speaks in praise of contentment with any kind of lodging. He does not engage in improper and unsuitable seeking for the sake of lodging. If he does not obtain lodging, he is not troubled; if he obtains it, he uses it without being greedy, infatuated, or obsessed, seeing the danger and possessing the wisdom of escape. Through that contentment with any kind of lodging, he does not exalt himself nor disparage others. That bhikkhu who is skillful, not lazy, clearly comprehending, and mindful in that regard is said to be one who stands in the ancient, primordial, noble lineage.

Furthermore, a bhikkhu is content with any kind of medicinal requisite for the sick and speaks in praise of contentment with any kind of medicinal requisite. He does not engage in improper and unsuitable seeking for the sake of medicinal requisites. If he does not obtain medicinal requisites, he is not troubled; if he obtains them, he uses them without being greedy, infatuated, or obsessed, seeing the danger and possessing the wisdom of escape. Through that contentment with any kind of medicinal requisite, he does not exalt himself nor disparage others. That bhikkhu who is skillful, not lazy, clearly comprehending, and mindful in that regard is said to be one who stands in the ancient, primordial, noble lineage. This is the meaning of the phrase: 'In this Sāsana, one should know the measure for the sake of contentment.'
399:
That monk is restrained in those four requisites and wanders in the village with restraint. 'That monk is restrained in those requisites' means that in regard to robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick, he is guarded, protected, watched over, and restrained. In this way, he is one who is restrained in those four requisites. Alternatively, it means he is guarded, protected, watched over, and restrained in regard to the sense bases (āyatanas). In this way also, he is one who is restrained in those sense bases.

'He wanders in the village with restraint' means that in the village, his body, speech, and mind are restrained, firmly restrained, thoroughly restrained, guarded, protected, watched over, and restrained. Therefore, it is said: 'That monk is restrained in those four requisites and wanders in the village with restraint.'

'Even if provoked to anger, he should not speak harsh words' means that even if he is abused, reviled, disparaged, struck, blamed, or accused, he should not respond with harsh or coarse words; he should not talk back; he should not revile in return to one who reviles; he should not be angry in return to one who is angry; he should not quarrel in return to one who quarrels. He should not engage in strife, he should not engage in quarreling, he should not engage in contention, he should not engage in dispute, he should not engage in verbal conflict. He should abandon, dispel, eliminate, and bring to an end strife, quarreling, contention, dispute, and verbal conflict. He should be one who keeps far away from, abstains from, refrains from, has emerged from, is released from, is fully liberated from, and is detached from strife, quarreling, contention, dispute, and verbal conflict, and he should dwell with a mind that has made no boundaries. Therefore, it is said: 'Even if provoked to anger, he should not speak harsh words.'

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
'Having obtained food and clothing at the right time,
one should know the measure for the sake of contentment in this Dispensation.
That monk is restrained in those requisites and wanders in the village with restraint;
even if provoked to anger, he should not speak harsh words.'

He should be one with downcast eyes, not restless of foot, devoted to meditation (jhāna), and very wakeful. Having developed equanimity and being possessed of a composed mind, he should cut off the tendency of thought and remorse (kukkucca).

'One with downcast eyes, not restless of foot'—how is one restless of eye? Here, a certain monk is restless of eye, possessed of restlessness of eye. Thinking, 'What has not been seen should be seen; what has been seen should be surpassed,' he goes from monastery to monastery, from park to park, from village to village, from town to town, from city to city, from country to country, from province to province, being devoted to looking at sights. In this way, he is one who is restless of eye. Alternatively, when a monk has entered the village and reached the street, he goes with unrestrained eyes, looking at elephants, looking at horses, looking at chariots...
400:
...looking at infantry, looking at women, looking at men, looking at boys, looking at girls, looking at shops, looking at the entrances of houses, looking upwards, looking downwards, and looking about in all directions. In this way also, he is one who is restless of eye.

Alternatively, a monk, having seen a form with the eye, grasps at its signs (nimitta) or grasps at its features (anubyañjana). Since covetousness and dejection, evil unwholesome states, might flow in upon one who dwells with the eye-faculty unrestrained, he does not practice for its restraint, he does not guard the eye-faculty, he does not achieve restraint over the eye-faculty. In this way also, he is one who is restless of eye.

Furthermore, some recluses and brahmins, while living on food offered out of faith, remain devoted to witnessing such unseemly shows as: dancing, singing, music, theatrical shows, ballad recitations, hand-clapping, cymbals, pot-drums, fairy shows, iron-ball acrobatics, bamboo-pole acrobatics, ceremonial bone-washing, elephant fights, horse fights, buffalo fights, bull fights, goat fights, ram fights, cock fights, quail fights, staff-fights, boxing, wrestling, sham fights, roll-calls, battle arrays, and seeing armies. In this way also, he is one who is restless of eye.

How is one not restless of eye? Here, a certain monk is not restless of eye, not possessed of restlessness of eye. He does not think, 'What has not been seen should be seen; what has been seen should be surpassed,' and he does not go from monastery to monastery, from park to park, from village to village, from town to town, from city to city, from country to country, from province to province, being devoted to long wandering or unsettled wandering for the sake of seeing sights. In this way also, he is not restless of eye.

Alternatively, when a monk has entered the village and reached the street, he goes with restraint. He goes without looking at elephants ...pe... without looking about in all directions. In this way also, he is not restless of eye.
401: Alternatively, a monk, seeing a form with the eye, does not grasp at its signs... he attains restraint over the eye-faculty. In this way, too, he is not one with a flighty eye. Or, some recluses and brahmins, having eaten the food given in faith... abstain from such spectacles that are thorns to the Dispensation, such as watching elephant troops, horse troops, and so on. In this way, too, he is not one with a flighty eye. This is the meaning of 'okkhittacakkhu' (one with downcast eyes). 'Na ca pādalolo' (nor is he restless in feet) means: how is one restless in feet? In this Dispensation, a certain monk is restless in feet, possessed of restlessness of feet, wandering from monastery to monastery... for the purpose of seeing forms, he is devoted to long journeys and unsettled wandering. In this way, too, he is restless in feet. Alternatively, a monk is restless in feet even within the Saṅgha's monastery grounds, possessed of restlessness of feet; not for a purpose, not for a reason, with an agitated and unpeaceful mind, he goes from one precinct to another, from one dwelling to another... and thus engages in talk about various kinds of existence. In this way, too, he is restless in feet. 'Na ca pādalolo' means: he should abandon restlessness of feet, dispel it, end it, and bring it to non-existence. He should be one who abstains, specially abstains, repeatedly abstains, has emerged, is released, specially released, and detached from restlessness of feet. He should dwell with a mind that has made no boundaries. He should be one who delights in seclusion, finds joy in seclusion, is devoted to internal tranquility of mind, does not neglect jhāna, is endowed with insight (vipassanā), nurtures wholesome states, meditates in a secluded dwelling, delights in jhāna, is constantly devoted to solitude, and regards his own welfare as important. This is the meaning of 'okkhittacakkhu na ca pādalolo'. In the phrase 'jhānānuyutto bahujāgarassa', 'jhānānuyutto' means: he is constantly devoted to jhāna for two reasons. He is devoted, specially devoted, repeatedly devoted, and well-devoted to the arising of the first jhāna not yet arisen... the second jhāna... the third jhāna... the fourth jhāna. In this way, too, he is devoted to jhāna. Alternatively, he frequents, develops, and cultivates the first jhāna that has arisen... the second jhāna...
402: ...the third jhāna, and the fourth jhāna. In this way, he is one devoted to jhāna. 'Bahujāgarassa' means: in this Dispensation, a monk, throughout the day, purifies his mind from obstructive states by walking and sitting. Throughout the first watch of the night, he purifies his mind from obstructive states by walking and sitting. Throughout the middle watch of the night, he lies down on his right side in the lion's posture, placing one foot on the other, mindful and clearly comprehending, having the thought of rising in mind. Throughout the last watch of the night, having risen, he purifies his mind from obstructive states by walking and sitting. This is one who is devoted to jhāna and possesses much wakefulness. In this Pali phrase 'upekkhāmārabbha samāhitatto', 'upekkhā' means: that equanimity in the fourth jhāna, the act of looking on, looking closely, evenness of mind, tranquility of mind, and neutrality of mind. 'Samāhitatto' means: that steadiness of mind, good steadiness, stability, non-wavering, non-distraction, the state of having an unscattered mind, tranquility, the faculty of concentration, the power of concentration, right concentration. 'Upekkhāmārabbha samāhitatto' means: based on equanimity in the fourth jhāna, he is one with a concentrated mind, an undistracted mind, and an unscattered mind. In the phrase 'takkāsayaṃ kukkuccañcupacchindeti', 'takka' refers to the nine kinds of thought (vitakka). They are: sensual thought, thought of ill-will, thought of cruelty, thought about relatives, thought about the country, thought about immortality, thought connected with compassion for others, thought connected with gain, honor, and fame, and thought connected with not being despised. These are called the nine thoughts. The basis of sensual thoughts is the perception of sensuality; the basis of thoughts of ill-will is the perception of ill-will; the basis of thoughts of cruelty is the perception of cruelty. Alternatively, the basis of thoughts, reflections, and intentions is ignorance, unwise attention, the conceit 'I am', lack of moral dread, and agitation. 'Kukkucca' means: fidgeting with the hands is kukkucca, fidgeting with the feet is kukkucca, fidgeting with both hands and feet is kukkucca. It is the perception of what is unallowable in what is allowable, the perception of what is allowable in what is unallowable, the perception of fault in what is faultless, and the perception of no fault in what is faulty. Such kukkucca, the act of being remorseful, the state of being remorseful, regret of mind, and mental scratching is called kukkucca.
403:
Furthermore, remorse (kukkucca), mental regret (vippaṭisāra), and mental irritation (manovilekha) arise due to two reasons: because of what has been done and because of what has not been done. How do remorse, mental regret, and mental irritation arise because of what has been done and what has not been done?

Remorse, mental regret, and mental irritation arise, thinking: "I have committed bodily misconduct, I have not performed bodily good conduct." Remorse, mental regret, and mental irritation arise, thinking: "I have committed verbal misconduct... I have committed mental misconduct... I have committed the taking of life, I have not performed the abstinence from taking life." Remorse, mental regret, and mental irritation arise, thinking: "I have committed the taking of what is not given... I have committed sexual misconduct... I have committed false speech... I have committed malicious speech... I have committed harsh speech... I have committed frivolous chatter... I have committed covetousness... I have committed ill-will... I have committed wrong view, I have not performed right view." In this way, remorse, mental regret, and mental irritation arise because of what has been done and what has not been done.

Alternatively, remorse, mental regret, and mental irritation arise, thinking: "I am not one who fulfills the virtues (sīla)"... "I am one who does not guard the sense-doors"... "I am one who does not know moderation in eating"... "I am one who is not devoted to wakefulness"... "I am not endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension"... "I have not developed the four foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna)"... "I have not developed the four right efforts (sammappadhāna)"... "I have not developed the four bases of power (iddhipāda)"... "I have not developed the five faculties (indriya)"... "I have not developed the five powers (bala)"... "I have not developed the seven factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga)"... "I have not developed the noble eightfold path (ariya aṭṭhaṅgika magga)"... "I have not fully understood the truth of suffering (dukkha)"... "I have not abandoned the truth of the origin (samudaya)"... "I have not developed the path (magga)"... "I have not realized the truth of cessation (nirodha)."

"One should cut off remorse and the basis of thought" means one should completely cut off remorse which is the basis of thought. One should entirely cut off, sever, uproot, eradicate, abandon, dispel, destroy, and bring to non-existence the thought (takka), the basis of thought (takkāsaya) such as thoughts of sensual desire and ill-will, and remorse (kukkucca). Thus it is said, "One should cut off remorse and the basis of thought."

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
"With downcast eyes, not restless of foot, devoted to meditation, much awake,
Practicing equanimity, with a concentrated mind, one should cut off remorse and the basis of thought."
404:
When admonished by words, one should be mindful and rejoice greatly; one should break the mental barrenness among fellow practitioners of the holy life. One should utter words that are wholesome and not beyond measure, and should not give rise to intentions because of the people's blame.

"When admonished by words, one should be mindful and rejoice greatly" means: Preceptors (upajjhāya), teachers (ācariya), fellow preceptors, fellow teachers, friends, acquaintances, companions, or associates admonish, saying: "Friend, this is not right for you, this is not attained by you, this is not suitable for you, this is not established in virtue." When thus admonished, one should establish mindfulness and rejoice in that admonishment, rejoice greatly, be glad, be delighted, desire it, accept it, long for it, wish for its arrival, and intensely yearn for it.

Just as a young woman or man, fond of ornaments, having bathed their head, would receive a garland of lotuses, jasmine, or great-flowered jasmine with both hands, and placing it upon the head, the highest part of the body, would rejoice, rejoice greatly, be glad, be delighted, desire it, accept it, long for it, wish for its arrival, and intensely yearn for it; in the same way, one should establish mindfulness and rejoice in that admonishment, rejoice greatly, be glad, be delighted, desire it, accept it, long for it, wish for its arrival, and intensely yearn for it.

"One should follow such a wise person who, like one pointing out hidden treasure, points out faults, who speaks reprovingly according to the fault, and who is sagacious.

For one who follows such a wise person, it is only for the better, not for the worse.

One should admonish in one's presence, one should admonish in one's absence, and one should restrain from unseemly actions. Such a wise person is loved by the good and disliked by the bad."

"When admonished by words, one should be mindful and rejoice greatly; one should break the mental barrenness among fellow practitioners of the holy life" means: Fellow practitioners (sabrahmacārī) are those who have the same actions, the same recitation (pātimokkha), and the same training. "One should break the mental barrenness among fellow practitioners" means one should break the mental barrenness which is the state of a struck mind towards fellow practitioners; one should break the five mental barrennesses (cetokhila), one should break the three mental barrennesses; one should break, shatter, and completely destroy the barrenness of lust (rāga), the barrenness of hatred (dosa), and the barrenness of delusion (moha).
405:
One should speak words associated with the wholesome; one should not exceed the limit. One should speak words arising from wisdom. One should speak and utter words that are beneficial, associated with the Dhamma, timely, with reason, and bounded. This is the meaning of "One should speak words associated with the wholesome." Regarding "one should not exceed the limit," there are two kinds of limits (velā): the time limit (kāla-velā) and the moral limit (sīla-velā). What is the time limit? One should not speak words that have passed the time, words that have passed the limit, or words that have passed the time limit. One should not speak words when the time has not yet arrived, words when the limit has not yet arrived, or words when the time limit has not yet arrived.

It is as stated in this verse:
"Whoever speaks excessively before the time has arrived,
He lies defeated, like the offspring of a cuckoo."
This is the time limit. What is the moral limit? One who is lustful should not speak; one who is angry should not speak; one who is deluded should not speak. One should not speak false speech, one should not speak divisive speech, one should not speak harsh speech, one should not speak, preach, recite, show, or address useless idle chatter. This is the moral limit. Thus, "One should speak words associated with the wholesome; one should not exceed the limit."

One should not be intent on the nature of people's talk. "People" refers to Khattiyas, Brahmins, Vessas, Suddas, householders, monastics, devas, and humans. One should not produce intention, should not produce thought, should not produce purpose, and should not produce attention towards the accusations, blame, reproach, infamy, dispraise, failure in virtue, failure in conduct, failure in view, or failure in livelihood of those people. This is the meaning of the phrase "One should not be intent on the nature of people's talk."

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
"When urged by words, being mindful, one should rejoice;
Among fellow practitioners, one should break the spike;
One should speak wholesome words, not excessively;
One should not be intent on the nature of people's talk."

Furthermore, there are five dusts in the world,
For the removal of which a mindful person should train;
One should conquer (abandon) lust for forms, sounds, tastes, smells, and touches.
406:
One should not produce attention—this is the meaning of the phrase "janavādadhammāya na cetayeyya." Therefore, the Blessed One said: "When urged by words, being mindful, one should rejoice; among fellow practitioners, one should break the spike; one should speak wholesome words, not excessively; one should not be intent on the nature of people's talk."

In the phrase "athāparaṃ pañca rajāni loke," "atha" signifies the connection of words, the combination of words, the completion of words, the union of syllables, the smoothness of consonants, and the sequence of words. "Five dusts" (pañca rajāni) refers to the dust of forms (lust for forms), the dust of sounds, the dust of smells, the dust of tastes, and the dust of touches.

Lust is the dust (the dust of defilements), but actual powder is not called dust;
"Dust" is a designation for lust.
Having abandoned this dust, the wise
Dwell in the Dispensation of the One free from dust.
Hatred is the dust, but actual powder is not called dust... (and so on) ... they dwell in the Dispensation of the One free from dust.
Delusion is the dust, but actual powder is not called dust... (and so on) ... they dwell in the Dispensation of the One free from dust.

"In the world" (loke) refers to the world of misery, the human world, the deva world, the world of aggregates, the world of elements, and the world of bases. This is the meaning of the phrase "athāparaṃ pañca rajāni loke."

In the phrase "yesaṃ satīmā vinayāya sikkhe," "for which" (yesaṃ) refers to the removal of lust for forms, lust for sounds, lust for smells, lust for tastes, and lust for touches. "Mindful" (satimā) refers to one who is endowed with this mindfulness, namely: mindfulness, recollection, constant mindfulness, mindfulness as the state of remembering, the state of bearing in mind, the state of non-drifting, the state of non-forgetfulness, the faculty of mindfulness, the power of mindfulness, right mindfulness, the factor of enlightenment that is mindfulness, and the one-way path. "Should train" (sikkhe) refers to the three trainings: the training in higher virtue, the training in higher mind, and the training in higher wisdom. What is the training in higher virtue? ... (and so on) ... this is the training in higher wisdom.

"For the removal of which a mindful person should train" means that a mindful person, for the sake of the removal, the further removal, the abandoning, the stilling, the relinquishing, and the further stilling of lust for forms, lust for sounds, lust for smells, lust for tastes, and lust for touches, should train in higher virtue, should train in higher mind, and should train in higher wisdom. Reflecting on and knowing these three trainings... (and so on) ... realizing what should be realized, one should train, should practice, should practice well, and should undertake and proceed. This is the meaning of the phrase "yesaṃ satīmā vinayāya sikkhe."
407:
One should endure lust (rāga) for visible forms, for sounds, for tastes, for odours, and for tangible objects. One should endure, repeatedly endure, overcome, suppress, exhaust, and subdue lust for forms, sounds, odours, tastes, and tangible objects. Therefore, the Blessed One said:

"There are five further dusts (defilements) in the world; a mindful person should train to remove those dusts. One should endure lust for forms, sounds, tastes, odours, and tangible objects."

A monk who is mindful and has a well-liberated mind should remove sensual desire in these things (such as forms, etc.). That monk, rightly reflecting on the Dhamma at the proper time, being of a concentrated mind, should destroy the darkness of ignorance (avijjā). (Thus, the Blessed One concluded the teaching, making Arahantship the culmination.)

Regarding "etesu dhammesu vineyya chandaṃ": "Etesu" refers to visible forms, sounds, odours, tastes, and tangible objects. "Chanda" refers to sensual desire (kāmacchanda) occurring in the strands of sensual pleasure, sensual lust (kāmarāga), delight in sensuality (kāmanandī), craving for sensuality (kāmatanhā), affection for sensuality (kāmasneha), the fever of sensuality (kāmapariḷāha), the infatuation with sensuality (kāmamucchā), the immersion in sensuality (kāmajjhosāna), the flood of sensuality (kāmogha), the yoke of sensuality (kāmayoga), grasping of sensuality (kāmupādāna) ... etc ... the hindrance of sensual desire (kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa). In these things, one should remove, repeatedly remove, abandon, dispel, destroy, and bring to non-existence that desire.

Regarding "bhikkhu satimā suvimuttacitto": "Bhikkhu" refers to either a noble worldling monk or a monk in higher training (sekha). "Satimā" refers to one endowed with mindfulness, which is called mindfulness (sati), recollection (anussati) ... etc ... right mindfulness (sammā-sati), the enlightenment factor of mindfulness (satisambojjhaṅga), and the one-way path (ekāyana-magga). One who possesses this mindfulness is called "satimā".

Regarding "bhikkhu satimā suvimuttacitto": For one who has attained the first jhana, the mind is released, specially released, and well-released from the hindrances. For one who has attained the second jhana, the mind is released, specially released, and well-released from initial and sustained thought (vitakka-vicāra). For one who has attained the third jhana, the mind is released, specially released, and well-released from rapture (pīti). For one who has attained the fourth jhana, the mind is released, specially released, and well-released from pleasure and pain (sukha-dukkha). For one who has attained the sphere of infinite space (ākāsānañcāyatana), the mind is released, specially released, and well-released from the perception of form (rūpa-saññā), the perception of sensory impact (paṭigha-saññā), and the perception of diversity (nānatta-saññā). For one who has attained the sphere of infinite consciousness (viññāṇañcāyatana)...
408:
...For one who has attained the sphere of infinite consciousness, the mind is (released) from the perception of the sphere of infinite space. For one who has attained the sphere of nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatana), the mind is (released) from the perception of the sphere of infinite consciousness. For one who has attained the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (nevasaññānāsaññāyatana), the mind is released, specially released, and well-released from the perception of the sphere of nothingness. For the Stream-enterer (sotāpanna), the mind is released, specially released, and well-released from personality belief (sakkāya-diṭṭhi), skeptical doubt (vicikicchā), adherence to rites and rituals (sīlabbata-parāmāsa), the underlying tendency to views (diṭṭhānusaya), the underlying tendency to doubt (vicikicchānusaya), and from the defilements that coexist with them. For the Once-returner (sakadāgāmī), the mind is released, specially released, and well-released from the gross underlying tendencies to sensual lust (kāmarāgānusaya) and aversion (paṭighānusaya), and from the defilements that coexist with them. For the Non-returner (anāgāmī), the mind is released, specially released, and well-released from the subtle fetters of sensual lust and aversion, the subtle underlying tendencies to sensual lust and aversion, and from the defilements that coexist with them. For the Arahant, the mind is released, specially released, and well-released from lust for form (rūpa-rāga), lust for the formless (arūpa-rāga), conceit (māna), restlessness (uddhacca), ignorance (avijjā), the underlying tendency to conceit (mānānusaya), the underlying tendency to lust for existence (bhavarāgānusaya), the underlying tendency to ignorance (avijjānusaya), from the defilements that coexist with them, and from all external signs (nimitta). Thus, the monk is mindful and has a well-liberated mind.

## Kālena so sammā dhammaṃ parivīmaṃsamāno
"At the proper time" means: when the mind is restless, it is the time for tranquility (samatha); when the mind is concentrated, it is the time for insight (vipassanā).

At the proper time, he uplifts the mind; again, at another time, he restrains it;
He gladdens it at the proper time; at the proper time, he should concentrate the mind.

That yogi, skilled in the proper times, remains equanimous at the proper time;
At what time should there be uplifting? At what time should there be restraint?

What is the time for gladdening? What is the time for tranquility like?
How is the time for the yogi's equanimity of mind shown?

When the mind is sluggish, uplifting should be done; when it is restless, restraint should be done;
When the mind is devoid of delight, it should be gladdened at that moment.

When the mind is well-gladdened, and is neither sluggish nor restless,
That is the time for tranquility; he should let the mind delight within.

By this aforementioned method, when the mind becomes concentrated,
Knowing that the mind is concentrated, he should remain equanimous at that moment.
409:
“Thus, the wise one who knows the time, who is skilled in the time, should properly note the sign of the mind from time to time.”

When that person properly investigates and contemplates the Dhamma from time to time—when properly investigating and contemplating the Dhamma as “All conditioned things are impermanent,” when properly investigating and contemplating the Dhamma as “All conditioned things are suffering,” when properly investigating and contemplating the Dhamma as “All things are non-self”... [pe] ... when properly investigating and contemplating the Dhamma as “Whatever is of the nature to arise, all that is of the nature to cease” (he dwells).

“Ekodibhūto vihane tamaṃ so, iti bhagavā” means—“Ekodi” refers to having a mind concentrated on a single object, an undistracted mind, an unshaken mind, the state of calm (samatha), the faculty of concentration (samādhindriya), the power of concentration (samādhibala), and right concentration (sammāsamādhi); this is called “ekodibhūto.” “Vihane tamaṃ so” means he should abandon the darkness of lust (rāga), the darkness of hatred (dosa), the darkness of delusion (moha), the darkness of wrong view (diṭṭhi), the darkness of conceit (māna), the darkness of defilements (kilesa), the darkness of misconduct (duccarita); he should abandon, specifically abandon, relinquish, dispel, destroy, and bring to non-existence that darkness which causes blindness, which causes lack of vision, which causes lack of knowledge, which obstructs wisdom, which is on the side of distress, and which does not lead to Nibbāna.

“Bhagavā” is a name called because of being worthy of respect. Alternatively, He is called “Bhagavā” because He has broken lust; He is called “Bhagavā” because He has broken hatred; He is called “Bhagavā” because He has broken delusion; He is called “Bhagavā” because He has broken conceit; He is called “Bhagavā” because He has broken wrong view; He is called “Bhagavā” because He has broken the thorn of defilements; He is called “Bhagavā” because He has broken the defilements. He is called “Bhagavā” because He has associated with, analyzed, and distinguished the Treasure of Dhamma. He is called “Bhagavā” because He has made an end of existences (bhava). He is called “Bhagavā” because He has a developed body, developed virtue, developed mind, and developed wisdom. Or, the Blessed One is called “Bhagavā” because He resorts to secluded dwellings in the depths of the forest, which are quiet, free from noise, with a breeze away from people, and suitable for seclusion. Or, the Blessed One is called “Bhagavā” because He is a partaker of the four requisites: robes, alms-food, dwellings, and medicines for the sick. Or, the Blessed One is called “Bhagavā” because He is a partaker of the essence of meaning (attharasa), the essence of Dhamma (dhammarasa), the essence of liberation (vimuttirasa), higher virtue (adhisīla), higher mind (adhicitta), and higher wisdom (adhipaññā). Or, the Blessed One is called “Bhagavā” because He is a partaker of the four jhānas, the four immeasurables (appamaññā), and the four formless attainments (arūpasamāpatti). Or, the Blessed One is called “Bhagavā” because He is a partaker of the eight deliverances (vimokkha), the eight bases of mastery (abhibhāyatana), and the nine successive attainments (anupubbavihārasamāpatti). Or, the Blessed One is called “Bhagavā” because He is a partaker of the ten perceptions (saññābhāvanā), the ten kasina attainments, the concentration of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānassatisamādhi), and the attainment of foulness (asubhasamāpatti). Or, the Blessed One is called “Bhagavā” because He is a partaker of the four foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna), the four right efforts (sammappadhāna), the four bases of psychic power (iddhipāda), the five faculties (indriya), the five powers (bala), the seven factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga), and the Noble Eightfold Path (ariya aṭṭhaṅgika magga). Or, the Blessed One is called “Bhagavā” because He is a partaker of the ten powers of a Tathāgata (tathāgatabala), the four kinds of intrepidity (vesārajja), the four kinds of analytical knowledge (paṭisambhidā), the six higher powers (abhiññā), and the six Buddha-dhammas.

This name “Bhagavā” was not given by His mother, father, brother, sister, friends, companions, relatives, kinsmen, ascetics, brahmins, or deities. This name “Bhagavā” is a realization-designation attained simultaneously with the attainment of Omniscience (sabbaññutañāṇa) at the foot of the Bodhi tree at the end of the path of Arahatship. Such is the meaning of the phrase “Ekodibhūto vihane tamaṃ so bhagavā.” Therefore, the Blessed One said: “A monk should subdue the desire, being mindful he should guard the mind, and while properly investigating and contemplating the Dhamma, being one with a concentrated mind, he should dispel that darkness.”

The Exposition of the Sāriputta Sutta is finished.
410:
This name “Bhagavā, Bhagavā” was not given by His mother, not given by His father, not given by His brother, not given by His sister, not given by His friends and companions, not given by His relatives and kinsmen, not given by ascetics and brahmins, and not given by deities. This name “Bhagavā” is a realization-designation of the Blessed Buddhas, attained together with the acquisition of Omniscience at the foot of the Bodhi tree at the end of the deliverances. Having a concentrated mind, He destroys the darkness; therefore, He is called “Bhagavā.”

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
'Having removed desire for those things,
The monk, being mindful and with a well-liberated mind,
While properly contemplating the Dhamma from time to time,
Being one with a concentrated mind, should destroy the darkness.'
(Therefore, He is called “Bhagavā.”)

## The Exposition of the Sāriputta Sutta, the sixteenth, is finished.

## The sixteen expositions of the suttas in the Aṭṭhakavagga are completed.

## The Mahāniddesa Pāḷi is finished.
